docs.markdown:
# Managed Databases & Backups

NineDeploy provides provisioning and lifecycle management for databases, encrypted database dumps, and attached-volume snapshots with offsite cloud storage.

---

## 🗄️ 1. Supported Managed Databases

| Engine | Version / Flavor | Features |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PostgreSQL** | 16 / 17 + `pgvector` | Full ACID, vector embeddings, relational indexing |
| **MySQL** | 8.0 / 8.4 LTS | High throughput, InnoDB storage |
| **MariaDB** | 11.4 LTS | Community SQL server with columnar support |
| **Redis / Valkey** | 7.x | Low-latency in-memory caching and message pub/sub |
| **KeyDB** | 6.3 (`eqalpha/keydb`) | Multithreaded Redis-compatible server (section 9) |
| **Dragonfly** | 1.x (`ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly`) | Multi-core Redis-compatible in-memory store (section 9) |
| **MongoDB** | 8.0 Community (pin `7.0` for the previous LTS) | Document-oriented NoSQL database; starts on Linux 6.19–7.0.13 too (below) |
| **ClickHouse** | 25.8 (`clickhouse/clickhouse-server`) | High-performance columnar analytics; backups since G1.8 (section 10) |
| **Meilisearch** | v1.53 (`getmeili/meilisearch`) | Full-text search engine; backups since G1.8 (section 10) |
| **RabbitMQ** | 4 Management (`rabbitmq:4-management`) | Message broker with AMQP; definitions backups since G1.8 (section 10) |

**MongoDB on Linux 6.19 through 7.0.13.** MongoDB 8.0 refuses to start on these kernels with the `mongo:8` image's own setting, `glibc.pthread.rseq=0`. The error is "Linux kernel versions 6.19 and newer has a known incompatibility" (SERVER-121912). The image's setting turns on TCMalloc's per-CPU caches, which crash there. NineDeploy starts MongoDB containers with `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.pthread.rseq=1`, so TCMalloc uses per-thread caches, as in MongoDB 7. It starts on every kernel. Kernel 7.0.14 and later also fixes the incompatibility. An existing database picks the setting up the next time it is started (Stop, then Start); Restart keeps the container's old settings.

---

## 🔗 2. Connection String Auto-Injection

- When a database is provisioned, NineDeploy generates cryptographically strong random credentials.
- In-memory linkers automatically inject environment variables into linked application services:
  - `DATABASE_URL` (e.g. `postgresql://user:pass@srv-postgres:5432/main`)
  - `REDIS_URL` (e.g. `redis://:pass@srv-redis:6379`)

---

## ☁️ 3. Offsite Backup Destinations

Automated backup jobs upload backups to S3-compatible cloud storage. Database dumps use streaming AES-256-GCM encryption:
- **Amazon S3 / AWS GovCloud**
- **Cloudflare R2** (Zero egress fees)
- **MinIO / Self-Hosted S3**
- **Wasabi / DigitalOcean Spaces**

The same destination stores attached-volume snapshots as `tar.gz` archives encrypted with the same streaming AES-256-GCM envelope as database dumps; downloads and restores decrypt transparently, and legacy plaintext archives written before encryption keep restoring unchanged. Snapshots taken before the encryption change remain plaintext on disk until they age out of retention — restrict access to the backup directory and bucket accordingly. Each uploaded backup records which destination holds its object, so switching the active destination does not orphan earlier recovery points — restores and remote deletions resolve the bucket that actually holds the object (rows whose destination was deleted fall back to the active one).

Retention counts completed recovery points separately from failed attempts and leaves running backups untouched. Failed attempts cannot evict the last successful backups.

Without a backup policy (below), the scheduler backs each running database up once a day and keeps the seven newest completed scheduled dumps. A dump that falls out of that window is removed together with its remote copy: the remote object is deleted first, through the destination its record names, and the record only once that delete succeeded. A record whose destination is unknown or unreachable is kept and retried on a later run, at most 100 remote deletes per run (or two per database, if that is more).

---

## 🗓️ 3a. Per-database backup policy

Each database can have its own **Backup schedule** (Database → Backups tab, `ninedeploy databases backup-policy`, or `GET`/`PUT /v1/databases/:id/backup-policy`):

| Field | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `enabled` | `false` turns scheduled backups off for this database. Manual snapshots still work. |
| `cron` | A 5-field cron expression (`minute hour day month weekday`) in the server's local time, checked with the same rule as scheduled jobs. A 6-field (seconds) pattern is refused. The UI offers daily (`0 3 * * *`), every 6 hours (`0 */6 * * *`) and weekly (`0 3 * * 0`). |
| `retainCount` | Completed scheduled dumps kept on the panel host, 1–365. |
| `retainRemoteCount` | Optional, 1–365. Off-site copies kept, counted over the dumps that actually have one. If you leave it out, a dump's remote copy is removed with the dump (the built-in rule). If it is higher than `retainCount`, older dumps stay restorable from the bucket after their local file is pruned. If it is lower, newer dumps keep their local file and lose only the remote copy. |
| `destinationId` | Optional. A specific backup destination for this database's scheduled dumps. Leave it out to use the active destination. Only an instance operator can choose a specific destination, because destinations are managed by operators. If that destination is deleted, the policy falls back to the active one. |
| `localOnly` | `true` keeps this database's scheduled dumps on the panel host only. It cannot be combined with `destinationId` or `retainRemoteCount`. |

- **Upgrades change nothing.** Policies live in their own table (`database_backup_policies`, migration 0067). A database with no policy row keeps the built-in schedule exactly: daily, seven kept, the active destination. `GET` reports such a database as `configured: false`.
- **Authorization:** reading a policy follows the database (the same as listing its backups). Saving one needs `admin` on the database, the same as taking a backup. Every save is audited as `backup.policy.update`.
- **Applied at once:** saving a policy re-arms that database's schedule immediately. The scheduler also resyncs every 15 minutes. A policy database is skipped by the built-in daily run.
- **Retention safety:** the newest completed dump, and the newest remote copy, are never pruned (both counts are at least 1). Failed attempts are bounded separately (seven kept) and can never evict a completed dump. Manual snapshots and running operations are never touched. A dump file still referenced by a kept record is never unlinked.
- **Missed-backup alert:** a database with a policy is judged against its own cadence (twice its interval, and never less than two days). A disabled policy is exempt.
- **Scope:** the policy governs **scheduled** dumps. "Backup now" still uploads to the active destination, and manual snapshots are only removed by hand.

---

### Replica destinations (G3.3)

A database's scheduled dumps can also go to up to three more backup destinations, for a copy in a second region or provider. Set them under **Database → Backups → Backup replicas**, or with `PUT /v1/databases/:id/backup-replicas` and `{ "replicas": [{ "destinationId": 2, "retainCount": 14 }] }`. Like naming a specific destination in the policy, this is for operators.

**How copies are made**
- After the main upload, the same encrypted dump is copied to each replica at `<prefix>/<file>`.
- Each replica keeps its own `retainCount` newest copies and deletes older ones there. A copy whose delete fails is tried again on the next run.
- A failure at one replica is logged and shown on the card, and never fails the backup or the other replicas.

**Limits**
- Scheduled dumps only, and not for a local-only policy. Manual backups go to the active destination as before.
- Restores read from the main copy. A replica is for getting a dump back by hand when that destination is lost.
- Taking a destination off the list leaves its copies in the bucket.

**Storage:** no migration is needed. The list and the log of copies are one settings row per database, `backup_replicas:<id>`.

## 💾 4. Volume Snapshots & Labels

Each managed Docker volume can be snapshotted (`tar.gz`), restored or downloaded from the Volumes tab:

- **Labels**: manual snapshots accept an optional operator label (up to 40 chars, defaulting to `manual`); scheduled runs are labeled `schedule-YYYY-MM-DD`. Labels surface on the Backups page so a mixed database/volume list stays readable.
- **Scheduling**: a recurring job can sweep multiple volumes in one pass, reusing the backup destination for off-site copies.
- **Safe restore**: restores refuse to run while a service is still live on that volume.

### Volumes on nodes

A volume lives on the host of the service that uses it. Volumes of a service placed on a node live on that node, and the volume routes take `?serverId=<node>` to work with them (without it they act on the panel host, exactly as before). These features need the node agent v0.15.2 or newer, which advertises `volume.manage`, `docker.runSpec` and `stream`. An older agent gets `422 node_agent_outdated` with an "update the node agent" message, and nothing else is sent to it.

- **List and create:** `GET /v1/volumes?serverId=` lists the node's managed volumes. `inUse` is true while a running container on the node mounts the volume. `POST /v1/volumes {name, serverId?}` creates a managed volume (`nd-svc-*` / `nd-db-*`) labelled `ninedeploy.managed=volume`. An existing volume answers `409 node_volume_exists`. `DELETE /v1/volumes/:name?serverId=` is unchanged.
- **Attachments, commands and the Docker socket on node docker services:** these now deploy through the agent's structured `docker.runSpec`. Any missing managed volume is created on the node first. An attached volume that a service or database on another host also uses is refused with `409 attachment_host_mismatch`, because each host has its own volume of that name. A database volume is never created by a service that attaches it. Bind mounts stay unattachable everywhere.
- **Compose stacks on nodes:** missing attached volumes are now created before `compose up`. Before this, a stack failed at `compose up` with "external volume not found" unless someone had created the volume on the node by hand. With an older agent nothing is created, and the volumes must already exist, as before.
- **Backups:** `POST /v1/volumes/:name/backups?serverId=` streams the volume from the node over the sealed stream channel. The backup lands in the same backups directory, with the same file name and format as a panel-host snapshot, encrypted at rest. The plaintext archive is never written to the panel's disk. It is uploaded off-site like any other backup. The row records `serverId`. Retention is counted per host, so node copies never push panel-host copies out. Scheduled backup jobs of a node service back its volumes up from the node.
- **Restore:** `POST …/backups/:bid/restore?serverId=` restores on the node through the same staging script, and refuses while any running container on the node mounts the volume. A backup taken on another host restores only with `?acrossHosts=true`.
- **Files:** the file manager works on panel-host volumes only. With `?serverId=` it answers `422 node_volume_files_unsupported` rather than touching the panel host's volume of the same name.
- **Rollback to 0.15:** node volumes stay on the node (`docker volume ls --filter label=ninedeploy.managed=volume`). Node volume backups stay on the panel and can be downloaded, but a 0.15 restore writes into the panel host's volume of the same name, not into the node. Restore node volumes only after upgrading again.

## 🛡️ 5. Restore Safety

- Restores can be initiated via Web UI or CLI (`ninedeploy backups restore <databaseId> <backupId>`).
- **Check a backup without restoring it.** A drill runs the engine's own reader over the dump (for example `pg_restore --list` or `redis-check-rdb`) in a throwaway container and records `passed`, `failed` or `unverifiable` (the check itself could not run, which says nothing about the file). Use **Check** on a backup row in the database's Backups tab, where the *Last check* column shows the newest verdict (web UI since G1.5), `ninedeploy backups drill <databaseId> <backupId>`, or `POST /v1/databases/:id/backups/drill` and `GET /v1/databases/:id/drills`. A drill needs `member` on the database. It does not restore anything, so it proves the file is readable, not that the data is what you expect.
- **Verify a backup by restoring it (R3), for every engine.** **Verify restore** in the Backups tab restores the backup into a throwaway container of the database's own engine image on the panel host and runs your query there. The CLI is `ninedeploy backups drill <databaseId> <backupId> --restore-query "SELECT count(*) FROM users" --expect 42`; the API is `POST /v1/databases/:id/backups/drill` with `{ backupId, restore: { query, expected } }`.
  - **Verdict:** `passed` only when the client's output, without headers, equals the expected value exactly. Rows are on separate lines.
    - PostgreSQL: psql's unaligned output, with `|` between columns.
    - MySQL and MariaDB: the client's batch output, with a tab between columns, values unescaped and NULL printed as `NULL`. The query runs in the `app` database, so qualify other schemas (`SELECT count(*) FROM shop.orders`). The whole `--all-databases` dump is restored, including its `mysql` schema.
    - MongoDB: the query is a mongosh script, for example `db.getSiblingDB('shop').orders.countDocuments()`. The expected value is what mongosh prints for its last expression; `EJSON.stringify(…)` prints one stable line. The whole archive is streamed into `mongorestore --stopOnError`.
    - ClickHouse: the query is SQL, and the expected value is `clickhouse-client`'s TabSeparated output: a tab between columns, and NULL printed as `\N`. The query runs in the `app` database. The whole backup archive is restored with `RESTORE ALL`.
    - Meilisearch: the query is an API path, for example `/indexes/movies/documents/1?fields=title`. The expected value is the JSON body a GET on that path returns. Search results carry a processing time, so documents and stats make stable probes. The dump is imported as the container starts.
    - RabbitMQ: the query is one `rabbitmqctl` list command, for example `list_queues -p shop name durable`. The expected value is what it prints without headers: a tab between columns, one row per line, and rows compare in any order. The definitions export is imported, and the query waits until every vhost, queue, exchange and binding it names exists. A definitions backup holds no messages, so probe names and settings, not message counts.
    - Redis, Valkey, KeyDB and Dragonfly: the query is one command per line, for example `GET greeting`. The expected value is what the command-line client prints: one line per value or list element, and an empty line for nil. The server loads the RDB backup as it starts. If it rejects the file (wrong signature, truncated or corrupt), the verdict is `failed`.
    - **Recovery duration:** a verification records how long the real restore took (`restoreMs` in the drill's details). The Backups tab shows it next to the verdict, and the CLI prints it on a pass. It measures the bounded container on the panel host, not a promise for a production restore.
    - `failed` means the restore or the query really failed, or the data differs.
    - `unverifiable` means the check could not run. Causes: the engine image could not be pulled, the container ran out of its bounds or its engine stopped, or the panel restarted mid-run. A backup larger than 512 MiB is refused up front, because the container has 1 GiB of scratch space for both the dump and the restored data.
  - **Isolation:** the container has no network, no published ports and no host mounts. It runs with all capabilities dropped, a read-only root and tmpfs storage only, and it is removed afterwards. The live database is never touched. The query and expected value are not stored, logged or audited.
  - **Role:** the probe tells you something about the backup's contents, so it needs `admin` on the database, the same role as download.
  - **Asynchronous:** a restore takes minutes, so the panel answers `202` with `status: "running"` at once.
    - The panel, CLI and SDK poll `GET /v1/databases/:id/drills/:drillId` (`databases.drill(id, drillId)` in the SDK) until the verdict lands. `--no-wait` returns right after the start.
    - One verification runs at a time per panel; another one gets 409 `restore_verification_busy`.
  - **Node databases:** their backups live on the panel too. If the engine image is not on the panel host yet, the panel pulls it first.
- Volume restores first check that the archive can be listed, then extract the whole archive into a hidden staging directory inside the volume and swap it into place with same-filesystem renames. Corrupt archives and extraction failures (including a full disk) abort before any existing data is touched; the transient staging copy means the volume needs space for both the old and the restored contents during a restore.
- Database operations use separate staging files. Failed decryption removes partial plaintext instead of retaining an unauthenticated dump on disk.
- Backup and restore operations hold a cross-process lock file (under `op-locks/` in the data directory), so an overlapping panel process — a systemd restart overlap or a second instance on the same data directory — cannot interleave a backup with a restore on the same database or volume; a busy lock answers 409, and a lock abandoned by a crashed process is reclaimed after its heartbeat goes stale.

## 📥 6. Dump import (0.14)

Import an existing dump into a managed database: **Database → Backups → Import**, `ninedeploy databases import <id> --file <dump>` (chunks, resumes with `--resume <import-id>`, and waits for the result), `ninedeploy databases imports <id> [--watch]`, the SDK's `databases.importFile()`, or `POST /v1/databases/:id/imports`. It needs `admin` on the database, the same floor as restoring a backup.

| Route | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `POST /v1/databases/:id/imports` | `{source:'upload', sizeBytes, sha256?, filename?, options}` → 201 with the advertised `chunkSize`; or `{source:'s3', destinationId, key, options}` → 202 (operators) |
| `PUT /v1/databases/:id/imports/:importId/chunks/:index` | One chunk, `application/octet-stream` |
| `POST /v1/databases/:id/imports/:importId/start` | Check size, sha256 and format, then run → 202 |
| `GET /v1/databases/:id/imports[/:importId]` | History (newest 50) or one import, for polling |
| `DELETE /v1/databases/:id/imports/:importId` | Cancel an `uploading` or `pending` import |

An import moves through `uploading` → `pending` (every byte is staged) → `running` → `completed`, `completed_with_warnings` or `failed`. `cancelled` and `expired` end an import that never started.

- **Uploads come in 8 MiB chunks** (`PUT …/imports/:importId/chunks/:index`, `application/octet-stream`). A single multi-GB request would hit Traefik's 60-second read timeout. Chunks arrive in order, and re-sending the last one is harmless. `GET …/imports/:importId` reports progress, so an interrupted upload can resume. Only the user who created an import may upload to it or start it.
- **Limits:** `NINEDEPLOY_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES` (default 10 GiB). The panel needs twice the dump size plus 512 MiB free under `<data dir>/backups/imports/`. The staging file is server-named, mode 0600, and deleted when the import completes, fails, is cancelled or expires (24 hours idle).
- **From a backup destination** (`{source:'s3', destinationId, key}`): instance operators only. The key must sit under the destination prefix. `GET /v1/backup-destinations/:id/objects?prefix=` lists candidates. The panel checks the object's size with a `HEAD` request, answers 202, and downloads it into staging in the background (`uploading` → `pending`). Then `start` it like an upload.
- **Formats**, detected from the file's first bytes (gzip is unwrapped):

| Engine | Accepted |
| :--- | :--- |
| postgres | `pg_dump -Fc` (restored with `pg_restore --no-owner --no-acl`), or plain SQL (`psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`). Tar and directory formats are refused. |
| mysql / mariadb | Plain SQL, fed to the client with its sandbox flag (`--system-command=OFF` / `--sandbox`). |
| mongo | A `mongodump --archive` file. `admin.*`, `config.*` and `local.*` are excluded. |
| redis / valkey / keydb | An RDB file, checked first with `redis-check-rdb` / `valkey-check-rdb` / `keydb-check-rdb` from the database's own image. Requires `options.confirmReplace: true`. |
| dragonfly | An RDB file, checked with `redis-check-rdb` from the Dragonfly image. Requires `options.confirmReplace: true`. Dragonfly must be able to load that RDB version; if it cannot, the import ends `completed_with_warnings` and the `pre-import` backup is the way back. |
| clickhouse, meilisearch, rabbitmq | Refused. |

- **Options** (`clean`, `singleTransaction` (postgres; on by default), `drop` (mongo), `confirmReplace`, `skipSafetyBackup`): a key that does not apply to the engine is refused.
- **Safety backup first:** `POST …/start` (answers 202) takes a normal database backup labelled `pre-import` before anything is imported. Skipping it is allowed only for an operator, or for a database created in the last 10 minutes.
- **After the import** the panel signs in with the credentials it holds. If that fails, the import ends as `completed_with_warnings`: the dump changed those credentials, and the `pre-import` backup is the way back.
- **Restarts:** an import running when the panel stops is marked `failed` ("interrupted by panel restart") at the next boot. Finished import records are kept for 90 days.
- **Audit:** `database.import.create`, `.upload` (the last chunk landed), `.start`, `.safety_backup`, `.complete`, `.fail` and `.cancel`, with the size, format, source and S3 key, never the contents.

**What the content checks are for.** The import runs with the database's own superuser or root account, inside the tenant's own container. That account can already reach a shell with SQL alone (for example `COPY … TO PROGRAM`), and a database admin already receives the same password from `GET /v1/databases/:id/credentials`. The privilege boundary is therefore the `admin` floor on the route. The checks below are defence in depth: they block client-side shell escapes and accidental damage to system schemas.

- **psql (operators too):** a plain SQL dump may contain only the meta-commands pg_dump writes (`\connect`, `\restrict` / `\unrestrict`, `\.`, `\set ON_ERROR_STOP on`). The file is lexed twice, with and without backslash escapes in string literals, and refused if the two readings disagree. Otherwise a `standard_conforming_strings` change could hide a meta-command.
- **mysql / mariadb (non-operators):** the dump may not name the `mysql`, `sys`, `performance_schema` or `information_schema` schemas, may not use client commands (`\!`, `source`, `connect`, `system`, `USE` of another database, …), and may not switch `sql_mode` to `ANSI_QUOTES` / `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES`. A client without a sandbox flag accepts imports from operators only. If a dump's views, triggers or routines carry a `DEFINER` the server refuses, re-dump with `--skip-definer` (mysqldump 8.0.21+) or ask an operator to import it.
- **Encrypted NineDeploy backups** (`NDBK1:` / `v<n>:` files): operators only, since the master key decrypts them. Anyone else should download the backup (it is served decrypted) and import that.
- **Rollback to 0.13** leaves staging files in `<data dir>/backups/imports/`. Delete them by hand (see [ROLLBACK.md](./ROLLBACK.md)). `pre-import` backups stay restorable.

## 🌍 7. Public access (0.14)

A managed postgres, mysql, mariadb, redis, valkey, keydb, dragonfly or mongo database can be reached from outside the host on a port of its own, behind a required IP allow-list and with optional TLS termination (**Database → Settings → Public access**, `ninedeploy databases public-access`, `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /v1/databases/:id/public-access`). Reading the settings needs `admin` on the database; turning access on, changing it or turning it off is operator-only. `GET /v1/databases/:id/credentials` then also returns `publicConnectionString`, and the database list shows `publicAccess: {enabled, port}`.

Public access exposes the database's **root (superuser) account**: create a limited user inside the database before you hand out an endpoint. The mechanism, the allow-list and port rules, the TLS modes and the rollback cleanup are described in [TRAEFIK_INGRESS.md §9](./TRAEFIK_INGRESS.md).

### Tunnels through the panel (G5.8)

You can reach a database, on the panel host or on a node, from your machine without public access:

```bash
ninedeploy tunnel db <db-id>                     # listens on 127.0.0.1, on the engine's port when it is free
ninedeploy tunnel db <db-id> --port 15432        # a port of your choice (0 picks a free one)
```

Then point `psql`, a GUI client or a local app at the address it prints, using the database's own credentials. The database port stays closed to the internet.

**How it works**
- Each local connection opens its own WebSocket to `GET /v1/databases/:id/tunnel`.
- The panel carries that connection byte for byte to the database container.
- For a database on a node, the node's agent (0.18.7 or newer, capability `tunnel.tcp`) opens the connection from inside the database container's network namespace. The panel and the agent talk over a single-use channel encrypted per tunnel. The agent connects only to a running container the panel started as a database. The node owner can turn tunnels off with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_TUNNELS=off`.

**Who may use it, and what is recorded**
- It needs `admin` on the database, the same as revealing its credentials. A scope-restricted API token must also be allowed to write databases.
- The database's own login still applies on top.
- Access is re-checked every minute, so a revoked seat, grant or token closes open tunnels.
- An idle tunnel closes after 30 minutes. One user can hold at most 32 open tunnels.
- Each tunnel is audited as `database.tunnel.open` and `database.tunnel.close`, with its duration and byte counts.

**Limits for now**
- `--bind` listens on another local address. Anyone who can reach that address can then use the tunnel.

### PgBouncer connection pooling

A PostgreSQL database on the panel host can get a PgBouncer sidecar that pools client connections, which helps apps that open many short connections. Turn it on under **Database → Settings → PgBouncer connection pooling** (web UI since G1.5), with `ninedeploy databases pgbouncer <id> enable|disable|status`, or with `GET /v1/databases/:id/pgbouncer` and `POST …/pgbouncer/enable|disable`. The listen port defaults to 6432 and can be set when enabling. The card shows the pooled connection URL to point apps at. Reading the status needs `member` on the database, and the full password in the URL needs `admin`; enabling and disabling start or remove a container on the host, so they are operator-only. Databases on nodes have no PgBouncer yet (`422 remote_database`).

## 🛰️ 8. Databases on nodes (0.15.3)

A managed database can run on a remote node instead of the panel host. Choose the node when you create it (Databases → New → host, `POST /v1/databases {…, serverId}`, `ninedeploy databases create --server <id>`). The node is fixed for the database's life. Without `serverId` nothing changes: every existing database stays on the panel host.

- **Who and where:** placing a database on a node is operator-only (`403 node_placement_operator_only`). The node must be online (`409 server_not_online`) and run agent v0.15.3 or newer with `db.manage` (`422 node_agent_outdated` otherwise, before anything is written; `403 node_feature_disabled` when its owner set `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASES=off`). A database on a node never adopts an existing volume: `existingVolume` is refused, and an existing `nd-db-<slug>-data` on the node answers `409 node_volume_exists`.
- **On the node** it runs as `nd-db-<slug>` with the volume `nd-db-<slug>-data`, on its own network `nd-dbnet-<slug>`, not on the node's shared `ninedeploy` network. A service on the **same node** that attaches it is connected to that network at its next deploy, so the injected `DATABASE_URL` (or the engine's variable) resolves there. Detaching disconnects it.
- **Responses** gain `serverId`, `serverName` and `reachable` (`null` for panel-host databases); `containerName` and `volumeName` keep naming the container and volume. `GET /v1/servers` counts each node's databases.
- **Status:** every 60 seconds the panel asks each node for its databases' state. A node that does not answer never changes a database's status; the database reports `reachable: false` instead.
- **Backups:** manual and scheduled backups, policies, off-site upload, restore, drills and dump imports work as for panel-host databases. The dump streams from the node over the agent's sealed stream channel into the panel's backups directory, in the same format and encrypted at rest; the backup records the node. A scheduled backup of a database whose node does not answer is recorded as failed; nothing falls back to the panel host.
- **Terminal (published 0.15.3–0.17.1):** a shell in the database container opens through the node's agent. Client mode answers `422 client_mode_unsupported`; open a shell and run the client there. The 0.18.2 client-terminal implementation is described in [Node operations](NODE_OPERATIONS.md#node-database-client-terminals-unreleased-0180).
- **Refused:** attaching it to a service on another host, the panel host included (`409 attachment_host_mismatch`), fan-out targets of a service that uses it (`409 fanout_database_host`), and moving it to another host. Public access (TLS end to end only) works with agent 0.18.11 or newer, PgBouncer with 0.18.12 or newer (see [NODE_OPERATIONS.md](./NODE_OPERATIONS.md#public-access-to-a-node-database)). To move one, back it up, create a database on the other host, and restore there.
- **The node** cannot be deleted while it hosts databases, even with `?force=true` (`409 server_hosts_databases`).
- **Rolling back** to a release before 0.15.3: the database keeps running on its node, but the older panel refuses to start, back up or restore it. See [ROLLBACK.md, "0.15.x multi-node rollback runbook"](./ROLLBACK.md) before you roll back.

**Panel-host attachments (0.15.3):** a panel-host database attached to a service (the attach route, a `.ninedeploy` manifest or a migration bundle) is now connected to the service's own network at the service's next deploy, so its `nd-db-<slug>` name resolves from the app. Before, only template databases were connected.

See [MULTI_NODE.md](./MULTI_NODE.md) for nodes, agent versions and the other node features.

## 🧵 9. KeyDB and Dragonfly (0.15.6)

Two more Redis-protocol engines. Create them like Redis (`POST /v1/databases {name, engine: "keydb" | "dragonfly", version?}`, `ninedeploy databases create`, Databases → New). Everything else about a Redis database holds for them: a generated password (shown under Credentials, encrypted at rest), a `redis://:<password>@<host>:6379` URI (every Redis client accepts it; there is no `keydb://`), the `REDIS_URL` alias when attached to a service, backups, scheduled backups and policies, drills, restore, dump import, public access (with TLS termination: `rediss://`), Web Studio (Redis Commander) and databases on nodes. No migration is involved: an existing install keeps every database exactly as it was.

| | KeyDB | Dragonfly |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Image (default) | `eqalpha/keydb:x86_64_v6.3.4` (`arm64_v6.3.4` on an arm64 panel host) | `ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v1.34.2` |
| Port, volume | 6379, `/data` | 6379, `/data` |
| Start | `--requirepass <pw> --dir /data` (KeyDB's own thread count) | `--requirepass <pw> --logtostderr --dir=/data --dbfilename=dump --df_snapshot_format=false --snapshot_cron=*/15 * * * *` |
| Interactive client | `keydb-cli` (Client button, `mode: "client"`) | `redis-cli`, which the Dragonfly image ships (Client button, `mode: "client"`) |
| In-container commands | `docker exec <db> keydb-cli …` | `docker exec <db> redis-cli …` (as for Redis) |
| Backup | `SAVE`, then a copy of `/data/dump.rdb` | `SAVE RDB`, then a copy of `/data/dump.rdb` |
| Drill | `keydb-check-rdb` in the KeyDB image (unverifiable if the image lacks it) | `redis-check-rdb` in the Dragonfly image (unverifiable if the image lacks it) |

- **Versions.** KeyDB publishes architecture-specific tags only; the default follows the panel host's CPU. For a node of the other architecture, or any other release, set `version` (for example `arm64_v6.3.4`). Dragonfly takes its release tag with the `v` (`v1.34.2`). Neither default is `latest`.
- **Backup and restore are one file.** Both engines persist as `/data/dump.rdb`: a backup is `SAVE` plus a copy of it; a restore stops the container, copies the backup over it and starts the container again (a graceful stop would otherwise write the old dataset over the restored file). Dragonfly is started with `--df_snapshot_format=false --dbfilename=dump` so that its snapshot is an RDB file with that name instead of its own timestamped `.dfs` set. A `SAVE` that answers an error fails the backup instead of copying a stale file. Dragonfly pads its dump with zeros to a multiple of 4096 bytes (a one-key dump is exactly 4096 bytes); that is a valid RDB file, which `redis-check-rdb` accepts and which loads normally, so the drill never judges the file's tail itself. A Dragonfly backup therefore restores only into Dragonfly (a backup belongs to its database), and an RDB written by Redis loads into Dragonfly only up to the RDB version it understands.
- **Dragonfly and the kernel.** Dragonfly asks for an unlimited locked-memory limit (`ulimit -l`) for its io_uring ring. NineDeploy starts the container with Docker's default limits; a kernel or seccomp profile without io_uring makes Dragonfly log a warning and use epoll, which is fine for a managed instance. If your host logs an error instead, raise the memlock limit for Docker (`default-ulimits` in `daemon.json`).
- **Periodic snapshots.** Redis saves on its own schedule; Dragonfly does not unless asked, so it runs with `--snapshot_cron` (every 15 minutes) and snapshots again on a graceful stop. A crash loses at most the last quarter hour, as with Redis' default save points.
- **On a node** the panel starts the container with the same arguments and pulls the same image. The node's agent must be v0.15.6 or newer: an older agent does not know the engine names, so creating a KeyDB or Dragonfly database on it answers `422 node_agent_outdated` before anything is created. Redis and Valkey on a node are unaffected by the agent's version.
- **Rolling back** to a release before 0.15.6 while a KeyDB or Dragonfly database exists: the older panel does not know the engine. The container keeps running, but while a running row of an engine the older panel does not know exists, the Databases list answers HTTP 500 for instance operators (members still see their databases), scheduled backups of it are recorded as failed, and it can be neither started nor backed up. Delete the row (or its data) before rolling back, or roll forward again. See [ROLLBACK.md](./ROLLBACK.md).


0.18.2 implements sealed node Web Studio for the supported SQL/KV engines; see [node Studio operations](NODE_OPERATIONS.md#node-database-web-studio-unreleased-0180). Its full acceptance is tracked separately from published 0.17.1.

---

## 📦 10. ClickHouse, Meilisearch and RabbitMQ backups (G1.8)

These three engines used to answer "backup not supported". Manual backups, scheduled backups and policies, off-site copies, download, restore and the **Check** drill now work for them on the **panel host** and **on nodes**. On a node the agent runs the same routines against its local Docker, with a temporary file on the node, and streams the result to the panel through the sealed channel, where it is stored encrypted like any backup. This needs an agent that advertises `db.dump.extra` (0.18.7 or newer); an older one gets 422 `node_agent_outdated` before anything runs. For a Meilisearch restore the agent reads the image and the data volume from the database container itself. Imports (section 8) remain refused for these engines.

| | ClickHouse | Meilisearch | RabbitMQ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What is backed up | Every user database (all but `system` and the information schemas), with data, through `BACKUP DATABASE … TO File(…)` | The whole instance as a Meilisearch dump (`POST /dumps`): indexes, documents, settings, API keys | The **definitions** only (`rabbitmqctl export_definitions`): users, virtual hosts, permissions, queues, exchanges, bindings, policies and parameters. **Not the messages in the queues.** |
| File | The backup zip | The `.dump` file (gzipped tar) | JSON |
| Restore | Each database is restored under a temporary name first. Only when all of them succeeded is each live database renamed aside and its copy renamed into place; the set-aside originals are dropped after every swap succeeded. A failure while restoring leaves the current data untouched; a failure while swapping renames that database's original back, and a database already swapped keeps its previous data as `<name>__nd_old`. Databases not in the backup are kept. | The database is **stopped**. A one-off container of the same image imports the dump into a new path on the same volume; only after it is healthy are the paths swapped and the old data removed. A failed import keeps the current data. The database is started again either way. | `rabbitmqctl import_definitions`, then the restore waits until every vhost, queue, exchange and binding in the file exists. The import **adds and updates**; objects created after the backup are not deleted. |
| Downtime | None | For the length of the import | None |
| Drill (**Check**) | `unzip -l` in the ClickHouse image | `metadata.json` read with `tar` in the Meilisearch image | The JSON parses and names a RabbitMQ version |

ClickHouse database names must consist of letters, digits and `_`; a backup or restore refuses others instead of quoting them. Large ClickHouse and Meilisearch operations may run for hours; the limit is six hours per step.

ClickHouse restore refuses to overwrite an existing `<name>__nd_restore` or `<name>__nd_old` database. A failed or interrupted restore can leave recovery databases behind; inspect their contents and resolve them manually before retrying. A failed promotion may require restoring the original name manually, and a partially completed multi-database restore is not an atomic transaction.

## ⏱️ 11. Point-in-time recovery (PostgreSQL, R3)

A dump restores the database as it was when the dump was taken. Point-in-time recovery restores it as it was at **any second** inside its window: just before a bad migration ran, or before a table was dropped. It is off by default; an upgrade changes nothing until you turn it on.

**Turning it on.** In the database's **Backups** tab, **Point-in-time recovery → Enable**. The CLI is `ninedeploy databases pitr enable <dbId> [--retention <days>]`, and the API is `PUT /v1/databases/:id/pitr` with `{ "enabled": true, "retentionDays": 7 }`. It needs `admin` on the database, and the database must be running.
- The database restarts once, now with WAL archiving on.
- Every finished WAL segment (PostgreSQL's change log) is gzip-compressed into a second volume, `<data volume>-wal`, on the panel host.
- At most **one minute** of committed work waits in a segment that is not archived yet (`archive_timeout` = 60 s). That minute is the most a recovery can miss.
- The first **base backup** (`pg_basebackup`) is taken right away. After that the panel takes one a day, and you can take one at any time with **Take base backup** (`ninedeploy databases pitr base-backup <dbId>`).

**Retention.** Base backups older than the retention (1–35 days, default 7) are deleted, together with the WAL only they need. The newest base backup is always kept. The window therefore reaches back about the retention, and forward to the newest archived segment. A gap in the archive splits the window.

**Status.** The card, `ninedeploy databases pitr status <dbId>` and `GET /v1/databases/:id/pitr` show:
- the recoverable window, the base backups and the archive size;
- whether archiving works: a failure newer than the last success is shown as **failing**, also lands on `lastError` and in the audit log, and the scheduler skips base backups until archiving works again.

**Recovering.** **Recover to a point in time…** in the card. The CLI is `ninedeploy databases pitr recover <dbId> --name <new database> [--to 2026-11-05T09:30:00Z]`, and the API is `POST /v1/databases/:id/pitr/recover` with `{ "name": "…", "targetTime": "…" }`. Without a time, the database is recovered to the latest archived point. The recovery needs `admin` on the database.
- **The database itself is never touched.** The recovery creates a **new** database in the same project, with its own credentials. You point your app at it, or copy what you need out of it.
- A base backup that finished before the target is restored into the new database's volume. The archived WAL is replayed up to the target in a networkless helper container. Only then is the new database started normally.
- It answers at once (202). The card polls the recovery, and the CLI waits for it, unless you pass `--no-wait`. `GET /v1/databases/:id/pitr/recoveries` keeps the history: the target, what PostgreSQL replayed to (the commit time of the first transaction **not** applied, or the end of the archive), the base backup it started from and the replay time.
- One recovery runs at a time on a panel.

**What is refused, and why.** A refused recovery keeps no new database behind; the reason is on the recovery row.
- **A time with nothing archived after it.** PostgreSQL stops a time recovery at the first transaction after the target, so it needs that transaction archived. "Nothing after … has been archived yet": recover to the latest archived point, or try again a minute later.
- **A time before the oldest base backup finished.** The answer names the earliest recoverable point.
- **A missing or damaged segment.** Every segment the replay needs is checked (`gzip -t`) before anything is created. A recovery to the latest point also checks that the replay really ended in the newest archived segment, because PostgreSQL itself would otherwise stop early at a gap without any error. A time before the damage can still be recovered.

**Limits.**
- **Panel-host PostgreSQL databases only.** Databases on nodes and preview copies answer 422 `pitr_unavailable`. The cluster must use the default 16 MB WAL segments and must not run with `wal_level = minimal`; enabling checks both.
- **The archive lives on the panel host, next to the database.** It protects against bad writes and deleted data, not against losing the host. Keep off-site dumps (section 3) for that.
- **Disabling deletes the archive and the base backups** (the database restarts without archiving). Deleting the database keeps the archive volume, like the data volume, until you remove it in **Volumes**. Enabling again later refuses to reuse such a left-over archive (409 `pitr_archive_exists`).
- **Restoring the data volume or the archive volume of a database with PITR on is refused** (409 `pitr_volume_restore_refused`). An older data directory under a live archive would write segment names the archive already holds with other contents. Disable PITR first, or recover to a point in time instead. A dump restore (`pg_restore` into the running database) is fine: it is just more WAL.
- **Rolling back the panel** to a version without PITR keeps the database archiving, because the container keeps its flags until it is recreated. Nothing prunes the archive in that version. Disable PITR before rolling back.
