docs.markdown:
# Competitor gap roadmap: 2026-10-27

This plan comes from a code-level analysis of the current releases of Coolify v4.5.0, Dokploy v0.30.10, CapRover v1.15.5, Dokku v0.38.32, Kamal v2.12.0 / kamal-proxy v0.10.2 and Komodo v2.3.4, plus Kubero, Canine, Tsuru, ZaneOps, Uncloud, Disco, Haloy and piku. Their repositories were cloned and read, not just their docs. Each gap below was checked against NineDeploy `main` (0.18.4). An item is counted as present only when it is reachable from the UI or the CLI, not merely implemented. The working notes and per-competitor evidence (file paths) are kept outside the repository.

The work runs **next to** the R2–R6 release sequence in [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md); it does not replace it. Items ship as **patch releases**, each a coherent slice. They follow the rule every release follows: additive migrations only, new behaviour opt-in or defaulting to the old behaviour, and `smoke:upgrade` extended to exercise the item after an upgrade.

Status: ⬜ not started · 🟨 in progress · ✅ done (with the release that shipped it)

---

## G1: Quick wins

Small items that close a visible gap against Coolify or Dokploy. Each one is a single patch release or less.

| ID | Item | Who has it | Our approach | Size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1.1 | **Inline Dockerfile.** Paste a Dockerfile instead of keeping one in the repo; also works with a plain image-less "Dockerfile only" service. | Coolify (`deploy_simple_dockerfile`), CapRover (`dockerfileLines`), Komodo | Nullable `dockerfileContent` on the build config (size-capped, validated like `composeContent`). The builder writes it into the build context before `buildx`; with no repo, the context is an empty directory. Panel and node builders. | S | ✅ unreleased (settings row instead of a column; written as `.ninedeploy.Dockerfile` and built with a per-deploy build-config override; builds on the panel host, a node service with Build on: panel) |
| G1.2 | **Self-hosted GitLab.** Repository and branch listing against any GitLab URL. | Coolify (OAuth app + system hook), Dokploy (`gitlabUrl`) | A `baseUrl` on `gitlab` sources, the same https and egress rules as Gitea. Webhooks already verify `X-Gitlab-Token`. | S | ✅ unreleased; also added GitLab branch listing, which had always fallen back to main/master |
| G1.3 | **Restart-loop limit.** Stop a container that keeps crashing and notify. | Coolify (`max_restart_count`, `RestartLimitReached`) | The collector already samples container state. Count restarts per window, stop at the limit (opt-in per service, off by default), emit a `restart_limit` event through `audit()` so notifications fire. | S | ✅ unreleased (panel-host docker services and PM2 services; settings row, no migration) |
| G1.4 | **Workspace-enforced 2FA.** | Coolify (`Team.is_two_factor_required`) | A workspace flag. Members without TOTP or a passkey are sent to enrolment after sign-in, and only enrolment routes answer until they finish. SSO sign-ins are exempt when the IdP enforces MFA (setting). | S | ✅ unreleased (settings row per workspace; the session must have signed in with a second factor, `amr: mfa`; SSO exemption per listed provider; API tokens keep working) |
| G1.5 | **Web UI for API-only features.** PgBouncer toggle, Loki log search, static egress IP, config and domain presets, FCM channel form, backup drill, email templates. | Rivals expose these in the UI | Cards in the existing tabs, calling the routes that are already mounted. No server change. | M | ✅ unreleased (PgBouncer, backup drill, log search, FCM, egress IP, email templates, domain presets as Settings → Integrations → Create a DNS record; config presets stay in the CLI, operator internals) |
| G1.6 | **SAML status.** ROADMAP.md lists SAML as shipped, but provider creation is refused (`SAML_UNAVAILABLE`). | Dokploy (enterprise) | Correct the docs now. The implementation (a vetted XML-DSig library with c14n and an AuthnRequest flow) becomes G3.6. | S | ✅ docs corrected |
| G1.7 | **Registry push webhooks.** Deploy when an image is pushed, instead of waiting for the 30-minute digest sweep. | Dokploy (Docker Hub and GHCR `registry_package`) | A per-service token URL, as for deploy hooks. The payload's repository and tag must match the service image; the digest is then resolved as the sweep does. | S | ✅ unreleased (Docker Hub, GHCR, Harbor, registry:2, generic; hashed token in a settings row; the next sweep re-baselines instead of resolving the digest in the request) |
| G1.8 | **Backups for the remaining engines.** ClickHouse, Meilisearch and RabbitMQ are offered but answer "backup not supported". | Coolify (ClickHouse native backup) | ClickHouse `BACKUP … TO File`, Meilisearch's dump API, RabbitMQ definitions export, each through the existing encrypted stream and restore path. | M | ✅ unreleased (panel host, and nodes whose agent has `db.dump.extra`, 0.18.7) |

## G2: Compose, routing and access

| ID | Item | Who has it | Our approach | Size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G2.1 | **A domain per compose service.** Today every domain of a stack routes to its main service. | Coolify (`docker_compose_domains`, `SERVICE_FQDN_<SVC>_<PORT>`), Dokploy (`createDomainLabels`) | A nullable `targetService` (and port) on the domain. The router targets that compose service; `null` keeps today's main-service routing. Magic variables gain the per-service form. | M | ✅ unreleased (settings row per domain instead of a column; picked in the domain's row under Service → Network → Domains) |
| G2.2 | **Maintenance mode and custom error pages.** | Coolify 4.5 (error-pages container + Traefik `errors` middleware), Kamal (`maintenance`, request pausing) | Per-service maintenance switch routing to a panel-served page (the wake route shows the pattern), plus optional custom 502/503/504 pages through Traefik `errors`. Request pausing is a follow-up. | M | ✅ unreleased (panel-host services; bypass list via ClientIP twin routers; settings rows; proven on Traefik 3) |
| G2.3 | **Put any app behind panel sign-in (forward auth).** | Dokploy (enterprise, oauth2-proxy), Canine | A Traefik `forwardAuth` middleware pointing at a panel endpoint that checks the panel session or OIDC and the caller's access to the service. No extra container. Per domain, off by default. | M | ✅ unreleased (panel session via one-time code + state cookie on the app domain; role re-checked per request; settings row per domain; OIDC sign-in comes through the panel login) |
| G2.4 | **Skip a compose build when its inputs are unchanged.** | Coolify (build fingerprint), Komodo (deploy-if-changed) | Hash the resolved compose, build contexts and env; reuse the recorded images when the hash matches. | S | ✅ unreleased (panel host and nodes; commit + resolved `docker compose config`; `NINEDEPLOY_COMPOSE_BUILD_SKIP=off` opts out) |

## G3: Data, secrets and integrations

| ID | Item | Who has it | Our approach | Size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G3.1 | **Move a service with its volume data** between the panel host and nodes. Today only configuration moves. | Dokploy (`transfer.ts`, tar streamed through the panel), Coolify (`VolumeCloneJob`) | Stop, then stream each volume as tar over the sealed agent channel with progress and a checksum, then deploy on the target. The source is kept until the operator removes it. | L | ✅ unreleased (docker services with the primary data volume, compose stacks with every named volume compose made; stopped first; archive → sealed node stream → restore → deploy; progress in a settings row) |
| G3.2 | **More secret managers through one generic mechanism.** | Dokploy (8 providers), Kamal (9, through vendor CLIs) | Add AWS Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager and 1Password Connect natively. Add an operator-only `exec` provider (Uncloud's idea: run a command with a timeout and read stdout) to cover the rest. | M | ✅ |
| G3.3 | **Backup replica destinations.** | Coolify (S3 replicas) | A backup policy may list extra destinations, each with its own retention. | S | ✅ unreleased (scheduled dumps; up to three; settings row per database with a copy log for retention) |
| G3.4 | **More log-drain targets.** CloudWatch, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Splunk HEC, Better Stack, New Relic, Axiom. | Dokploy (Vector, config checked by `vector validate`), Coolify (Fluent Bit, CloudWatch) | Generate a Vector sink config from the drain rows and validate it in a throwaway container before switching. | M | ✅ unreleased (native formatters on the existing HTTP shipper instead of Vector — same queue/retry/egress guard, no extra container; no CHECK on the type column, so no migration) |
| G3.5 | **More DNS record providers.** Route53, OVH, Porkbun, Hetzner DNS. | Dokploy (5 providers) | New drivers behind the existing DNS driver interface. | S each | ✅ |
| G3.6 | **SAML that actually works.** | Dokploy (enterprise) | Use a maintained XML-DSig and c14n library, add an SP-initiated AuthnRequest, and lift `SAML_UNAVAILABLE`. | M | ✅ unreleased (@node-saml/node-saml 5.1.0, release-age checked; InResponseTo bound and spent once; an identity signs in only the account it was linked to, as OIDC) |
| G3.7 | **More notification channels.** Mattermost, Google Chat, Matrix, PagerDuty, Opsgenie. The last two are ROADMAP item 7. | Dokploy (Mattermost) | New channel types in `notifier.ts`. | S | ✅ |

## G4: Fleet operations (approved 2026-10-27)

Several of these were listed under "Not planned for now" in ROADMAP.md. Coolify spent most of 2026 here. **The owner approved all of G4 on 2026-10-27.**

| ID | Item | Who has it | Our approach | Size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G4.1 | **More Linux distributions.** RHEL, Alma, Rocky, Fedora, Alpine (and SLES/Arch later) for `install.sh` and SSH bootstrap. | Coolify, Dokploy | Distribution detection with package-manager branches; the systemd unit and the Alpine OpenRC variant; extend the installer test matrix. | M | ✅ RHEL family, Fedora, Alpine (Docker mode), openSUSE/SLES and Arch (Docker from the distribution's packages; Node for bare-metal from NodeSource RPMs via zypper, or Arch's LTS packages) |
| G4.2 | **OS security updates from the panel.** | Coolify 4.5 (unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic, reboot detection) | A typed agent op group for listing updates, enabling automatic security updates and reporting a pending reboot. Never an automatic reboot. | M | ✅ apt + dnf, panel host and nodes (NODE_OPERATIONS.md) |
| G4.3 | **Create servers through cloud APIs.** Hetzner first, then DigitalOcean and Vultr. | Coolify (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Vultr, Hostinger) | Create the VM with cloud-init that runs the existing SSH bootstrap, then enrol the agent. API tokens in the vault. | L | ✅ Hetzner, DigitalOcean and Vultr (MULTI_NODE.md) |
| G4.4 | **Heroku and Paketo buildpacks.** | Dokploy, Dokku, Kamal | A `buildpacks` build pack wrapping `pack build`, checksum-pinned like Nixpacks. | S | ✅ |
| G4.5 | **GitHub Actions runners on your own servers.** | Coolify 4.4 (`generate-jitconfig`, one container per job, dind or Sysbox) | Through the GitHub App: on `workflow_job` queued, start a just-in-time runner container on a build node. This could be a cheaper first step for R5. | M | ✅ panel host or one node per App (node owner opts in), no Docker in jobs (GITHUB_APP.md §7.1) |
| G4.6 | **Interface translations.** Turkish and English first. | Coolify (20 languages), CapRover | Add an i18n layer to the web app, extract strings route by route, ship the Turkish locale. | L | ✅ layer + Turkish locale; every page extracted, the service Network tab and Domains included (TRANSLATIONS.md) |
| G4.7 | **A larger template catalog.** Dokploy has 586, CapRover 361, Coolify 352, NineDeploy 305. | — | A converter for Dokploy blueprints (`template.toml` + compose) next to the Coolify mirror, with every stack smoke-run before promotion as in 0.15.7. | M | ✅ converter; 20 Dokploy entries promoted after smoke runs and a closed-by-default review (2026-10-29, 2026-10-31 and 2026-11-01); further rounds are catalog upkeep, see TEMPLATE_MIRRORS.md §3 |

## G5: Ahead of the field

When this plan was written (2026-10-27), none of the Docker-based rivals had these. That no longer holds as a group claim: Coolify 4.7.0 (2026-11-09) scans images, Coolify and ZaneOps stage pending changes, and Komodo syncs resources. See [plans/COMPETITIVE_ROADMAP_2026-11.md](plans/COMPETITIVE_ROADMAP_2026-11.md) §10.

| ID | Item | Inspiration | Size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G5.1 | **Image vulnerability scanning.** Trivy in a throwaway container after each build and on a schedule, with a severity summary and an optional gate on critical findings. | Kubero | M | ✅ unreleased (docker services on the panel host and on nodes with the deploy gate; panel host Compose stacks with the gate before the running stack is replaced; Swarm services on schedule and on request, report only) |
| G5.2 | **Pending changes tray.** Edits accumulate as field-level changes, are reviewed as a diff and applied atomically on deploy. This fits protected lanes and approvals. | ZaneOps, Coolify "changes pending" | M | ✅ unreleased (service settings; tags and variables apply directly) |
| G5.3 | **Instance-wide GitOps.** The whole instance (projects, services, domains, grants) as files in a repository, with a drift diff, an alert and an optional write-back of UI edits. | Komodo Resource Sync | L | ✅ unreleased (projects, services, domains, project grants; drift + alerts + apply without deletes; write-back is an export to commit, the panel does not push) |
| G5.4 | **Sentry-compatible error ingest** per project, grouped by fingerprint and linked to the deploy that introduced it. | Canine | M | ✅ unreleased (per service DSN; migration 0105; envelope + store, gzip/deflate/br; release → deploy, else the live one; new/regressed issues alert) |
| G5.5 | **Deploy freeze.** An admin block on deploys for a project or environment, with a reason and an expiry, checked by the queue. | Tsuru event blocks | S | ✅ unreleased (operator only; held deploys wait as queued and start when it ends) |
| G5.6 | **Autoscale on schedules and right-sizing hints.** Cron-scheduled replica floors, and memory and CPU limit suggestions from the metric history. | Tsuru | M | ✅ unreleased (weekly floor windows in a time zone; hints are advisory) |
| G5.7 | **Certificates shared across node proxies,** so any ingress node can serve any domain. | Uncloud 0.21 | M | ✅ unreleased (opt-in; the panel's ACME certificates for hosts each node routes; cross-node routing itself is not part of it) |
| G5.8 | **`ninedeploy tunnel`.** Forward a local port to a service or database through the panel, so database ports stay closed. | Haloy, Disco | S | ✅ unreleased (`ninedeploy tunnel db` and `tunnel service`; databases and docker services on the panel host and on nodes; node targets over an encrypted agent channel) |

---

## Order of work

1. **G1** in the order listed. Each item is self-contained and ships when its gates pass.
2. **G2.1 and G2.2.** These are the most visible to template users.
3. **G3** in parallel where it does not touch the same files. G3.1 waits for R2's node lifecycle work to settle, because both change node runtime transitions.
4. **G4**, item by item, after the owner decides.
5. **G5**, interleaved where a release has room.

docs.title: GitHub Apps
docs.description: The complete upstream guide to github apps, synchronized with the product repository.
docs.markdown:
# GitHub App

Since 0.13, NineDeploy can deploy GitHub repositories through a **GitHub App** instead of a personal access token (PAT). This is the recommended setup for GitHub and GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES):

- **Short-lived tokens.** Every clone uses an installation token that GitHub expires within an hour. The token is scoped to one repository with `contents: read`, and it is never written to the database.
- **One webhook for every service.** The App's single webhook deploys every linked service. You no longer paste a secret into each repository.
- **Routing by repository id.** A renamed or transferred repository keeps deploying, and the service's clone URL is corrected automatically.
- **Feedback on GitHub (opt-in per service).** Commit statuses for each deploy, and one PR comment per pull request with the preview URL and the outcome.
- **Remote nodes can clone private repositories.** A node receives a per-job token and never holds a long-lived credential.

Existing PAT, deploy-key and webhook setups keep working unchanged. Nothing changes for a service until an operator links it to an App.

---

## 1. Setup

Registering an App is **operator-only**, because its private key can mint tokens for every repository its installations reach. Any number of Apps can be registered; they are unique per API base URL and App id.

### 1.1 One-click setup (github.com)

The panel needs a public domain, because GitHub must reach its webhook URL. Set it under **Settings → Security** (panel domain) first. On a `localhost` panel the setup refuses to start with `panel_origin_local`.

1. Open **Sources → GitHub Apps → Create GitHub App**.
2. Choose **Personal account** or **Organization**. For an organization, enter its login.
3. Press **Continue on GitHub**. GitHub opens with the App pre-filled:
   - permissions: contents and metadata `read`, pull requests and commit statuses `write`;
   - events: `push` and `pull_request` (GitHub always sends `installation` events to Apps);
   - webhook URL `https://<panel>/v1/hooks/github-app/<key>`, callback URL `/github-apps/callback`, setup URL `/github-apps/installed`.
4. Confirm the App name on GitHub. GitHub sends the browser back to `/github-apps/callback`, and the panel saves the App: its id, private key, webhook secret and client secret are stored encrypted.
5. Press **Install the App**, pick the account and the repositories. GitHub returns to `/github-apps/installed`, which syncs the installations.

The setup state is signed, expires after one hour, can be used once, and belongs to the user who started it. If the callback reports that the state was already used or has expired (for example, because the panel restarted in between), start the setup again. GitHub's code is also single-use.

The CLI cannot drive the browser flow. `ninedeploy github-app list` prints the panel URL to open.

### 1.2 Manual entry (GHES, or an existing App)

Use **Sources → GitHub Apps → Add manually (GHES)**, the CLI, or the API:

```bash
ninedeploy github-app add-manual --name "NineDeploy (GHES)" --app-id 12 --key-file ./app.private-key.pem \
  --web-base-url https://github.example.com --api-base-url https://github.example.com/api/v3
```

```http
POST /v1/github-apps
{ "name": "NineDeploy (GHES)", "appId": 12, "privateKey": "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----\n…",
  "webBaseUrl": "https://github.example.com", "apiBaseUrl": "https://github.example.com/api/v3" }
```

- Omit both base URLs for github.com. For GHES give both; giving only one is refused, so a GHES App's JWT is never sent to `api.github.com`.
- The panel signs a JWT with the key and calls `GET /app` before saving. A key that is not a PEM private key is refused with `400`. A key belonging to a different App is also refused.
- Leave the webhook secret empty and the panel generates one and points the App's webhook at itself (`PATCH /app/hook/config`). This needs a public panel origin. If you pass `webhookSecret` (the CLI reads `NINEDEPLOY_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), the panel stores it and leaves the App's webhook configuration alone.
- The CLI never takes a key on the command line: use `--key-file` or `NINEDEPLOY_GITHUB_APP_KEY`.
- Base URLs must be `https`. A GHES host on a private address is blocked by the egress guard unless the server runs with `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`; `http` is accepted only with that setting.

### 1.3 Maintenance

| Action | UI (Sources → GitHub Apps) | CLI | API |
|---|---|---|---|
| List / show | App card | `github-app list`, `github-app show <id>` | `GET /v1/github-apps`, `GET /v1/github-apps/:id` |
| Sync installations | **Sync** | `github-app sync <id>` | `POST /v1/github-apps/:id/installations/sync` |
| Replace the private key | **Rotate key** | `github-app rotate-key <id> --key-file new.pem` | `PUT /v1/github-apps/:id/private-key` |
| Re-point the webhook after a domain change | **Webhook sync** | | `POST /v1/github-apps/:id/webhook/sync` |
| New webhook secret | | | `POST /v1/github-apps/:id/webhook-secret/rotate` |
| Rename, OAuth client fields | | | `PATCH /v1/github-apps/:id` |
| Forget the App | **Delete** | `github-app remove <id>` | `DELETE /v1/github-apps/:id` |

Responses carry metadata only (`webhookUrl`, `installUrl`, `hasPrivateKey`, `hasClientSecret`, permissions, events), never a secret. Deleting an App removes its installation rows and service links. The generated sources stay, so services keep their source, but their clones run anonymously and private repositories fail closed. The App itself stays on GitHub; delete it there too if you no longer need it.

---

## 2. Installations

Each installation (an account or organization where the App is installed) becomes a **source** named `gh-app:<account>` with type `github_app`. The source holds no token; clones mint one.

- **Sync** reads `GET /app/installations` from GitHub; the list GitHub returns is the only input. The `/github-apps/installed?installation_id=…` page syncs every App and never trusts the query parameter.
- Installation webhooks keep the list current without a sync:
  - `installation.created` adds the installation and its source;
  - `installation.deleted` marks it removed;
  - `installation.suspend` / `unsuspend` set or clear the suspended state;
  - `installation.new_permissions_accepted` refreshes the stored permissions;
  - `installation_repositories.added` / `removed` are audited, naming the linked services they affect.
- Installation rows are never hard-deleted. A removed or suspended installation stops minting tokens; reinstall or unsuspend it on GitHub and sync.
- Testing a `github_app` source (**Test installation**, `ninedeploy sources test <id>`, `GET /v1/sources/:id/test`) proves the App key and reads the installation: `{ok, provider: "github_app", login, repositorySelection, permissions, suspended}`.
- `GET /v1/sources/:id/repos` lists the repositories the installation can see. Each row carries GitHub's numeric `repoId`.
- The read-only MCP tool `list_github_installations` lists Apps and their installations (operator, coarse tokens only).

---

## 3. Linking services

A service is **App-driven** when it has an enabled link on a live installation. The link stores GitHub's numeric repository id; webhooks are routed by that id, never by URL.

### 3.1 New services

In the Deploy Wizard, pick the `gh-app:<account>` source. The repository picker lists what the installation can see. After the service is created, the wizard links it to the picked repository by id before the first deploy. If the link is refused (for example, the repository is not in the installation's selection), the wizard warns and still deploys; the first clone links the service lazily anyway.

A service on a `github_app` source with no link is linked automatically on its first clone, with feedback switched off.

### 3.2 Migrating an existing PAT or webhook service

Migration never cuts anything off:

1. **Migrate.** Service → Settings → GitHub App → pick the installation → **Migrate to GitHub App**. CLI: `ninedeploy services github <id> --migrate <sourceId>`. API: `POST /v1/services/:id/github/migrate {sourceId}`.
   - The panel resolves the repository id through the installation and creates the link. It remembers the current source as `previousSourceId` and copies the deploying webhook's watch paths.
   - The service's own source and webhooks stay as they are. While the installation is live, deliveries to the per-service webhook are skipped (`{ok: "skipped", reason: "github_app_linked"}`), so one push never deploys twice.
2. **Finalize (optional).** **Finalize migration**, `--finalize`, or `POST /v1/services/:id/github/finalize`. The App source becomes the service's source and its per-service webhooks are switched off. It is refused (`409`) unless the link is enabled and the installation is live, because deploys would otherwise stop. Afterwards, delete the old webhook on GitHub too.
3. **Revert.** **Revert to previous source**, `--unlink`, or `DELETE /v1/services/:id/github`. The previous source comes back, every deactivated webhook is switched on again, and the link is removed.

**The 409 revert rule:** revert is refused with `409` when the source it would restore is the App installation's own source, that is, a service created on (or finalized onto) the App with no earlier source. Cloning through that source would re-create the link on the next deploy, so the unlink would not stick. Attach another source to the service first, or disable the link instead (`PUT /v1/services/:id/github` with `enabled: false`). The UI keeps the reason on screen.

### 3.3 Link settings

| Setting | Who | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Re-link, `enabled`, `tokenScope`, `watchPaths` | operator | `PUT /v1/services/:id/github`; Settings card (scope and enabled) |
| Commit statuses, PR comments | service admin | `PATCH /v1/services/:id/github/feedback`; Settings card; `--status on\|off`, `--pr-comment on\|off` |
| Required CI workflow paths | service admin | `PATCH /v1/services/:id/github/feedback` with `requiredWorkflows`; Settings card |
| Read the link | any viewer of the service | `GET /v1/services/:id/github` (`{link}`; `link.active` says whether the App drives deploys) |

PR previews follow their parent service's link; linking a preview directly is refused.

### Required CI workflows (0.17.1)

In the GitHub App card, enter up to ten exact paths such as `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, one per line. The API/SDK accepts `requiredWorkflows: [".github/workflows/ci.yml"]` on the feedback PATCH. An empty array disables the policy for future candidates. All existing links default to an empty array (additive migration 0094).

The App installation needs **Actions: read** and **Contents: read**. Newly created App manifests request these permissions. For an existing App, add Actions read in GitHub and have the installation owner accept the permission update before enabling required CI. A missing permission holds deployment; it never counts as success.

The worker captures the policy and repository identity, moves the candidate to `awaiting_ci`, and resolves a manual branch deployment to an exact commit once. Every selected workflow must finish with `success` for that commit. A newer run or rerun attempt supersedes an earlier success. Missing or pending workflows wait; completed failures, cancellations, skips and neutral results fail the candidate. Retry by rerunning CI and creating a new deployment. Workflow paths, not display names or arbitrary commit-status labels, identify the requirements.

Normal deployments accept `push`, `workflow_dispatch` or `merge_group` workflow runs. PR previews inherit their parent's policy and require `pull_request` runs on the parent repository for the exact preview head SHA; `pull_request_target` is never accepted. Fork previews still need the existing human approval and receive no parent repository token. Workflows whose path/branch filters do not produce a run for this commit leave the candidate waiting. This is workflow-level gating, not branch-protection or per-job check enforcement.

CI runs **before** lane approval. An early approval of a mutable branch is cleared when the candidate is pinned; the admin then reviews the actual SHA. After a long review, CI is checked again when its receipt is over a minute old. The checkout uses that SHA even if the branch advances. Changing the repository, branch or installation invalidates the candidate. Existing candidates retain their captured required paths; cancel and redeploy to adopt a changed policy. Disabling/suspending a linked App does not bypass an already captured CI requirement.

Polling uses at most four concurrent checks, 30-second retries and a two-hour deadline, independently of build slots. Leases and results survive restarts; a request interrupted by shutdown is eligible again within a minute. GitHub errors, malformed or truncated results never permit deployment. Service/global deploy lists show waiting candidates; service history includes safe CI reasons and run/attempt receipts. The global queue includes CI waits only with `includeCi=true` (set automatically by the current SDK), preserving the original response for older clients. Cancellation and newer deployment replacement prevent late poll responses from reviving old work. CI evidence does not freeze build settings, environment values or built artifacts; immutable artifact promotion remains separate work.

`tokenScope` is `repository` by default: the clone token covers only the linked repository. Set it to `installation` when the repository has **submodules in sibling repositories** of the same installation; the token then covers every repository the installation can see.

---

## 4. Coexistence with per-service webhooks

- An unlinked service is unchanged: its per-service webhook (`/v1/hooks/:id`) deploys it as before.
- An App-driven service skips its per-service webhook deliveries. The App webhook applies the same gates: branch, `[skip ci]` markers, the link's watch paths, the deploy guard, SHA de-duplication and the race guard.
- When the installation is suspended or removed, or the link is disabled, the per-service webhook takes over again automatically.
- Pull requests from forks are refused by repository id (`external_pr_repository`). Previews from the App webhook use the same preview lifecycle as the per-service webhook.
- When the push payload shows a renamed or transferred repository (same host and id, different clone URL), the panel updates the service's repository URL and audits `service.repo_renamed`.

---

## 5. Commit statuses and PR comments

Both are **off by default** and switched on per service (service admin role).

- **Commit statuses:** `pending` when a deploy starts (only when the commit SHA is known), then `success`, `failure` or `error` (cancelled). The context is `ninedeploy/<slug>`, or `ninedeploy/<parent-slug>/preview` for a PR preview. The target URL is the service's first domain.
- **PR comments (previews only):** one comment per pull request, marked `<!-- ninedeploy:preview:<parentId> -->` and updated in place with the preview URL, the outcome and the short SHA. A deleted comment is re-created. When the preview is torn down, the comment says so.
- Feedback is observational: a GitHub error is logged (redacted) and never fails a deploy.
- The Checks API is not used in 0.13. The manifest flag `checks` only requests the permission.

---

## 6. Remote nodes

An App repository can be deployed to a remote node (docker services) when:

- the node agent is **v0.13.0 or newer** and advertises the `git.credential` capability;
- the panel reaches the agent over the **sealed** (encrypted) transport;
- the node has **git 2.31 or newer** (the credential is passed with `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, which older git ignores).

Per job, the panel mints a repository-scoped `contents: read` token and sends it inside the sealed `git.ensure` / fetch / reset operands. The agent applies it only through the git child process environment (`http.<origin>/.extraheader`): never in argv, never in `.git/config`, and redacted from every output line. When the job finishes the panel revokes the token (`DELETE /installation/token`).

An older agent, or an unsealed transport, gets today's refusal with an instruction to update the agent; nothing is minted.

**PATs and deploy keys on nodes (0.15.2).** A PAT or deploy-key source is still refused on nodes by default. Two ways forward: build the service on the panel and ship the image (`buildOn: panel`, panel 0.15.3), or allow that source on nodes (`allowOnNodes`, with your password), which sends the PAT or key to the node for one clone at a time and needs node agent v0.15.2. Unlike an App token, a PAT is not revoked after the clone. See [PRIVATE_REPO_GUIDE.md §10](./PRIVATE_REPO_GUIDE.md) and [MULTI_NODE.md §6](./MULTI_NODE.md).

---

## 7. Token model and security

| Token | Scope | Lifetime | Stored |
|---|---|---|---|
| App JWT | the App | 9 minutes | no (signed per call) |
| Clone token | one repository, `contents: read` (or the installation with `tokenScope: installation`) | GitHub's expiry (1 hour); reused until 5 minutes before it | in memory only |
| Node job token | one repository, `contents: read` | one job, then revoked | no |
| Listing token | `metadata: read` | as above | in memory only |
| Feedback token | one repository, `statuses: write` / `pull_requests: write` | as above | in memory only |

- The private key, webhook secret and client secret are encrypted at rest (and re-encrypted by master-key rotation). No route returns them, and audit entries carry ids and names only.
- A token is never sent to a host other than the App's: the clone URL's host must equal the App's web host, otherwise the clone is refused ("Refusing to send a GitHub App token to <host>").
- Every App, installation and Gitea call goes through the egress guard. Private destinations are refused unless `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`.
- Tokens are redacted from clone output, API errors and agent output.

### Audit actions

| Action | Actor | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `github_app.create` | operator | App registered (`via: manifest` or `manual`) |
| `github_app.update` | operator | renamed, OAuth fields changed, or webhook re-pointed (`changed: ["webhook"]`) |
| `github_app.rotate_key` | operator | private key replaced |
| `github_app.rotate_webhook_secret` | operator | new webhook secret registered on GitHub |
| `github_app.delete` | operator | App forgotten |
| `github_app.sync` | operator | installations synced (counts in meta) |
| `github_installation.created` | system | installation added by webhook |
| `github_installation.removed` | system | installation removed (webhook, or `detectedBy: sync`) |
| `github_installation.suspended` / `.unsuspended` | system | installation suspended or resumed on GitHub |
| `github_installation.permissions_updated` | system | new permissions accepted on GitHub |
| `github.repos_changed` | system | repositories added to or removed from an installation; names the affected services |
| `service.github_link` | operator, admin or system | service linked or re-linked, feedback toggled (`change: feedback`), or linked lazily on first clone |
| `service.github_migrate` | operator | PAT/webhook service linked to the App |
| `service.github_finalize` | operator | previous source detached, webhooks switched off |
| `service.github_unlink` | operator | reverted to the previous source |
| `service.repo_renamed` | system | clone URL corrected after a rename or transfer |
| `github_app.runners_update` | operator | self-hosted runner settings changed (§7.1) |
| `github_app.runner_stop` | operator | a runner container stopped from the panel |
| `github_runner.failed` | system | a queued job's runner could not be started (error in meta) |

System entries have no actor, so only operators see them.

### 7.1 Self-hosted Actions runners (G4.5)

An App can run GitHub Actions jobs on the panel host or on one node. Each job gets a just-in-time runner: a single-use registration bound to one runner, which takes one job and exits. Its container is then removed.

**Set up**

1. Give the App what it needs:
   - Subscribe it to the **Workflow job** event.
   - Grant the runner permission:
     - an organization installation needs **Self-hosted runners: write** (organization permission);
     - a personal installation needs **Administration: write** (repository permission), because GitHub offers no narrower one for repository runners.
   - A new App gets all of this when **Also allow self-hosted Actions runners** is on in the setup form. For an existing App, add the event and permission on GitHub and accept them on each installation.
2. On Sources, open the App's **Self-hosted Actions runners** section, turn **Run jobs on this panel** on, and save. The section lists anything still missing.
3. Ask for the runner in a workflow: `runs-on: [self-hosted, ninedeploy]`, using one of your configured labels.

**Which jobs are taken**

A queued job is taken only when all of these hold:

- its `runs-on` names at least one configured label;
- every other label in it is one of GitHub's defaults (`self-hosted`, `linux`, and the host's architecture);
- its repository is private, unless **Allow public repositories** is on;
- its repository is on the repository list, if a list is set.

Other jobs are left for other runners.

GitHub, not only the panel, enforces the repository rules:

- **Repository runners** (a personal installation) serve only the repository they were registered for.
- **Organization runners** are registered in a runner group the App owns, named `NineDeploy runners (App <id>)`. The panel creates the group and keeps it open only to the allowed repositories: the repository list, or every repository the installation sees, without public ones unless allowed. GitHub hands an organization runner any queued job its group may serve, so without its own group a job from another repository could take the runner.
- Custom runner groups need GitHub Team or Enterprise. On another plan, no organization runner starts, and the section shows the error.

**Isolation and limits**

- **No Docker access:** the runner container never gets the Docker socket. Workflows that use `container:`, `services:` or `docker build` therefore do not run on it; use GitHub-hosted runners for those.
- **Its own network:** the container runs on its own bridge network, `nd-gha-runners` (interface `nd-gha0`), not on any service network. Runners cannot reach each other.
- **Firewall rules:** before every start, the panel makes sure these rules are in place:
  - `INPUT -i nd-gha0 -j DROP`: nothing reaches the host itself, such as the panel, databases or a Docker API.
  - `DOCKER-USER -i nd-gha0 -d <range> -j DROP` for 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254/16 (cloud metadata), 100.64/10, 127/8 and 224/4: nothing reaches private networks or other containers.

  Internet access stays open, which GitHub and package registries need. The rules are checked again on every start, so a firewall reload or a reboot does not leave runners unguarded.
- **No rules, no runner:** if the panel cannot apply the rules, the runner does not start. That happens when iptables is missing, or when the panel runs in its own network namespace and cannot see `nd-gha0`. `NINEDEPLOY_GHA_RUNNERS_UNISOLATED=1` lets runners start without the rules. Set it only if you accept runners that can reach the host and the LAN.
- **Resource limits:** a pid limit, plus the CPU and memory limits you set.
- **IPv6:** the runner network is created with IPv6 off, even on a daemon that enables it for new networks, because the firewall rules are IPv4. A runner does not start on an existing `nd-gha-runners` network that has IPv6 or another bridge name; remove that network and the panel recreates it.

**On a node**

**Run on** in the section picks where this App's runners start: the panel host, or one node. A node runs jobs only after its owner opts in. They set `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_GHA_RUNNERS=on` for the node's agent, which must be 0.18.7 or newer (capability `gha.runner`). Until then, the section names the reason, and no job is registered on GitHub.

- Isolation is the same as on the panel host. The agent creates the same `nd-gha-runners` network and starts the same container: no Docker socket, the same limits.
- The agent itself lives in a container, so its own iptables would not guard the host. It puts the same firewall rules on the node's host instead, through the privileged `nsenter` helper that OS updates use. The rules are checked before every start, and no runner starts when they cannot be put in place. A node has no equivalent of `NINEDEPLOY_GHA_RUNNERS_UNISOLATED`.
- The just-in-time configuration travels to the agent only inside a sealed request. It is written to a 0600 env file for `docker run`, and never appears in argv.
- **Runners at once** counts the App's runners on every host. While the node does not answer, its jobs wait for the next minute's sweep.
- Changing **Run on** is refused (`409 runners_active`) while the App still has runners on the old host. Stop them, or let their jobs finish, first.
- `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_GHA_RUNNERS=off`, or unsetting it, takes the capability away again.

**Queue and upkeep**

- **Runners at once** limits how many runner containers an App has. Further jobs wait in memory; every minute the panel starts those that are still queued on GitHub. An unverifiable job status stays pending for a later sweep.
- The waiting list does not survive a panel restart. GitHub keeps such a job queued until some runner takes it, or for 24 hours.
- After 10 minutes, a running runner is removed only when GitHub confirms it is idle or its registration is gone. Busy or unverifiable runners are retained; an operator can still stop one explicitly. Job duration follows the workflow's [`timeout-minutes`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#jobsjob_idtimeout-minutes) and GitHub's [self-hosted execution limits](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits), rather than container creation age.

**Image**

`ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner`, pinned by digest (`GITHUB_RUNNER_IMAGE` in `@ninedeploy/schemas`). When GitHub requires a newer runner version, the runner updates itself at start.

**Troubleshooting**

- **A job stays queued:**
  - Check the section's problem list, then the App's **Recent deliveries** for `workflow_job`. An `ignored` answer names the reason: `labels_not_ours`, `labels_unmatched`, `public_repository`, `repository_not_allowed` or `runners_disabled`.
  - A start that failed is audited as `github_runner.failed`.
- **`403` when the runner registers:** the installation has not accepted the runner permission.


---

## 8. Troubleshooting

- **"The panel's address is http://localhost…, which GitHub cannot reach"** (`panel_origin_local`): set the panel domain under Settings → Security, or use manual entry with your own webhook secret.
- **Callback says the setup state was already used or expired:** start the setup again from Sources. The state lives in memory, so a panel restart in between invalidates it.
- **"GitHub refused the App credentials"** (`github_app_rejected`): the App id and key do not match, the key was revoked on GitHub, or the GHES base URL is wrong. Rotate the key.
- **Clone fails with "not found or no access":** add the repository to the installation's repository access (GitHub → Settings → Installed GitHub Apps → Configure), and check that the installation is not suspended. For a failing submodule in a sibling repository, set the token scope to `installation`.
- **"Refusing to send a GitHub App token to <host>":** the service's repository URL is not on the App's GitHub host. Fix the URL or use a different source.
- **Pushes do not deploy:** check the App's **Advanced → Recent deliveries** on GitHub. `401` means the webhook secret differs (run **Webhook sync**, or rotate the secret). `404 Unknown webhook` means the App was deleted from the panel or the webhook URL is stale (run **Webhook sync** after a domain change). An `ignored` answer with `no_linked_service` means no enabled link matches the repository id.
- **Remote node refuses an App repository:** update the node agent to v0.13.0 or newer (re-run its bootstrap from the Servers page), and make sure the sealed transport is in use.
- **A GHES or Gitea host on the LAN is refused:** the egress guard blocks private addresses. Set `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1` on the server if that is intended.

---

## 9. Rolling back to 0.12

Rolling back the panel image to 0.12 is safe; the 0.13 tables and the `sources.base_url` column are ignored.

- **Migrated but not finalized** services keep their PAT and per-service webhook, which 0.12 uses as before.
- **App-only services** (created on, or finalized onto, a `github_app` source) clone anonymously on 0.12, so private repositories fail closed. No secret is exposed. Re-attach a PAT or deploy key to keep deploying, or switch the per-service webhooks back on.
- The 0.12 source test answers "Unknown source type" for `github_app` sources, and their type label is blank.
- `/v1/hooks/github-app/*` answers 404, so GitHub records failed deliveries until you upgrade again.
- Gitea base URLs are ignored; the Gitea test is "not supported" again.

Upgrading back to 0.13 restores everything: the links, Apps and installations are still in the database.

---

## 10. Gitea

0.13 adds a **base URL** to Gitea sources (Sources → New source → Gitea → *Gitea base URL*, the card's *Base URL · edit*, `ninedeploy sources add --base-url https://git.example.com`, or `baseUrl` on `POST`/`PATCH /v1/sources`). With it:

- **Test token** calls `GET <base>/api/v1/user` and reports `{ok, provider: "gitea", login, name}`;
- the Deploy Wizard lists your repositories (`<base>/api/v1/user/repos`, following the `Link` header) and their branches.

Without a base URL the test keeps its old answer, now with the message "Set the Gitea base URL to enable the live test". The base URL must be `https` (`http` only with `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`), without credentials, query or fragment; `PATCH` with `baseUrl: null` clears it. A base URL on any other source type is refused.

docs.markdown:
# Moving from Coolify, Dokploy or CapRover

`ninedeploy import plan` reads another platform's API and shows what NineDeploy would create. For each item it also lists what NineDeploy cannot carry over and what needs a person. It is read-only: it creates nothing in NineDeploy and changes nothing on the source. `ninedeploy import apply` then creates what a saved plan describes. It never touches the source.

| Step | What it does | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Plan | Read the source and list each service, domain, environment variable name, volume and database, with every unsupported option | Available (CLI) |
| 2. Apply | Create the planned services and databases in NineDeploy, resumably, with a receipt per item, and leave the source untouched | Available (CLI) |
| 3. Data | Move database contents, checksummed; then deploy, switch DNS and add the domains as the last step | Databases available (CLI); volumes and the domain cutover by hand for now |

## Run a plan

The command runs on your machine. The source credential stays there: it is read from an environment variable or a hidden prompt, never from the command line, and it is never written to the plan.

```bash
# Coolify: turn on Settings → Advanced → API access, then create a token with "read" (Keys & Tokens).
NINEDEPLOY_IMPORT_TOKEN=… ninedeploy import plan coolify --url https://coolify.example.com

# Dokploy: create an API key for the organization (Profile → API keys).
NINEDEPLOY_IMPORT_TOKEN=… ninedeploy import plan dokploy --url https://dokploy.example.com

# CapRover: the dashboard password (NINEDEPLOY_IMPORT_OTP for a two-factor code; otherwise it is asked for).
NINEDEPLOY_IMPORT_PASSWORD=… ninedeploy import plan caprover --url https://captain.apps.example.com
```

`--json` prints the plan as JSON, and `--out plan.json` also saves it. Leave the variable unset and the command asks for the credential without echoing it.

## Apply a plan

```bash
ninedeploy import plan caprover --url https://captain.apps.example.com --out plan.json
ninedeploy import apply plan.json                      # shows what it would create; creates nothing
ninedeploy import apply plan.json --yes --project 3 --dotenv blog=./blog.env   # creates them
```

`import apply` uses the panel the CLI is signed in to (`ninedeploy login`). It reads the plan file only, so it needs no source credential. Edit the plan first if you want different names or fewer items.

**What it creates**
- Each service that has something to deploy from: an image, or a repository and branch, with its port, replicas, limits, health path and first volume.
- Each database with a NineDeploy engine. It is created empty. The source's version is used when the source runs the same image (for example `postgres:14.5`); otherwise the panel's default is used.

**What it does not do**
- **It does not deploy anything.** Deploy each service when its environment is complete.
- **It does not add domains.** Adding a domain makes NineDeploy request a certificate, and the request would fail while DNS still points at the old platform. With the Cloudflare integration on, adding a domain would also change your DNS. Domains move at the cutover, step 3.
- **It does not invent environment values.** A plan holds names only. Pass `--dotenv <service>=<path>` with a `.env` file to set a service's values through the panel's `.env` import. Variables with no value are listed in the receipt; they are not created empty.

**The receipt**
- It is saved next to the plan as `plan.receipt.json` (`--receipt` to choose the file).
- It records each item's state (`done`, `skipped`, `failed`), its NineDeploy id and notes: what still needs a person, and which domains wait for the cutover. It never contains a value.
- Running the same command again repeats only what is not `done`. Each item is written as pending before the panel is called. Creates are sent with `reuseExisting`, so a run that stopped halfway picks up your own idle service or database of the same definition instead of failing on the name.
- A receipt is tied to one panel and one source. Apply refuses a receipt from another one.

## Move the data

```bash
ninedeploy import data plan.json                                  # the order, and a dump command per database
ninedeploy import data plan.json --dump pgreal=pgreal.dump --yes  # imports it
```

Without `--yes`, `import data` prints the order that loses no writes, and the dump command to run on the source host for each database:

1. A day ahead, lower the TTL of each domain's DNS record.
2. Stop writes on the source. A dump of a live database misses every write made after it.
3. Take the final dumps.
4. Import them with `--dump <database>=<file> --yes`.
5. Deploy each service and check it is healthy. Connection strings copied from the source may still name its database hosts: attach the new database to the service (it sets `DATABASE_URL` or the engine's own variable at deploy), or edit them.
6. Switch DNS, then add each domain in the service's Domains tab.

**The dump commands**
- The commands produce what the panel's import accepts: `pg_dump -Fc`, `mysqldump` or `mariadb-dump` of the app's database, a gzipped `mongodump --archive`, or an RDB snapshot.
- They read credentials from the database container's own environment, inside single quotes, so no password appears in the output or in your shell history.
- The CapRover commands were run against a live CapRover v1.16.0: a PostgreSQL 16 one-click app with 500 rows arrived with the same row count and checksum. The Coolify and Dokploy commands follow their source code.

**The import**
- Each file goes through the panel's chunked dump import with its sha256 declared. The panel checks the hash before it restores anything.
- The receipt records the import id, sha256 and size.
- Once the receipt has an import id, retrying after an upload/status error checks that same job: unfinished uploads resume, running jobs are awaited, and completed jobs are recorded without restoring again.
- If that job's status cannot be read, its id stays in the receipt for another retry instead of starting a replacement.
- A different dump is refused while a prior import id is recorded. Inspect it with `ninedeploy databases imports <database-id>`; use `ninedeploy databases import <database-id> --file <file>` for a deliberate new import.
- A database whose data is already in is not imported again. The same file is skipped, and a different file is refused; use `ninedeploy databases import` directly if you mean it.
- ClickHouse has no dump import, so move its data by hand.

**Volumes** are not moved yet. Copy their files from the source host, then upload them in the service's Volumes & Storage tab.

## What a plan contains

- **Services**, each with:
  - a kind: image, Git or compose;
  - the fields a NineDeploy service would be created with: repository and branch, build pack, base directory, port, replicas, CPU and memory limits, health path, first volume;
  - its domains, with whether each had HTTPS. A host the source generated for itself is marked as staying behind: CapRover's `<app>.<root domain>`, Coolify's `sslip.io` hosts and Dokploy's `traefik.me` hosts;
  - its environment variable **names**;
  - its volumes.
- **Databases**, each with the matching NineDeploy engine and the source image, which carries the version.
- **Issues** on every item:
  - `✗ unsupported`: no NineDeploy equivalent;
  - `! manual`: a person must do something;
  - `· info`: worth knowing.

**What a plan never contains:** variable values, database passwords, registry passwords, Git credentials, tokens or keys. Some sources return these to any authenticated client: Dokploy returns decrypted env values and database passwords, and CapRover returns Git passwords and SSH keys. The importer reads names and drops the rest. It also removes `user:password@` from every URL.

## Per source

**Coolify**
- A plain `read` token is enough. Values that need `read:sensitive` (env values, compose YAML, passwords) are never requested.
- A compose stack from a one-click template is listed without its compose file. Paste the file into a new compose service, or look for the app in the NineDeploy Hub.
- Databases are read from `/databases`, so KeyDB, Dragonfly and ClickHouse are included. SQLite has no managed equivalent.

**Dokploy**
- The plan covers the organization the API key belongs to.
- Builds with Heroku and Paketo buildpacks map to the same NineDeploy build packs.
- An uploaded ("drop") application cannot be read over the API; re-upload it as a ZIP source.
- For a Gitea source the URL must be entered by hand, because the record does not include the Gitea host.
- libSQL has no managed equivalent.

**CapRover**
- A one-click database (marked by its template tag) is listed as a database.
- An app built by CapRover from an upload or the CLI, with no repository on record, has its image only inside CapRover. Push its source or image somewhere NineDeploy can reach first.
- A custom nginx config, pre-deploy script and Swarm service override have no equivalent and are listed as such.
- An app that was registered but never deployed has no image or repository to carry. It is listed for a person to complete.

## How the adapters were checked

The field mappings were written against the source code of Coolify v4.7.0, Dokploy v0.31.0 and CapRover v1.16.0, and are tested with fixtures derived from that code.

- **CapRover v1.16.0 was also run live.** A plan was made against a fresh instance with an app from a repository, an image app with a host port and a one-click PostgreSQL. Its responses are kept as a test fixture, with secret values replaced. That run found three things the source reading had missed:
  - an app that was never deployed runs CapRover's placeholder image, which is not planned as its image;
  - a stopped app (0 instances) is flagged as stopped;
  - the version is read from `versionInfo`.
- **Coolify and Dokploy have not yet been run against live instances.**

If a plan looks wrong for your version, please open an issue with the plan's `source.version`.

docs.markdown:
# Instance GitOps (G5.3)

One YAML file in a git repository describes the instance:

- its projects,
- their services (identity and source),
- their domains,
- their project grants.

The panel compares the file with the instance on a schedule and shows the drift. When the drift changes, it raises an alert. On request it applies the file through the ordinary API.

It is set up under **Settings → GitOps** by an operator, or through `/v1/gitops`.

## The file

```yaml
version: "1"
projects:
  - slug: shop
    name: Shop
    workspace: main          # workspace slug; optional
    description: The web shop
    services:
      - slug: api
        name: api
        type: docker         # docker | compose
        image: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
        port: 3000
        domains: [api.shop.example.com]
      - slug: web
        repoUrl: https://github.com/acme/web
        branch: main
        domains: [shop.example.com]
    grants:
      - { email: bob@example.com, role: admin }   # viewer | member | admin
```

**Managed fields**
- A service field you leave out is not managed: the panel keeps whatever it has.
- Domains are hostnames on path `/`.
- Grants are project grants (no environment).

**Validation**
- The file is limited to 256 KiB and must use the schema exactly; unknown keys are refused.
- Each project slug, service slug, domain and grant may appear only once.
- The secret scanner of the service manifest runs over the file. Secrets and environment values stay in the panel.

**Reading the file**
- The panel reads the file from a shallow checkout of the configured branch, with the same egress rules as a deploy checkout.
- For a private repository, pick a git source; its credential is used for the checkout.
- A path that resolves outside the checkout, for example through a symlink, is refused.

## Drift

Each difference is one of three kinds:

| Change | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `missing` | In the file, not in the instance. |
| `extra` | In the instance, not in the file. Covers projects the file does not name, and services, domains and grants of the projects it does name. |
| `changed` | In both, with different fields. Each changed field shows the value in the instance and the value in the file. |

**When the panel checks**
- Every *interval* minutes while scheduled checks are on.
- Whenever someone presses **Check now** (`POST /v1/gitops/check`).

**Alerts**
- A drift that differs from the previous check is audited as `alert.gitops_drift`.
- A file that cannot be read is audited as `alert.gitops_failed`. It is raised once, until a read succeeds again.
- Both reach the channels that receive alerts, including PagerDuty and Opsgenie as warnings.

## Applying

**Apply the file** (`POST /v1/gitops/apply`) reads the file again and calls the ordinary routes with the operator's own credentials, in this order:

1. Projects are created or updated: name, description and workspace.
2. Services are created in their project, or their managed fields are patched.
3. Domains are added.
4. Project grants are created, or their role is changed.

Every check those routes make still applies: slug rules, image policy, domain ownership and grant caps. A refused step is reported with its reason, and the other steps still run.

Applying never deletes. `extra` items stay until someone removes them in the panel.

A service whose slug belongs to a service outside the project is reported and left alone.

## Write-back

To bring edits made in the panel back to the repository:

1. Export the panel as the file: **Export the panel as the file**, or `GET /v1/gitops/export` (YAML; `?format=json` answers `{ file }`).
2. Commit the result.

The panel does not push to the repository itself. It holds no write credential for it.

## Storage

The configuration and the last check are settings rows (`instance_gitops`, `instance_gitops_check`). There is no migration.

# Developing on macOS and continuing work from another computer

Use a Mac for native desktop packaging and Keychain acceptance. Panel/API unit
tests and source audits can also run on Windows or Linux. The production
installer and systemd/UFW behavior still need Linux; a Mac is not a replacement
for those runtime checks.

This guide describes a reproducible setup, not a claim that this checkout was
tested on a physical Mac. The November 9 handoff was prepared on Windows.
The hosted macOS checkpoint below records which native CI checks subsequently passed.

## Native server regressions on hosted macOS

The [manual server audit workflow](../.github/workflows/macos-server-audit.yml)
checks backend filesystem, SQLite, scheduler, image and LFS regressions on a
native macOS runner. It installs the root frozen lockfile, builds the server and
its workspace dependencies, and runs 25 focused test files plus four controlled
Docker CLI integration files. Docker CLI is installed without starting a daemon;
all native CLI cases use private configs and loopback fixtures.

Use **Actions → macOS server audit → Run workflow** on main, or an authenticated
GitHub CLI:

```sh
gh workflow run macos-server-audit.yml --repo ninedeploy/ninedeploy --ref main
gh run list --repo ninedeploy/ninedeploy --workflow macos-server-audit.yml --limit 3
```

Download the run's audit artifact for exact source SHA, OS/architecture, tool
versions and logs. The runner uses .node-version, the root pinned pnpm and
GOMAXPROCS=4. No GUI, deployment, real registry or Docker daemon is started.
This focused lane is separate from full release/coverage acceptance and normal
Keychain/desktop checks. It does not resolve the round73 Windows worker fault.

Native server checkpoint (November 10): [run 42813045891](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/42813045891)
passed at source `f71b619db87cd34350a9e15ac2c6c12ac45c6467`: macOS 26.7.2 arm64,
Node 26.12.1, pnpm 11.23.0 and Docker CLI 29.9.2. Frozen install, five-project
workspace/server build, typecheck, 307 unit tests in 24 files and 20 controlled
native CLI tests in four files passed. The downloaded environment/logs match
the run SHA and counts; see the [receipt](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/round89_receipt.json)
and [retained normalized text diagnostics](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/round89_macos_42813045891).
The result records hosted native arm64 evidence, not physical Mac, Intel,
normal Keychain persistence or full release acceptance. The successful install
reported an optional ssh2 crypto-binding build failure on Node 26's V8 API and a
pre-build workspace MCP bin-target warning. Native SSH acceleration and the
post-build MCP executable link were not certified by this focused lane.

### Fresh workspace MCP executable

The MCP package now exposes a tracked `bin/ninedeploy-mcp.mjs` launcher so
pnpm can create its command link during a fresh install, before TypeScript has
created `dist/index.js`. Build is still required before starting the server.
The Mac setup helper verifies the workspace command after its root build.

```sh
node scripts/check-workspace-mcp.mjs
```

This read-only smoke removes every casing of the API token name from child
environments, including Windows lowercase/mixed-case aliases. The parent
environment is unchanged. The child
entrypoints deliberately refuse startup with the required-token message; those
exit-1 refusals mean the launcher resolved, and the checker itself exits zero.
No panel or credential is contacted. Cold/prebuilt/offline-reinstall fixtures,
MCP's full 52-test coverage gate and actual npm-layout packing passed locally.
The package was packed for inspection, not published.

Fresh MCP native Mac checkpoint: [run 42819090055](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/42819090055)
passed at `e20be68c60bb53e9737fc40612e8a31bc4d71ab0` on macOS 26.7.2 arm64 with
Node 26.12.1/pnpm 11.23.0. The real workspace launcher resolved, all three cold
install/reinstall cases passed, and the 307-unit/20-native-CLI groups passed
again: 330 tests across 29 files. The install log no longer reports the MCP bin
creation warning. See the [receipt](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/round90_receipt.json)
for exact identity and original/normalized diagnostic hashes. This is native
workspace-launcher evidence, not npm publication, full release, physical Mac or
SSH native-acceleration acceptance.

Diagnostic environment checkpoint: [run 42823382868](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/42823382868)
passed at source `66c9f4cbaedf46c04110e181eef9b5fa668db021` on macOS 26.7.2 arm64.
All four workspace cases, including uppercase/lowercase/mixed-case and empty
credential variables, passed alongside 307 unit and 20 native CLI tests: 331
tests in 29 files. See the [receipt](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/round91_receipt.json).
The parent environment was not modified and fixture probes made no API calls.

The earlier optional ssh2 build warning traces through Dockerode/Testcontainers
[development dependencies](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/round91_ssh2_dependency.log).
No direct apps/packages source imports were found; this warning was not a
confirmed backend startup failure. Native SSH acceleration remains unverified.

## Full backend unit verification on native macOS

Run **macOS server full unit audit** manually from GitHub Actions, or use:

```bash
gh workflow run macos-server-full-unit-audit.yml --ref main
```

This separate workflow uses the selected commit, the repository's Node/pnpm
versions, a frozen install, workspace dependency builds and server typecheck.
It runs the configured server unit suite with one worker and coverage disabled:

```bash
pnpm --dir apps/server exec vitest run --coverage=false --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=verbose
```

The job has a 90-minute budget; individual test/hook timeouts remain those in
`apps/server/vitest.config.ts`. Its artifact records the expected test files,
config hash, source/event SHA, environment, complete logs and workspace MCP
checks. The four controlled Docker CLI test files run separately. Docker CLI is
installed before the unit suite; no Docker daemon, GUI or deployment is started.

Use the existing **macOS server audit** for the shorter focused regression lane.
Neither workflow substitutes for coverage, the full root release gate, normal
Keychain behavior, signing/notarization or acceptance on a physical Mac.

## Open the same source revision

On a fresh Mac checkout:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy.git
cd ninedeploy
git status --short
git rev-parse HEAD
```

For an existing checkout, inspect `git status --short` first and preserve local
work before updating. On `main`, when clean, `git pull --ff-only origin main` gets the
pushed handoff without creating a merge. Record the commit in the Mac's results.

Install Node using the exact version in [`.node-version`](../.node-version).
The supported security range is enforced by
[`scripts/check-node-version.mjs`](../scripts/check-node-version.mjs).
Use the pnpm version in the root `package.json` (`pnpm@11.23.0` at this handoff).
If Node is installed but pnpm is missing:

```sh
npm install --global pnpm@11.23.0
node scripts/check-node-version.mjs
pnpm --version
```

Install Apple's Command Line Tools with `xcode-select --install` if
`xcode-select -p` fails, finish its installer, and retry. Use the Mac's native
terminal architecture (`uname -m`): install native Node/dependencies rather than
copying Windows `node_modules`, build output or Electron binaries.

Install/start your Linux-container Docker environment only if you will exercise
the panel's Docker runtime. Check `docker context show`, `docker info` and
`docker compose version` before any deployment smoke. The panel controls the
selected daemon; use an isolated daemon for runtime acceptance, as
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) requires.

## Check and bootstrap

The helper runs from any working directory. Its default mode only checks
prerequisites; `--install` explicitly installs the locked dependencies and
builds both projects. It does not start a panel, Docker daemon or GUI.

```sh
node scripts/dev-macos.mjs --check
node scripts/dev-macos.mjs --check --docker  # also check a Linux Docker engine
node scripts/dev-macos.mjs --install
```

The root workspace and `desktop/` have **independent lockfiles**. Root install or
build does not install/build Electron. The helper runs root
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and `pnpm build`, then installs, typechecks,
tests and builds `desktop/` separately. It never updates either lockfile.

Do not copy `.env`, `.data`, master keys, database files, production backups,
tokens or signing certificates between computers as a development setup step.
Use disposable local configuration and fixtures. A copied SQLite database also
needs its original encryption keys; a clean development installation does not.

## Panel/API development

After the workspace build:

```sh
pnpm typecheck
pnpm lint
pnpm turbo run test --concurrency=1
```

Tests that write coverage must run serially. Do not launch a second full suite
while the first is writing. The server test configuration supplies a fresh data
directory for each invocation.

For a focused audit, run the relevant Vitest files in `apps/server`, for example:

```sh
cd apps/server
pnpm exec vitest run test/lib/webhooks.test.ts test/runtimeState.test.ts --coverage=false
cd ../..
```

To run the app, prepare a **local** `.env` following
[Quickstart: local development](QUICKSTART.md#-3-local-development-from-source).
Run `pnpm dev` and `pnpm dev:web` in separate terminals. This starts the panel
and its background plugins against your configured Docker daemon; do that only
after selecting your development daemon.

For the complete repository gate, run `pnpm release:check`. A successful desktop
unit suite or an individual audit scope is not a full release verdict.

## Desktop development and native acceptance

From `desktop/`, use the project's existing commands:

```sh
cd desktop
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm build
pnpm start                         # interactive unpackaged app
CSC_IDENTITY_AUTO_DISCOVERY=false pnpm dist
pnpm smoke                        # packaged app, temporary user-data directory
```

`pnpm dist` builds Intel and Apple-silicon DMGs according to
[`electron-builder.yml`](../desktop/electron-builder.yml). Run the packaged app
matching the current Mac's architecture. Building both architectures on one
computer does not prove that both launch natively.

The smoke script uses a disposable loopback panel and the Chromium debugging
port 9339. Close any earlier smoke instance before another run. It checks the
launcher, bridge isolation, encrypted token storage, restart and instance
removal. It does not sign into a production panel.

Test the **installed copy** too, rather than only `release/mac*/NineDeploy.app`:

1. Mount the DMG matching the Mac's architecture in Finder.
2. Copy `NineDeploy.app` to your chosen Applications directory and eject the DMG.
3. Run the smoke against that copy, using its real executable path, for example:
   `pnpm smoke /Applications/NineDeploy.app/Contents/MacOS/NineDeploy`.
4. Open the installed app normally and check its instance list, adding/opening
   a development instance, sign-out, removal and Cmd+Shift+O.
5. Record macOS version, architecture, source commit, app/signing state and
   whether a token actually survived a normal quit and restart.

For unsigned local builds, follow the normal macOS Privacy & Security approval
if needed. Do not disable Gatekeeper or use a sandbox-disable flag as acceptance.
Signing/notarization is optional for local development. Certificate/Apple API
secrets belong in the existing Desktop workflow's secret inputs, not in Git or
this guide; see [Desktop signing](DESKTOP.md#installing).

### Keychain: acceptance versus fallback

Leave `ND_SMOKE_KEYCHAIN_UNREACHABLE` unset when checking a real Mac's persistence.
If the unlocked login Keychain grants access, the token must survive a normal
quit/restart and disappear after instance removal.

The existing CI workflow sets `ND_SMOKE_KEYCHAIN_UNREACHABLE=1` because its
unsigned app cannot keep its Keychain key on that runner. That mode verifies
safe fallback, **not persistent sign-in**. If a local unsigned build encounters
the same problem, record it separately; do not turn on that flag to call the
normal persistence check passed. A signed build or explicit Keychain access
may be needed to close the remaining acceptance gap.

## Handoff: audit state on November 9, 2026

The first seven requested scopes were reviewed: settings ownership, Swarm
recovery, runtime reconciliation, backup scheduling/policy, restore
verification/drills, node sleep coordination and webhook delivery.

- **F1034:** webhook delivery replay IDs now include provider and service scope.
  Previously the same ID could suppress another service's legitimate event.
- **F1035:** unreadable local/fan-out Docker inspections no longer report a
  container missing without Docker's explicit missing-container/object reply.
- Seven permanent regression cases were observed failing before the changes
  and passing afterward. The combined seven-scope run passed **519 tests in
  23 files**; server typecheck/build, scoped lint and `git diff --check` passed.
- **F1036:** failed image-removal accounting now credits an image only when
  follow-up inspection explicitly confirms absence; unknown inspect errors no
  longer claim reclaimed space. Its before-proof failed on current code and
  four new permanent regression cases were observed red before the patch.
  The expanded verifier passed three consecutive runs; all 76 tests in the
  four-file release-image scope passed afterward.
- These were Windows/local observations. Hosted CI, Linux runtime and
  physical-Mac results must be recorded separately for the pushed commit.

The user authorized continued proof-led audit rounds with independently chosen
scopes until asked to stop. The second completed scope covers
`apps/server/src/lib/releaseImageRetention.ts`, `releaseRecords.ts` and their
`imageInventory.ts` dependency, plus their tests. F1036 was fixed and verified
in that round. The next selected scope is `apps/server/src/lib/backupReplicas.ts`
and `test/lib/backupReplicas.test.ts`. Continue by recording current Git status, reading any
existing ledger, and writing a failing executable proof before editing source.

The earlier working tree also contained panel IP-access policy, portable
service settings and several focused server fixes. The user requested those
existing changes be included in the commit/push for cross-machine continuation;
their validation must not be inferred from the 519-test audit result.

### Local handoff checks and remaining boundary

The handoff also passed workspace typecheck, lint and build; the full web suite
passed **2,800 tests**, SDK **388 tests with 100% coverage**, schemas **803**,
database **84**, plugin SDK **7**, MCP **49**, and CLI **1,067**. The first SDK run
failed its coverage floor because the new panel-access methods had no tests;
authenticated read/update/lockout-error transport tests closed that gap without
lowering thresholds. A manifest UI test failed once in a complete web run;
the unchanged file passed all 139 cases in isolation and the next complete web
run passed. No assertion or timeout was weakened.

The targeted server run covering the changed features and release-image scope
passed **1,793 tests in 27 files** before F1036's narrow patch. Desktop
typecheck, **27 unit tests** and bundling passed on Windows. The macOS setup
helper passed Node syntax and Biome checks, its help command ran, and its Mac
check refused Windows as intended. Native Mac bootstrap/DMG/Keychain execution
remains unverified.

The complete `pnpm release:check` did **not** finish green: its server coverage
step was refused because another Vitest process already owned
`apps/server/coverage`. That process was left running; its lock/report directory
was not deleted, overridden or redirected. Run the full gate after that owner
finishes (or in this fresh Mac checkout) and record the result for this commit.
This is a development handoff, not a certified release.

For each next audit round, retain `prove_*`, `verify_*` and a ledger; run the
verifier three times; promote High/Critical and race/ownership findings into
the normal suite. Preserve unrelated edits. Do not commit runtime data or
credentials. The `.temp_files/` directory is ignored by default; any explicitly
committed handoff evidence is selected individually, not the entire historical
scratch directory.

### Continued audit evidence through November 9, round 14

The following additional fixes were committed and pushed after the initial
Mac handoff. Counts are per bounded scope run, not unique aggregate coverage.
Each fix includes a before-proof, three independent verifier runs, a permanent
regression and successful server typecheck/build plus scoped lint.

| Finding | Change | Commit | Scope tests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F1037 | Recheck replica retention policy before each delete | `54f9e936` | 48 |
| F1038 | Reject truncated encrypted envelopes before opening output | `ee5b225a` | 186 |
| F1039 | Fill short S3 multipart reads; abort premature EOF | `b0432ce8` | 152 |
| F1040 | Cancel unused S3 cache-miss response bodies | `3a8e9e8d` | 86 |
| F1041 | Resolve Compose workspaces under a filesystem root | `8c6d71ab` | 126 |
| F1042 | Restore absent paths during failed system-import rollback | `9ceaf094` | 27 |
| F1043 | Give concurrent source uploads separate pending files | `1881b72f` | 35 |

F1039's first six-file scope run failed an existing real-timer slow-download
test; an unchanged repeat passed all 152 tests. Both logs are retained, and
this is not claimed to be a demonstrated failure on the base revision.

Additional passes produced no new confirmed defect: file-command input (74
tests), remote backup selection (114), cross-process locks (9), release records
(30), and panel upstream reachability/sleep callers (41). Source was not changed
for these passes. The lock implementation's documented residual stale-takeover
window is not claimed resolved.

Current-round evidence is selected under
[`.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/`](../.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/).
Ledger files record exact commands, failed attempts and environment boundaries.
Use `git log` to identify any later rounds before resuming. These focused
Windows checks do not replace the still-required full release gate, native Mac
DMG/Keychain checks, Linux installer checks or live Docker/provider acceptance.

### Optional native Linux-container probe regression

The continued audit also ran the real BusyBox probe on Windows Docker Desktop's
Linux engine. F1044 covers an uncommon compatibility edge: a server emitting
informational responses despite the probe's HTTP/1.0 request. The client now
reads through them to the final status; 101 protocol switching remains unready.
This is not a claim that compliant HTTP/1.0 servers normally send Early Hints.

With Linux Docker reachable and `busybox:1.36` already available locally, run
the committed integration test explicitly from the repository root:

```sh
pnpm exec vitest run --config .temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/F1044.integration.config.ts --reporter=verbose
```

The normal server suite excludes integration tests. This test creates only
UUID-named internal networks and fixture containers, publishes no host ports,
and removes its owned resources. Its fixture uses `--pull=never`; preload the
image intentionally before running on a fresh Mac. The independent native
verifier exercised seven final-status/error cases three times; 26 neighboring
unit tests passed. This does not exercise Electron or macOS Keychain.

### Further audit checkpoints through round 54

Additional committed evidence is under `.temp_files/audit_continuous_20261109/`:
