docs.markdown: # Node operations: readiness, metrics and logs Release target: 0.18.2. Readiness and log capabilities first shipped in the 0.17.0 agent; later additions below identify their required capabilities. Capability negotiation is authoritative; the panel and agent update independently. Update both to use the new node operations. ## Readiness Service → Settings → Healthcheck now offers two opt-in modes for plain Docker services, on the panel host or a node: | Mode | Verdict | | --- | --- | | Default (`http` or the existing NULL) | Existing behaviour, unchanged. On a node this checks stable container state and an image/command healthcheck when present. | | HTTP readiness (`http-strict`) | The configured path must return HTTP 2xx or 3xx. Redirects are not followed; a 4xx/5xx or missing response fails. | | TCP readiness (`tcp`) | The container's configured port must accept a TCP connection. This does not establish application readiness beyond that connection. | | Container running / command | Existing explicit modes, unchanged. | HTTP/TCP readiness requires a container port. A small `busybox:1.36` helper shares only the workload's network namespace, targets loopback, and publishes no port. It has a read-only root, no added capabilities, no mounts or credentials, and bounded CPU, memory, process count and execution time. Helpers are removed after an attempt, including failure. The first attempt may need the image pulled; operators can pre-pull it to avoid that startup delay. A remote agent must advertise `docker.probe`. The panel refuses unsupported opt-in probes at queue time and checks again before starting the container. Both new agent operations require sealed transport. Existing services keep their default mode until an operator changes it. Swarm and Compose retain their own healthcheck lifecycles; the new modes apply to plain Docker services. The node builder still checks crash loops and Docker health, then requires the readiness probe to pass before the new candidate can take traffic. Readiness is a deploy-time check, not a continuous availability monitor. ## Routing-load confirmation The next agent increment targets 0.18.2 and advertises `proxy.routingAck`. Routed primary-node deployments and fan-out targets require this live capability and sealed transport before changing routing; update the agent as well as the panel. There is no silent fallback to a file-write acknowledgement for these deployments. The managed routes and generation marker share one atomic dynamic file. The agent checks enabled definitions and the actual HTTP/TLS response generation through the proxy's loopback-only internal route, bounded to 15 seconds and 4 MiB per observation. Only a hash receipt crosses back to the panel. It does not accept a caller-selected container, command, API path or external address. If a dynamic-write response is lost or the load cannot be confirmed, either runtime may already receive traffic. A confirmed rollback allows candidate retirement; an unconfirmed rollback fails the deployment and keeps both generations. The deployment log identifies the retained candidate; resolve the proxy problem before manual cleanup. Ordinary fleet edits and unrouted workers keep their existing compatibility behavior. This is separate from workload readiness, and does not enable node canary or autoscaling. Fan-out applies explicit HTTP/TCP readiness and its configured timeout on each target, including the resolved container port of a source build. The target's previous generation stays live until readiness and routing-load confirmation pass, followed by a two-second request drain. Target updates check both the target generation and the primary runtime owner; stale work cannot restore a deleted/replaced target or publish after a service stop. A target failure is reported independently; the primary deployment and other targets continue. Routed fan-out with published host ports is refused before replacing a target; remove that host-port mapping to allow overlapping generations behind Traefik. Default node readiness remains container state unless HTTP/TCP is selected. ## Fan-out recovery after restart Routed fan-out targets also require the sealed `docker.recovery` capability (agent target 0.18.2). Migration 0097 adds a durable transition journal before image preparation or container creation. Each transition records both generation names and their immutable Docker IDs; managed service/deployment labels allow recovery of a candidate created immediately before a panel crash. Cleanup uses the recorded ID, so reusing a container name cannot delete another container. Only transitions begun with this journal are recovered. Older retained containers with no journal still require operator review; they are not adopted by guessing ownership from their names. The panel checks pending transitions one second after boot, then every minute. A live deploy/recovery holds a renewable 90-second lease. A replacement panel waits for that lease to expire. Failures retain both possible serving generations and back off from one minute to one hour. Settings → Fan-out recovery shows the reason and retry time. An operator can retry immediately; retry bypasses the backoff, never another active lease. Viewer access is read-only. Recovery reads the current target and service owner, repeats stable readiness (including explicitly configured HTTP/TCP probes), confirms loaded routing and drains requests before retiring an obsolete generation. An unhealthy, uncommitted candidate can roll back to a confirmed healthy previous generation. Once retirement is committed, recovery cannot roll back to that obsolete generation. Unknown identity, stopped services, changed owners and unavailable nodes retain their records for review; recovery never starts a stopped runtime. Removing a target preserves its journal until routing removal and both known generations can be confirmed. Explicit service or node deletion removes the journal through its foreign key; this mechanism does not promise orphan cleanup after those destructive operations. `GET /v1/services/:id/targets/recovery` returns pending entries to authorized service readers. Operator-only `POST` on the same path retries eligible entries and returns recovered/held counts plus remaining entries. SDK methods are `fanout.recovery(id)` and `fanout.retryRecovery(id)`. Recovery records expose neither lease tokens nor immutable container IDs. This increment covers routed fan-out Docker targets; primary-runtime cleanup, Swarm and canary/autoscaling remain separate work. Recorded Docker artifact fan-out uses the same journal and routing guards; see [artifact promotion](DEPLOYMENTS.md#docker-artifact-promotion-0171). ## Resource history The collector now samples the existing `agent.stats` operation for nodes hosting services. Node collection runs independently of local samples, at most once per collector cycle, with at most four requests in flight, bounded requests and shutdown cancellation. A failed node does not erase local samples or block the other nodes. Missing/malformed data stays unknown. CPU and memory for a node service are persisted in the same history and fed to the same alert rules as local services. Serving replicas are summed only when their complete sample is available. Host identity is part of the cache key: identically named containers on different Docker daemons never share a sample. The service metrics route retains its existing resource visibility checks. Monitoring's Local Host totals stay local; selecting a node uses the existing node-specific live endpoint. Samples from different hosts are never summed into the panel host's allocation figures. The published 0.17.0/0.17.1 releases retain 24 hours. The next observability increment adds opt-in 1–90 day history with rollups; see [resource history and export](OBSERVABILITY.md). Remote Swarm task aggregation, fan-out destination history and node-only database history remain separate work. ## Immutable controller resource samples (0.19.0 development) The development agent adds sealed `docker.metrics` for CPU/memory controller decisions. This is separate from the existing `agent.stats` history path and is not available in the published 0.18.2 agent. Requests bind an explicit node, service/deployment and up to ten full Docker IDs with expected names. The agent checks managed labels, running state, restart counts and configured resource limits before and after one bounded sample. CPU limits use NanoCPUs or the quota/period configuration; memory limits use HostConfig.Memory. An unlimited memory container reports a zero limit, never the host RAM as its allocation. The node owner can disable this read-only operation with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_CONTAINER_METRICS=off`. The capability disappears from the ping and the operation refuses execution. Older agents receive an update hint; current agents with the operation disabled receive an owner-disabled hint. Missing, duplicate, replaced, malformed or late samples remain unavailable. There is no fallback to panel-host statistics or names alone. Sampling uses one deadline, at most two concurrent samplers and at most 64 KiB per command. Run `pnpm smoke:container-metrics --image=ninedeploy-local:YOUR_LOCAL_BUILD` against a current built image. This creates an isolated Docker daemon with no host socket, a same-name panel decoy and disposable node workloads; it verifies configured limits and refusal after stop, generation mismatch and same-name replacement. All owned containers and their volumes are removed afterward. Node autoscaling and scale to zero remain unavailable until their fenced runtime, readiness, routing and recovery acceptance is complete. ## Ordered container lifecycle (0.19.0 development) The development agent adds the sealed `docker.lifecycle` operation for managed plain Docker containers. A command binds a service/deployment, an increasing revision, a request ID and up to ten full container IDs with expected names. The fixed actions are Start and Stop. The agent verifies ownership labels and the complete target set before any effect, addresses Docker by immutable ID, then verifies the result before returning its receipt. Application readiness and loaded routing remain separate controller steps. The accepted revision and semantic intent are committed before Docker runs. Each service has a private SQLite journal under the agent working directory: `.agent-work/.lifecycle/service-.sqlite`. The generated agent command mounts that working directory at `/var/lib/ninedeploy-agent` on both host and container. Preserve it when replacing the agent. The image's anonymous `/data` volume does not hold this ordering state. A newer accepted revision refuses older requests after restart; a conflicting reuse of a revision is refused. An exact retry returns the original receipt, which records completed work rather than a fresh readiness observation. An interrupted effect retains its accepted intent for the same retry or a newer command. Corrupt or unavailable storage is an error. SQLite write transactions serialize effects across agent processes sharing the same state directory. Other services have independent journals. One deadline includes queueing, storage and Docker calls. Pending work is bounded to 16; timed-out work holds its queue position until an already-started child drains. The node owner can disable the capability and operation with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_CONTAINER_LIFECYCLE=off`. `pnpm smoke:container-lifecycle --image=ninedeploy-local:YOUR_LOCAL_BUILD` uses the generated agent command's persistent working-directory layout, an isolated Docker daemon and independent agent processes. It exercises delayed Start after Stop, exact retry, concurrent Start/Stop, hard crash after a Docker effect, same-name replacement and owner-disabled refusal, then removes its owned containers and volumes. Current manual node lifecycle paths still use their existing operations. Panel command persistence, revision allocation and conversion of competing deploy/Stop/scale/wake callers remain R2 work. Node autoscaling and sleep stay unavailable until that integration, routing and recovery acceptance is complete. ## Log drains Node Docker/Compose primary runtimes and their named replicas are tailed through `docker.logsSince`, never through the panel host's Docker daemon. The agent must advertise this capability. Cursors include the node identity; moving a runtime cannot cause another host's logs to be treated as already delivered. New runtimes start without backfill. Each remote poll is bounded to 1,000 recent lines and 256 KiB (long lines may be clipped); PM2 files and secondary Compose services remain outside this path. The next observability increment replaces the volatile delivery cursor with an encrypted per-destination queue and durable cursor. Captured batches survive restarts and source-container removal, failed destinations retry independently, and full queues pause capture without evicting pending logs. Destination edits block existing batches from being sent to a different receiver. Source rotation before capture can still lose history. See [durable captured-log delivery](OBSERVABILITY.md#durable-captured-log-delivery) for limits, explicit discard, key rotation and CLI/API controls. ## Availability in the UI The Servers page and Docker deployment wizard show HTTP/TCP readiness, log drains, canary, autoscaling, scale to zero and file browser availability for the selected host. Fields omitted by an older panel are shown as unknown. This is a capability view; the deploy API revalidates the target when the job runs. For 0.18.2, node canary availability requires all five sealed-agent capabilities described in [Node canary](DEPLOYMENTS.md#node-canary-unreleased-0180), including owner-enabled proxy traffic observations. Per-service requirements are one replica, HTTP readiness, domain routing and no published host ports. Node autoscaling and scale to zero remain later R2 work. The live worker rechecks support before candidate launch; a cached availability indicator does not authorize deployment. ## Validation Run the normal workspace checks. The real-Docker smoke uses the current compiled agent and a disposable workload; it checks a TCP-open/HTTP-503 application stays unready, HTTP 200 passes, no host port is published, telemetry/logs contain the workload, and probe helpers are removed: ```sh pnpm build node scripts/smoke-node-operations.mjs --image=ninedeploy-local:YOUR_LOCAL_BUILD node scripts/smoke-multinode.mjs --image=ninedeploy-local:YOUR_LOCAL_BUILD --node-operations-only --no-swarm ``` On Windows the statistics operation runs in the supplied Linux NineDeploy image, with current compiled server/packages mounted read-only and the Docker socket. The script removes only its uniquely named workload. It does not certify upgrade, cross-host networking or a published release. The focused multi-node command uses separate panel and node Docker daemons. It checks the sealed deploy path, refuses an unready HTTP release while the previous release stays routed, reads persisted node memory through the API, and receives actual node logs at an HTTP drain. Other multi-node features, build packs and Swarm are outside this focused command. ## Following work from the platform comparison 1. Immutable release records: versioned Compose, configuration and encrypted environment snapshots; artifact-based approvals and CI checks before deploy. 2. Real restore-into-database drills, measured recovery time and preview data anonymisation/seed policies. 3. Remote Docker canary/autoscaling, the remaining node tools and private networking. 4. Authenticated HTTP MCP/OAuth and a reviewed AI proposal → validation → PR/apply → measured outcome flow. 5. Competitor migration previews, resource budgets/usage and cloud provisioning. These remain planned work, not capabilities delivered by this increment. 0.18.2 also journals routed plain-Docker **primary** node transitions (migration 0098). The same sealed recovery/routing capabilities and immutable-ID safety rules apply. The worker preserves journalled candidates across panel restart, and Settings exposes Primary runtime recovery with a lease-safe retry. Fresh readiness and loaded routing precede retirement; Stop, cancellation and changed placement remain authoritative. Recovery does not replay node builds, hooks or additional-node deployments. See [Deployments](DEPLOYMENTS.md#primary-docker-transition-recovery-unreleased-0180) for state choices and exclusions. ## Node container inspection and files (0.18.2) Service and database Manifest/Files views target their recorded node explicitly. Instance operators can inspect a container, generate its runtime Compose manifest and list/read/write/create/delete files through the sealed `docker.containerTools` capability. The agent resolves the container name once and uses its immutable Docker ID for the operation. Missing capabilities, unsealed transport, an unknown node or an unconfirmed response never fall back to the panel daemon. Node routes use `/v1/servers/:serverId/containers/:container`, with `/inspect`, `/compose`, `/files`, `/files/content` and `/files/dir` suffixes. An older panel returns 404 for this namespace. The local `/v1/containers` routes reject a host query rather than ignoring it. Node file reads and writes are limited to 1 MiB decoded content; wrapped base64 is normalized before transport. Oversized or unreadable files are refused without returning an editable partial/empty file. Directory metadata preserves exact whitespace in names and includes empty files. File operations still require the workload's usual shell/head/stat/find/base64 utilities and permissions. SDK container methods take an optional final `{ serverId }` argument. For example, `containers.inspect(name, { serverId: 7 })`, `containers.readFile(name, path, { serverId: 7 })` and `containers.writeFile(name, input, { serverId: 7 })`. CLI `services inspect ` and `services compose ` automatically use the service's host. Panel caches and editor state are separated by host, so identically named containers do not share file content. The node owner can disable these operations with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_CONTAINER_TOOLS=off`; the capability disappears from the sealed ping and the agent refuses the operation too. The Servers/wizard support view reports `features.containerTools`; an older panel omitting the flag remains unknown. Node-volume files and database Web Studio use the separate capabilities below. Node canary uses the separate [R1 requirements](DEPLOYMENTS.md#node-canary-unreleased-0180); node autoscaling and Swarm task file selection remain later runtime-parity work. ### Node volume files (0.18.2) Instance operators can browse, read, write, create directories and delete paths on a selected node through sealed `volume.files` / `volume.fileTool`. Routes use `/v1/servers/:serverId/volumes/:name/files`, with `/content` and `/dir` suffixes. The legacy panel-host file routes reject `?serverId`; an older panel returns 404 for the new namespace. There is no local fallback. The node owner can disable this capability with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_VOLUME_FILES=off`. Support views expose `features.volumeFiles`; update the agent to 0.18.2 when unavailable. These tools support existing managed volumes on Linux Docker's local driver without external driver options. Other drivers/options are refused with 422. A missing volume returns 404 and is never auto-created by browsing. The helper pins the selected volume through its first live bind and checks both metadata and the current device/inode through isolated read-only probes before and after the file operation. A changed identity returns 409. File operations cannot redirect that pinned bind into a replacement volume. Helpers mount only the selected volume, have bounded commands/lifetimes, and require nonce/immutable-ID ownership confirmation for cleanup. Unconfirmed cleanup is reported; helpers self-exit within 150 seconds after startup. Reads and writes allow at most 1 MiB decoded content. Binary bytes and whitespace in names are preserved, empty files are listed, and wrapped base64 is accepted. Oversized reads never return an editable partial file. Paths outside the volume and symlinks escaping it are refused; deleting a terminal symlink deletes that link itself. Operations are ordinary live filesystem edits: coordinate with the workload when editing data files. Volume snapshots retain their separate support boundary. The Volumes page host selector and a service's recorded host choose the file browser target. Host changes clear the editor and use distinct query caches. Unavailable nodes show the actual refusal with a retry action. SDK file methods take an optional final `{serverId}` argument. CLI examples: ```sh ninedeploy volumes files nd-svc-app-data --server 7 --json ninedeploy volumes read nd-svc-app-data config.json --server 7 --output config.json ninedeploy volumes write nd-svc-app-data config.json --server 7 --file config.json ninedeploy volumes mkdir nd-svc-app-data archive --server 7 ninedeploy volumes delete-file nd-svc-app-data archive --server 7 ``` CLI reads preserve exact binary stdout; `--output` refuses an existing local file unless `--force` is supplied. Delete prompts for the exact path unless `--yes` is explicit. `pnpm smoke:volume-files --image=` runs the actual helper CRUD/binary/limit/symlink/missing-volume controls on an owned Docker-in-Docker daemon. Public API, two-daemon isolation, CLI and browser acceptance are separate checks. ### Node database client terminals (0.18.2) The database Client action uses the recorded database ID and node. Operators can open PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Redis, Valkey, KeyDB and Dragonfly clients through `POST /v1/terminals` with `target: {kind: 'database', databaseId, mode: 'client'}`. The node needs `db.manage`, `db.client`, sealed terminal transport and its Docker Engine API. Support views expose `features.databaseClients`. Missing support returns a refusal before creating a client; there is no panel-host fallback. Unsupported engines retain the separate container Shell action. Preparation and attachment both recheck support. The agent verifies the managed-database labels, database ID, slug, running state and immutable container ID, then opens the fixed engine-specific command against that ID. Stored credentials travel only through the sealed channel and remain in the pending session's memory; client passwords use Docker exec environment variables rather than client command arguments. Terminal history and audit records do not contain the client payload. This does not change other database provisioning commands. The node owner can disable clients with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASE_CLIENTS=off`, or disable database operations with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASES=off`. Both preparation and attachment enforce these switches. An already prepared ticket cannot attach to a replacement container with the same name. Existing terminal authorization, single-use tickets, resize, termination and connection limits still apply. SDK `terminals.create` allows at least 60 seconds for database client creation; other terminal modes retain their normal timeout. Larger custom timeouts and an explicit disabled timeout remain respected. `onReady` confirms the terminal transport: automated interactive clients must also wait for their CLI prompt and each command's response. The panel title identifies the node. Database Web Studio is described below. `pnpm smoke:database-clients --image=` runs actual API and SDK queries against all seven default engine images on owned Docker-in-Docker hosts, including password refusal, same-name local/node isolation, old-agent refusal, owner switches, single-use tickets and container replacement controls. `--case=postgres` or `--case=engines --engine=keydb` narrows the run. This smoke does not certify every engine version, browser behavior or the full release matrix. ## Node database Web Studio (0.18.2) An operator can launch Adminer for PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB or Redis Commander for Redis/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly from the database page. Both the panel and node agent must support sealed `db.studio`; an old or owner-disabled agent is refused with an actionable message. `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASE_STUDIOS=off` disables Studio on that node; `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASES=off` disables it with other database operations. The helper uses the verified private database bridge, resolved image identity and fixed internal port, with no published host port. Access uses the panel-origin proxy in a separate noopener tab. SQL driver/server/user/database defaults contain no password; SQL Studio still asks for the database password. A node Studio request never falls back to a local helper. The standard bootstrap keeps its default Docker bridge. For private Studio access, the agent connects its own verified container to the database bridge with a lower gateway priority, preserving its original outbound route. This automatic attachment needs Docker Engine API 1.48 or newer. The agent identifies itself through Docker's default container-ID hostname; customized hostnames need an operator-provided compatible network arrangement. Native/host-network agents and existing manual connections are left unchanged. Stop removes only the endpoint carrying this Studio resource's ownership alias after confirming the helper is gone. A preparing receipt is durable. If preparation or cleanup cannot be confirmed, retry from the same database page or use Stop Studio; the panel retains the receipt until confirmed node cleanup. Database stop/restart/recreate/delete share the lifecycle lock and confirm Studio cleanup first. A busy operation returns 409 rather than queueing another browser mutation. Explicit forced record deletion reports possible node orphans. SDK `databases.startStudio` permits at least 240 seconds and returns `port: null` on a node. Stop permits at least 270 seconds to include an outstanding preparation and cleanup. Larger configured budgets and `timeoutMs: 0` retain their meanings. Browser requests include the path-scoped Studio cookie. The cookie follows the authenticated API key or login session; deletion, expiry, individual revocation, loss of operator scope/access, token-version changes and the instance epoch invalidate it. Reopen existing Studio tabs after this upgrade. All seven supported engines passed real default-bootstrap browser data workflows and the uncached local matrix. An earlier opaque browser exception remains unreproduced; vendor Studio pages retain their narrow-screen layout limitations. Release artifact certification and publication status are tracked in [Competitive delivery](COMPETITIVE_DELIVERY.md). ## Database resource telemetry (0.18.2) The database page requests `/v1/stats?databaseId=`. The response is access-scoped, excludes host metrics and other containers, and identifies the database and its recorded node. Database-only nodes are collected too. Samples older than 90 seconds, failed or missing samples, and stopped databases are never displayed as live zero metrics. The panel distinguishes waiting, unavailable, stale and stopped states and can retry. The SDK requires the scoped resource receipt; an older panel that ignores the filter must be upgraded. The unfiltered stats endpoint retains its panel-host behavior. ## Agent capacity and readiness budgets (0.18.2) Sealed agent calls honor a canonical positive Retry-After of 1–60 seconds on HTTP 429, with at most two retries and one original request deadline. The encrypted request and nonce are reused; already-executed requests remain protected by replay refusal. Unsupported headers, other HTTP failures, transport errors and legacy plaintext calls are not retried. Cancellation also stops a capacity wait. The agent operation route permits at most 1,000 requests/minute. Invalid authentication/validation retains a separate 120/minute rejection response budget, including concurrent failures; unrelated peers have independent buckets. The panel request limits, sealed authentication, nonce replay checks and original request deadlines remain in force. Remote readiness RPCs and diagnostic log retrieval share the remaining readiness deadline. Replies arriving after it cannot admit a candidate. HTTP/TCP readiness still requires explicit configuration; container-state readiness alone does not establish HTTP application readiness. Packaged Docker health uses the configured `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PORT` and `/agent/ping` for agent role, or `NINEDEPLOY_PORT` and `/health` for panel role. ## Public access to a node database A database on a node can be reached from outside on a port of that node, the same way as one on the panel host: **Database → Settings → Public access**, or `PUT /v1/databases/:id/public-access`. Operators only, behind a required IP allow-list. How it works: - The node's agent runs the same sidecar as the panel host: a Traefik container `nd-dbpub-` that publishes one port of the node and proxies TCP to the database. - The sidecar joins only the database's own bridge `nd-dbnet-`, never the node's shared network, so it reaches that database and nothing else. - Before it proxies anything, the agent checks that `nd-db-` is the managed database with that id. - Its configuration lives under the agent's home (`dbproxy/`). It restarts with the node's Docker. Clients connect to the node's address. The credentials' `publicConnectionString` uses it. Limits on a node: - **TLS end to end only (`tlsMode: none`).** The certificates are on the panel, so `terminate` is refused (`422 unsupported_tls_mode`). The client and the database still negotiate TLS between themselves. - **Ports.** The port may not be the agent's port, 80, 443 or 22. It may not be a port a service on that node publishes. As on the panel host, it must differ from every other database's public port. - **No panel reconcile.** The panel's reconcile does not restart a node's sidecar; the node's Docker restarts it. - **Turning off needs the node.** Turning access off is refused while the node cannot confirm it (`502 node_unreachable`), because the port would stay open. Deleting the database removes the sidecar on a best-effort basis. Requires agent 0.18.11 or newer (`db.publicAccess`) and a sealed transport. The node owner turns it off with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PUBLIC_DATABASES=off`; `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASES=off` turns it off together with every other node database feature. ## PgBouncer for a node database A postgres database on a node can have the same PgBouncer sidecar as one on the panel host: **Database → Settings → PgBouncer**, or `POST /v1/databases/:id/pgbouncer/enable` (database admin). How it works on a node: - The node's agent runs `nd-pgb-` on the database's own bridge `nd-dbnet-`. Services attached to the database are on that bridge too. - It publishes no port of the node. Attached services connect to `nd-pgb-:6432`, or to the port you chose; the pooled connection string names it. - Before creating the sidecar, the agent checks that `nd-db-` is the running managed database with that id. - The database password travels only in a sealed request. The config is copied into the container, and the temporary files are deleted at once. Turning it off, or deleting the database, is refused while the node cannot confirm the sidecar is gone (`502 node_unreachable`, `502 node_pgbouncer_cleanup_unconfirmed`); `?force=true` on the delete names what was left. Requires agent 0.18.12 or newer (`db.pgbouncer`) and a sealed transport. The node owner turns it off with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PGBOUNCER=off`; `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_DATABASES=off` turns it off together with every other node database feature. ## OS security updates (G4.2) Operators can see each host's pending package updates and turn automatic **security** updates on or off: - **Panel host:** Settings → System → *OS security updates*. - **A node:** Servers → node panel. The card reads nothing until you press **Check updates**: every read runs a short-lived helper container on the host. **What it shows** - the distribution and package manager; - the pending updates, security ones first; - whether automatic security updates are on; - whether the host is waiting for a reboot and, on Debian or Ubuntu, which packages asked for it. **Refresh package lists** runs `apt-get update` or `dnf --refresh` first. **What switching it on does** | Package manager | On | Off | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | apt (Debian, Ubuntu) | Installs `unattended-upgrades` if it is missing. Writes `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades` (periodic list updates and unattended upgrades). Writes `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52ninedeploy-no-reboot`, which sets `Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "false"`. The distribution's default origins are its security pockets. | Rewrites `20auto-upgrades` with unattended upgrades set to `0`. The package stays installed. | | dnf (Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma) | Installs `dnf-automatic` (or `dnf5-plugin-automatic`) if it is missing. Sets `upgrade_type = security` and `apply_updates = yes` in `/etc/dnf/automatic.conf`. Enables the `dnf-automatic.timer` (or `dnf5-automatic.timer`). | Disables the timer. | Other package managers (Alpine, Arch, SUSE) are reported as unsupported; nothing is changed there. **Never a reboot.** NineDeploy does not reboot a host and turns unattended-upgrades' own automatic reboot off. The card shows **Reboot required** when the host reports it: - on Debian or Ubuntu, from `/var/run/reboot-required`; - on dnf hosts, from `needs-restarting -r`. Without it, the card says the host cannot tell. Plan reboots yourself. **How it runs** Each action is a fixed script, picked by name. Nothing a caller sends reaches a shell. - The script runs in a privileged helper with `--pid=host` that enters PID 1's namespaces with `nsenter -t 1`, the same helper as host shells. - The image is `NINEDEPLOY_HOST_SHELL_IMAGE`, or else the proxy image that is already on the host. - On a node, the agent runs it through the sealed op `host.packages`. The node's owner can refuse it with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_HOST_PACKAGES=off`; the panel then answers `403 node_feature_disabled`. - An agent older than 0.18.6 gets `422 node_agent_outdated`. - One action runs per host at a time; a second one answers `409 os_updates_busy`. **Routes and audit** (operator only): - `GET /v1/os-updates[?refresh=1]` and `POST /v1/os-updates/auto {enabled}` for the panel host; - `GET /v1/servers/:serverId/os-updates[?refresh=1]` and `POST /v1/servers/:serverId/os-updates/auto {enabled}` for a node. Switching is audited as `os_updates.auto_enable` or `os_updates.auto_disable`. ## Move a service with its data (G3.1) `PATCH /v1/services/:id { serverId }` moves only the configuration: the next deploy starts the service on the new host with an empty volume. **Service → Settings → Move with data** (`POST /v1/services/:id/move`, operators) also moves the data: 1. The service must be stopped, with no deployment running and no extra volume attachments. Its primary volume `nd-svc--data` must be on the current host. Docker services and compose stacks; Swarm and PM2 are refused. 2. The host change is that same PATCH, with every check it makes: attached databases stay on their host, and a volume of the same name already on the target is refused. 3. The volume is archived on the source, created on the target and restored there. Node archives travel over the agent's sealed stream channel, which checks the size and sha256 end to end. The temporary archive under the backups directory is deleted afterwards. 4. The service is deployed on the target. The request answers 202 at once. `GET /v1/services/:id/move` reports `copying`, then `deploying`, then `done` with the deployment id, or `failed` with the reason. After a failed copy the service stays on the target, undeployed; moving it back is a plain host change, because the source volume is never deleted. Remove the old volume from the Volumes page once the service runs on the target. The state is the settings row `service_move:`; there is no migration. A **compose stack** moves every named volume compose created for it, `ndcmp-_` (found by compose's own `com.docker.compose.project` label), one after the other; `GET …/move` lists them in `volumes` and counts them in `copied`. Each one is created on the target with compose's project and volume labels, so the stack's `up` there adopts it. A stack with a volume that has a fixed `name:` is refused (`move_fixed_volume_names`), because that volume would be left behind. External volumes and bind mounts are not moved. A node on either end needs agent 0.18.7 or newer with the `volume.compose` capability; its owner can turn it off with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_VOLUME_COMPOSE=off`. The agent transfers such a volume only when Docker says compose created it for the project its name starts with.

# Node request-rate autoscaling implementation plan

Status: agent observation accepted; panel adapter and durable observation consumption implemented, controller integration pending. Memory autoscaling has real single-node and PostgreSQL acceptance; those results do not accept request-rate autoscaling.

Schema contract: `servingTrafficOpen` and `servingTrafficSnapshot` model ordinary serving generations separately from canary steps. Validation rejects missing/duplicate/wrong-generation replicas, unsupported fields, invalid source/counter shapes and incomplete coverage declared complete. All 802 schema tests in 40 files passed locally.

Agent observation acceptance — 2026-11-01: development source `7716cf93099e8c374ed1c1e175ce6c012b19f77e` implements separately sealed `proxy.servingTraffic.open/sample/finish/close` operations. It reuses the bounded reservation/log engine with a serving-only counter, without synthetic canary targets or altered canary operands/receipts. The node owner must opt in through `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PROXY_TRAFFIC`; the capability's planned release floor is 0.19.0. Serving elapsed time follows the observed sequence markers, excluding verification after the end marker. The delayed-verification regression failed before that timing adjustment.

[Hosted Docker/Traefik run 41323263997](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41323263997) passed all nine observation controls through the actual sealed HTTP agent. Independent inspection recomputed request/target/routing hash bindings from immutable fixture identities: 20 serving requests counted, five unrelated requests excluded, all 25 HTTP responses successful, both replicas served, and a separately completed zero-traffic window was verified. Loaded but unrouted configuration, proxy restart, changed routing, stopped replica, plaintext and owner-disable controls refused observation. No active windows remained and all five owned resources were removed. The first fixture looked for the panel's default proxy during a node recheck; the corrected helper uses the observed node proxy ID for both HTTP and HTTPS. Its regression failed before the fix while the panel-default control passed. Evidence: `.temp_files/rps-serving/hosted-green-41323263997/independent-verification.json`.

[Full CI 41323263845](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41323263845) passed 17,854 tests in 1,130 files, real Docker/PostgreSQL integration and the complete Docker/runtime job on the same source head. The local eight-file routing/deployment admission suite passed 112 tests; the routing-helper/smoke/matrix suite passed 13 tests. Five deployment/routing boundary regressions failed before the additional admission checks. Server typecheck, targeted lint and actionlint passed. The hosted-only observation smoke is mandatory in normal CI and future versioned images. This is source/agent observation evidence, not a numbered release, production cutover or RPS scaling acceptance.

The same final-head CI's normal-deploy artifact independently retained 1,892 HTTP 200 responses across HTTP, strict HTTP, TCP, running and command readiness, with previous and replacement responses in every trace and confirmed owned cleanup. Evidence: `.temp_files/rps-serving/ci-panel-health-41323263845/independent-verification.json`. This is isolated Host-header HTTP acceptance, not production DNS/TLS certification.

The agent portions of steps 1–2 below are implemented and observed. Step 3 has a private panel adapter and real SQLite-backed boundary tests; its transport boundary is mocked in those tests. Steps 4–6 now include durable one-use observation consumption, per-serving-replica RPS calculation, decision/controller integration, capability-gated capacity preparation and support reporting. `NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING_ACCEPTED` in `lib/autoscaler.ts` is true after the hosted 1→2→1 and source-loss acceptance in [CI 41464316996](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41464316996). That run completed successfully on `31c598ec4901963b963a1a5558580e02b1c15a1b`; subsequent development still needs its own final-source certification. This acceptance does not enable node sleep/wake or complete the wider R2 matrix.

Panel adapter implementation — 2026-11-01: `openNodeServingTraffic` accepts the selected running deployment, with matching immutable capacity, serving count and port. Before and after awaited operations it checks runtime ownership, service configuration, database bridges, queued/building/deploying work, lifecycle intents, preparation and transition journals, and the current node routing render. It refuses fanout because a node-local counter cannot measure traffic served elsewhere. Sealed capability preflight is followed by another context check before reservation. Snapshot binding retains request, target, source, proxy, routing, epoch and sequence identities; unavailable or regressing coverage is never substituted with zero.

Cancellation closes known windows even while idle; cleanup uses its own bounded call without the cancelled signal. A total observation deadline supplements the agent's existing expiry. Overlapping calls are refused, returned snapshots cannot mutate internal continuity checks, and a successful final receipt closes the client. Invalid unbound opening receipts are never used to close a foreign window; unknown reservations remain subject to agent expiry.

Local panel-adapter validation: 190 tests passed across eight files, including 52 new adapter cases against migrated in-memory SQLite. The suite covers real routing rendering and runtime-owner changes, sealed capability refusal, database placement changes, deployment/Stop conflicts, idle/in-flight cancellation, overlap, foreign receipts, unavailable sources and mutable receipt isolation. Server typecheck and targeted lint passed. Local Docker was not accessed (`DOCKER_HOST=tcp://127.0.0.1:9`). These focused checks do not certify a new release or hosted RPS scaling.

Durable consumption implementation — 2026-11-01: migration `0119_node_serving_traffic_receipts` retains consumed request/window identities per deployment. Finishing a panel observation now persists its bound completed receipt before returning it. A transaction rechecks runtime ownership/capacity and rejects duplicate request/window IDs and counter intervals at or below the source's retained high watermark. Source watermarks apply across agent epochs; a new proxy source may start a new sequence without forgetting the previous source. Canonical uint64 counters are stored as fixed-width decimal text and ordered through a covering source index, without floating-point conversion. The housekeeping step `serving-traffic-receipts` deletes a receipt 7 days after consumption unless it is the newest for its service, node and source; that row holds the high watermark, so an older interval stays refused after its own row is gone. Every row also cascades with its deployment or service.

Consumption checks the panel-captured observation interval and sample freshness before validation, before writing and before returning. Routing is checked before and after the transaction; an intervening change may spend a receipt but cannot return decision evidence. The per-replica rate is `serving.requests * 1000 / elapsedMs / serving.length`; a fully verified zero remains distinguishable from unavailable coverage. The next controller step must bind these records into durable autoscale admission and reset sustained decision windows when source, owner, route, configuration or replicas change. Persisting an observation does not itself authorize a scale mutation.

Validation of this increment: 219 focused tests passed in nine server files and all 76 database tests passed in 30 files. A new adapter replay regression failed on the previous panel adapter because its second instance accepted the same completed window. The fixed path rejects it. A separate-process SQLite fixture verifies persistence across actual process restarts and that two independent clients accept only one competing consumption; its temporary files are removed after the processes exit. Migration tests upgrade an existing deployment, retain data, verify uniqueness/cascade behavior and prove the covering-index query plan. Typecheck, targeted lint and a no-schema-drift generation check passed. Full hosted acceptance of this new increment is still required.

The preceding panel-adapter head `2fcfcbbf390bca48f56cbab2a38f7cf92e43b166` separately passed [hosted observation run 41334052103](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41334052103): nine real sealed-agent/Docker/Traefik cases, both immutable replicas, verified zero, 25 HTTP 200 responses, no remaining windows and five owned resources removed. Hash bindings were independently recomputed. This exercises the agent observation path, not the new consumption ledger or RPS scaling.

The same preceding head's [full CI 41334052085](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41334052085) finished with Docker/runtime and Docker/PostgreSQL integration passing, but source tests failed solely because `nodeServingTrafficContext.ts` was missing from the static Swarm runtime-reader inventory: 17,907 tests passed and one failed. The module already rejects Swarm before agent contact. Adding its documented classification reproduced red/green locally; all 65 Swarm/adapter tests passed on corrected panel head `88753950`. Full CI was restarted; the failed run is not full certification. Its independently checked normal-deploy trace contains 1,916 HTTP 200 responses across all five readiness modes, with previous and replacement responses in every mode and owned cleanup confirmed. Evidence: `.temp_files/rps-serving/ci-panel-health-41334052085/independent-verification.json`.

## Confirmed boundaries

- Ordinary serving observations require matching deployment labels and a managed HTTP load-balancer route containing exactly the selected replica URLs. Missing routes, another generation, incomplete leaf sets and weighted canary routes refuse observation rather than returning zero. Maintenance bypass routing is held; the HTTP twin is counted when it actually reaches a selected leaf. Five new Docker-boundary assertions failed before these admission checks; the covering eight-file suite passed 112 tests after the change. The nine-case hosted follow-up includes a loaded but unrouted configuration control.

- `engine/builders/nodeAutoscaleDeployment.ts` prepares RPS capacity only after a sealed `proxy.servingTraffic` capability check (step 5, 2026-11-02). Older agents are refused with a `measure node request rate` reason before any effect. The deploy pipeline also requires the capability before it selects the capacity path for an RPS service, and keeps RPS services on the existing deployment path while `NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING_ACCEPTED` is false.
- Hosted acceptance (2026-11-02): CI and the release workflow run `scripts/smoke-node-canary.mjs --autoscale-rps-only` with default panel settings: public API and sealed agent on isolated daemons, with 1→2 under load and 2→1 on measured low traffic. A source-loss control restarts the agent with `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PROXY_TRAFFIC=off`, then holds for 90 s with a null value and no scale-down despite low traffic. Every routed request must return 200.  Its first hosted run (41457498775) timed out on scale-up with 14,628 requests, all HTTP 200. The decision generation included `targetHash`, which hashes the whole request including its unique `requestId`. Every window therefore restarted the sustained window. The generation now leaves it out; serving identities and `routingGeneration` still bind each window. A decider regression that varies `targetHash` per window failed before the fix. After that fix, [CI 41464316996](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41464316996) passed: 1→2 at 23.5 rps per replica, the source loss held 2 replicas for 90 s with no value, then 2→1 at 0.6 rps. All 6,232 requests returned 200, and both immutable replicas served. `NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING_ACCEPTED` is now true; a temporary panel preview variable used for this run was removed. Setting the constant false withdraws node RPS from the pipeline, the worker and every reported surface.
- Step 6 (2026-11-02): `GET /v1/services/:id/autoscale` returns `supportedMetrics` from `autoscaleSupportedMetrics` in `lib/autoscaler.ts`, which also holds the gate. With acceptance withdrawn, a node service with `rps` reports `node request-rate autoscaling is not available yet` with a null value and desired count, never a pending evaluation or zero. With the accepted gate on, RPS is included in node-supported metrics. The panel card disables an unsupported metric unless it is the stored one. The CLI lists "Metrics here" and warns when `autoscale set` stores a metric that does not act. Flipping the gate updates every surface.
- `lib/nodeAutoscaleWorker.ts` holds RPS while `NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING_ACCEPTED` is false. The capacity-preparation check alone is not enough: capacity prepared under cpu or memory stays valid when the metric is switched to rps without a redeploy. Turn the gate on after step 6 and the hosted smoke.
- `lib/requestRate.ts` is a panel-local analytics counter. It cannot attest a remote proxy source, loaded routing configuration or immutable serving replicas.
- `lib/nodeProxyTrafficClient.ts` requires an unfinished canary deployment. A selected running deployment is deliberately refused.
- The existing `proxyTrafficOpen` contract still requires stable/canary sets and a canary step. Ordinary observations use the separate `servingTrafficOpen` contract and capability.
- `lib/nodeProxyTrafficDocker.ts` already verifies immutable container identities, proxy restart identity and loaded HTTP/HTTPS routing. Preserve these checks in the new observation path.

## Ordered implementation

1. Add a separate, capability-advertised serving-traffic observation contract. Bind node, service, selected deployment, immutable serving targets, loaded routing generation and a unique observation request. Keep existing canary requests and receipts compatible. Do not invent a candidate or reuse a canary step for ordinary traffic.
2. Reuse bounded proxy log transport and request-sequence markers. Count only requests attributed to the selected serving leaves. Return completed coverage, elapsed duration, source/proxy identity and target/routing hashes. Missing logs, attribution, sequence boundaries, capability or owner opt-in must hold scaling; they must never become zero RPS.
3. Add the panel adapter with before/after placement and runtime-owner checkpoints. Accept selected running deployments, reject queued deploy/lifecycle conflicts, changed targets, routing, database topology and source restarts. Close windows on cancellation and failure; preserve the agent's bounded expiry backstop.
4. Feed completed fresh windows into the existing durable autoscale admission/controller. Compute requests per second per serving replica. Reset sustained scale windows across source, route, owner, target, config and serving-count changes. Reject repeated receipts, incomplete coverage and stale or future samples.
5. Permit RPS capacity preparation only after the required serving-traffic capability is confirmed. Retain old-agent refusals, immutable spare preparation, readiness, route confirmation, drain ordering and database attachment fencing.
6. Expose precise held reasons and accurate supported metrics through the existing API/panel/SDK/CLI surfaces. Do not report unsupported RPS as a live zero measurement.

## Required evidence

- Contract and agent tests: running-generation observations, unrelated service traffic exclusion, missing markers, log loss/rotation, malformed attribution, proxy restart, replaced replica and stale routing refusal.
- Panel and decision tests: sustained up/down windows, duplicated receipts, owner/deploy/Stop races, cancellation cleanup, no traffic versus unavailable source, capability-disabled and older-agent controls.
- Public API smoke on an isolated GitHub runner: create RPS-configured capacity, generate controlled proxy load, observe one-to-two scale-up, reduce load, observe two-to-one scale-down, prove both immutable replicas served, and retain continuous HTTP outcomes and cleanup evidence. Include a source-loss control that holds scaling.
- Repeat with PostgreSQL readiness, then add the accepted scenarios to candidate-image release gates. Run the final uncached release matrix on the final code revision. No local Docker access is required for this plan.

## Decision integration — 2026-11-02

`lib/nodeServingTrafficSample.ts` opens one 10-second window per autoscale tick on the serving replicas named by the deployment's capacity receipt (`node_autoscale_capacity`), at the service port, against the node's current routing render, then finishes and consumes it. A refusal at any point throws and holds the tick; it never becomes a zero reading. A service without a routed domain is refused before a window opens. The window is always closed.

`lib/nodeAutoscaleWorker.ts` reads that sample for `metric: rps` and the container-metrics sample for cpu and memory. `measureNodeServingTraffic` accepts only a complete, fresh receipt bound to the node, service, selected deployment and exact serving names, and computes `requests * 1000 / elapsedMs / replicas`. `lib/nodeAutoscaleDecision.ts` runs it through the same sustained window as cpu and memory. The window restarts when the replica set, proxy source, proxy, agent epoch, routing generation or target hash changes. A repeated receipt does not advance it. The receipt's request ID and serving identities become the admission evidence, so `admitNodeAutoscale` and the controller are unchanged.

Tests: `test/lib/nodeAutoscaleDecision.test.ts` (sustained up, verified zero scaling down, window reset per identity, repeated, incomplete, foreign and stale receipts), `test/lib/nodeServingTrafficSample.test.ts` (window inputs, close on refusal, Swarm/placement/capacity/route refusals) and `test/lib/nodeAutoscaleController.test.ts` (an RPS decision completes through durable admission and the controller; a refused window holds with no transition).

docs.markdown:
# Node scale to zero and wake (R2)

## Standalone catcher collection — local development checkpoint, 2026-11-08

The production sleeper's `recoverCatchers` poller also discovers never-bound candidates on nodes with an already persisted wake credential and no sleeping cohort. Collection runs after demand scheduling, at most one job at a time, with a five-minute interval per node. It creates neither a wake credential nor a replacement catcher. Unsupported, unsealed or opted-out agents are refused before a fresh admission barrier is created.

A durable `collecting` maintenance phase blocks new sleep/wake admission while bounded, exact-key inventory is retained as retirement-only identities without service metadata. The existing ordered loaded-routing acknowledgement, drain and immutable-ID retirement fence still govern every removal. Lost replies keep targets in the journal for replay after restart, including targets absent from the next inventory. A foreign-key container is not an inventory member. The existing 64-entry inventory and 256-member retained-snapshot limits still apply; uncertainty holds the journal. Ordinary sleeping-cohort maintenance keeps its readiness and replacement requirements.

This extends the existing text phase and JSON snapshot representation without a SQL migration. An older panel refuses the unfamiliar phase rather than completing the barrier. Local component and native collection evidence are distinct from hosted automatic idle/Stop/wake acceptance and publication; those broader requirements remain open.

## Lost preparation replies — local development checkpoint, 2026-11-07

Catcher maintenance now requires the separately advertised, sealed `wake.catcher.inventory` operation before preparing another generation. An agent without that capability keeps maintenance held until upgraded; ordinary demand polling and wake retain their existing requirements.

Inventory reads at most 64 managed catcher identities for the exact node wake key, including older images and stopped candidates. It never starts or removes a container. The panel records unknown identities as retirement-only members of its durable maintenance intent before preparing again. Actual retirement still requires readiness, confirmed ordered routing, drain and the agent's immutable-ID fence. An uncertain or incomplete inventory holds the operation. More than 64 inventory entries or 256 retained snapshot members requires operator review.

This closes the lost-reply/image-change identity gap within an existing maintenance intent. Standalone collection without a sleeping cohort is described above. Local tests and native Docker/sealed-HTTP inventory checks are separate from hosted end-to-end retirement, upgrade and release acceptance; those broader gates remain required.

Current release checkpoint: [v0.18.17](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/releases/tag/v0.18.17) was published from `91017c3405398666aa78f168751e0baa62a9b42f`. Its [release run](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41666599464) completed with all nine runtime cohorts and 18,373 source tests passing. The sleep/wake cohort passed on attempt 2; the unchanged image also passed [isolated automatic acceptance](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41683897308). The first automatic idle/Stop timeout remains unresolved. Preserve that failed attempt alongside the passing evidence.

## Diagnose an automatic idle timeout

Run the original manual-wake → lost-routing-acknowledgement → automatic-sleep sequence on one isolated GitHub-hosted runner, using an immutable published image:

```sh
gh workflow run serving-traffic.yml --repo ninedeploy/ninedeploy --ref main -f sleep_cohort=true -f immutable_image=ghcr.io/ninedeploy/ninedeploy@sha256:c19bafb5a4c04508994b4ce3009319dc15dd1882233a509e40ac6b88be2d1dd0
```

The diagnostic job retains the original per-case deadlines (15/12/20 minutes) and real five-minute idle requirement. It pulls the digest without rebuilding. Its script revision and the image's embedded source revision are separate identities and must both be recorded.

Download the `automatic-sleep-cohort-<run-id>` artifact. The automatic case includes bounded public status observations, a journal snapshot after the actual Stop, traffic/audit records and owned cleanup. On failure, `automatic-sleep-failure.json` records the automatic journal phase, idle decision age, remaining lease and a fixed reason class. Raw exception text, wake keys, worker tokens and agent credentials are excluded. Failure to collect diagnostics preserves the original test failure.

Automatic transitions live in `nodeSleepTransitions`; `/lifecycle` reports manual intents. Use the automatic journal to distinguish missing idle coverage, expiry before Stop, restoration and failed wake readiness. These diagnostics read the owned fixture's state and preserve the production timers and readiness checks. Local Docker execution remains refused by the smoke's hosted-runner guards.

## Historical pre-release checkpoints

Status, 2026-11-03: durable node authority, ordered sleep/wake effects, guarded demand and staged catcher retirement have component acceptance. The [two-service cohort 41616036959](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41616036959) passed actual five-minute idle, Stop/Start, failed strict HTTP readiness, new-process recovery, Basic Auth/IP denials, agent opt-out and Stop during wake, with 2,328 valid responses. The [pre-Stop transport fault 41627779632](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41627779632) restored the application after a lost real loaded-routing acknowledgement, with 640 valid responses. The latest [public automatic-cycle cohort 41634736108](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41634736108) passed ordinary API settings, production timers, genuine idle after a real traffic reset, automatic Stop, readiness-held demand wake and panel restart, with 791 valid responses and settled audit events. All three had zero 502/connection errors. The public automatic candidate passed all required [CI 41643863613](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41643863613) and serving-traffic checks on frozen head `65d15f69f71eb0e63e59dd1600e7455089e331a8`. [PR #25](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/pull/25) merged to main as `977390d7279268b3ab8dffd0dde133fa40668c01`; normal main plugin timers now activate eligible configured nodes. It is not in a numbered release. Manual Sleep now continues to refuse node placement. Final combined release/upgrade/artifact checks remain open. Sections below retain exact source identities; [DEPLOYMENTS.md](DEPLOYMENTS.md) documents the released activation limit.

## Why the panel-host mechanism does not carry over

- **Idle evidence.** The panel host counts requests from its own Traefik access log (traffic analytics). A node's access log never reaches the panel. The node serving-traffic windows used by RPS autoscaling ([NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING.md](NODE_RPS_AUTOSCALING.md)) are bounded reservations of at most 60 s with gaps between them. A zero there proves only that window was idle, not the minutes before it. Sleeping on that would stop a service that is in use.
- **Wake path.** A sleeping panel-host domain routes to the panel's own wake endpoint (`/_nd/wake`, `modules/wake.ts`) over the local Docker network. On a node, the panel calls the agent and the agent never calls the panel. A node proxy cannot assume a route to the panel, and the panel's Traefik does not know node domains.

## Decisions

1. **Continuous idle watch (new sealed agent operations).** `proxy.idleWatch.open/sample/finish/close` is a separately advertised capability under the existing owner opt-in `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PROXY_TRAFFIC=on`. It reuses the serving-window engine with `purpose: 'idle'` and windows of 1 minute to 1 hour (`idleWatchOpen`). A window counts requests to the selected serving leaves continuously between its start and end sequence markers. The engine releases a window that is not sampled within 30 s, so the panel samples every 15 s; that is the lease. Because `sleepAfterMinutes` can reach 24 hours, the panel chains windows. It opens the next window before finishing the previous one, so the next start counter is below the previous end counter, and requires the same source, proxy and agent epoch. Overlapping chained receipts therefore leave no unobserved gap. A proxy restart, source change, routing change, lease lapse, agent restart or any refusal ends coverage, and the idle clock starts again. A service sleeps only after a verified zero count over continuous coverage of `sleepAfterMinutes`. Unavailable coverage never counts as idle, the same rule RPS uses.
2. **Node wake catcher.** The agent prepares private generation names, `ninedeploy-wake-g-<nonce>`, on the node's `ninedeploy` network. A previous selected catcher is retained through stable readiness, ordered route acknowledgement and retirement proof; names fenced as retired are never reused. Legacy `ninedeploy-wake` remains a compatibility identity. Each catcher runs the agent's own pinned image with no host mounts or Docker socket. It answers valid keyed requests with the "waking up" page: `503`, `Retry-After`, a self-reloading HTML body and HEAD support. Opaque wake tokens map to services only on the panel. Bounded demand counters emit bounded Docker-log records, and reads bind the immutable container plus its current process start time.
3. **Routing.** A sleeping node domain routes to the catcher after the domain's own middlewares, so basic auth and IP allow lists still run before anything wakes, as on the panel host. Routes are written through the panel-rendered node dynamic config and confirmed with `proxy.routingAck` before any container stops.
4. **Wake.** For each node with sleeping services, the panel polls the sealed `wake.demand` operation every 2 s. On demand it acquires the service runtime owner and starts the recorded serving count by immutable ID through the ordered node lifecycle. It then waits for readiness, restores the routes with routing confirmation, and records `service.wake`. The visitor's page reloads into the app. A cross-host redirect is not used, because a non-GET body cannot be replayed anyway.
5. **Sleep effect order.** Sleep follows a strict sequence:
   1. reserve the runtime owner;
   2. switch routes to the catcher;
   3. confirm routing;
   4. stop the serving members by immutable ID with a sleep intent, distinct from Stop;
   5. record `service.sleep`.
   
   A failure at any step before the containers stop restores the routes, and the service stays awake.
6. **Authority.** Explicit Stop, deploy and Restart supersede sleep and wake, as on the panel host. The autoscaler holds while a node service sleeps; nothing sleeps during a deploy, canary or autoscale transition. Fan-out and Swarm services stay refused with their own reasons.

## Ordered implementation

1. Agent: the `proxy.idleWatch` contract and capability, on the bounded log transport and sequence markers. Cover lease lapse, restart, source change and refusal with tests, and add a hosted observation case (continuous zero, a single request breaks the zero, proxy restart resets coverage). *Implemented 2026-11-02:*
   - `lib/nodeIdleWatch.ts` and `agentOps/idleWatch.ts`.
   - Agent tests: `test/agentOps/idleWatch.test.ts` (two-minute verified zero under a 15 s lease, a single request, lease lapse, overlapping chain, owner disable).
   - Hosted cases in `scripts/fixtures/serving-traffic-agent.mjs`: a verified zero over one minute, a chained window broken by one request, and a proxy restart ending coverage.
   - The agent now also closes serving and idle windows when it shuts down.
2. Agent: the `ninedeploy-wake` catcher (an idempotent ensure/remove operation, pinned image, no mounts) and the sealed `wake.demand` operation. Cover token bounds, expiry and missing-catcher refusal. *Implemented 2026-11-02:*
   - `src/wakeCatcher.ts`, `lib/nodeWakeCatcher.ts` and `agentOps/wakeCatcher.ts`, under the capability `wake.catcher` (same owner opt-in; `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_CONTAINER_MUTATIONS=off` also turns it off).
   - The catcher runs the agent's own image by ID as `65534:65534`, read-only, with all capabilities dropped and no published port. It has no volume or bind mount. The image declares `VOLUME /data`, which Docker would otherwise satisfy with a writable anonymous volume. The first hosted run (41511827062) caught exactly that, so `/data` is shadowed by an empty 64 KB tmpfs with mode `0555`. The smoke asserts that writes to `/data`, `/` and `/app` fail. Removal uses `rm -fv`.
   - Service containers share the proxy network, so demand counts only when a request carries the node's wake key. The `x-nd-wake-key` header is added by the panel-rendered Traefik middleware, and the key comes from `wake.catcher.ensure { key }`. The container gets it in its environment, and its label holds only a hash. Any other request gets a 404 and writes no line.
   - It writes at most one `ND-WAKE` line per token per second and 20 a second in all. `wake.demand` aggregates those lines from the catcher's Docker log since a cursor. A read that fills the 2,000-line tail is flagged `truncated`, so the panel never treats it as all the demand.
   - A missing, stopped or unlabelled catcher is refused rather than reported as no demand, and a same-name container it did not create is never touched.
   - Hosted check: `scripts/smoke-wake-catcher.mjs` in CI and on the release image.
3. Panel: the node idle clock in the sleep tick, using the idle watch. Report hold reasons (capability, coverage, opt-in) through sleep status. Never sleep on unavailable coverage. *Read-only scheduling, transport and coverage calculation implemented 2026-11-02; public status and runtime effects remain open:*
   - `lib/nodeIdleWatchClient.ts` uses the shared sealed observation client with its own idle schemas, capability and receipt frame. It retains before/after runtime, owner, route, topology and conflict checks, cancellation cleanup, source continuity and one-use finalization. Idle windows do not enter the autoscale receipt ledger.
   - A normal node deployment does not require autoscale spare capacity to be observed. Its serving names/count/port and database placement are checked in the panel; the sealed agent verifies the live immutable serving IDs and deployment labels. RPS observations still require their complete capacity receipt.
   - `lib/nodeIdleCoverage.ts` accepts only completed zero-request windows. A chain requires overlapping sequence markers, unchanged source/proxy/epoch, serving IDs, routing and runtime context. A gap, traffic, replacement, lease loss or validation failure resets coverage.
   - Chained durations are not added together: monotonic panel timestamps bracketing each opening RPC give a conservative union-duration lower bound. Opening latency and overlapping seconds cannot inflate the idle proof. Repeated and superseded completions are refused, with exact uint64 counter comparisons.
   - `lib/nodeIdleWatchService.ts` resolves all serving members through sealed `docker.identity` before opening each window. Both `docker.recovery` and `proxy.idleWatch` are required. Runtime owner/configuration checks surround discovery, and the bound transport rechecks deployment, topology and route eligibility before reserving any window.
   - `lib/nodeIdleScheduler.ts` samples every 15 seconds independently per service. It opens a successor before finishing its predecessor, resets on traffic/refusal/lease lapse, closes ineligible or superseded generations, and aborts/cleans up during server shutdown, including late opening replies. One slow node cannot block another service's lease tick. Missing current service state discards all coverage.
   - Each node reserves paired slots for at most eight active services within the agent's sixteen-window limit. Other services report capacity waiting with no idle value. Backing-off failures do not reserve empty slots or starve healthy services. Refusals retry after one minute instead of generating a request and warning at every lease tick.
   - `plugins/sleeper.ts` starts the node read-only observer separately from the existing one-minute panel-host sleep tick. The scheduler's internal status distinguishes unavailable coverage (`idleMs: null`), a verified traffic reset (`idleMs: 0`) and a completed idle proof. `idleSatisfied` is observation evidence, not mutation authority. Public status, wake reachability, route changes and runtime mutation effects remain pending; node sleep stays refused until those steps and hosted acceptance pass.
   - Transport/coverage foundation validation: 222 server tests passed in ten files covering idle transport/coverage, existing RPS observation/consumption/sample/controller/admission, agent idle watch and the Swarm runtime-reader inventory. Server typecheck and targeted lint passed. Agent transport is mocked in panel adapter tests; the agent idle tests use the real observation engine with a fake Docker I/O boundary. This is local source validation, not hosted node sleep/wake acceptance. Local Docker was not accessed (`DOCKER_HOST=tcp://127.0.0.1:9`).
   - Scheduler/helper validation: 230 focused tests passed in eleven server files, including the real Fastify plugin's 15-second cadence and shutdown. Scheduler tests use the actual idle-watch engine, counter and coverage calculator with fake Docker I/O; they verify five-minute continuous coverage, pending unverified tails, traffic, lease/source loss, late replies, concurrency, paired capacity and refusal backoff.
