The same queue interleaving independently reproduced on a pre-Stop failure: the catcher ACK was lost, the controller restored a ready application and marked sleep aborted, but a queued ordinary writer restored the catcher. Its ready-app control passed; the final routing assertion failed. Restoration now settles its fallback inside the acknowledged routing slot and compares the exact ordered generation transactionally, using the same guard as wake and explicit Start/Restart. A newer bound or unbound reservation holds restoration for retry rather than completing an obsolete ACK. Recovery restores the app and never resumes the old idle decision or issues Stop.

The unchanged queued restoration regression passed after the fix. The covering run passed **99 tests in six files** across sleep, wake, poller, explicit settlement, authority and the Swarm reader inventory; server typecheck and scoped lint passed. The first filtered reproduction invocation had incorrectly escaped Windows arguments and was stopped without being counted as evidence; the corrected invocation failed on the intended routing assertion with 12 other tests skipped. These tests substitute agent I/O and do not certify the real-Docker pre-Stop failure path.

### Real idle acceptance: concurrent metadata readers

The dedicated real-idle fixture uses the production scheduler/client and a real five-minute window, real immutable Stop/Start, strict HTTP readiness failure, an independent traffic observer and recovery through a new Node/HTTP-agent process. It keeps credentials outside public artifacts and does not seed dormant state. [Run 41609229034](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41609229034) on `4a65b21c7bcbd0d89ec6806358cc1eb4f19eae86` failed: the serving-request reset control passed, but four `SQLITE_BUSY` errors prevented continuous idle coverage. All four owned containers and the network were removed. Artifact: `.temp_files/node-sleep-wake-41609229034/`. No Stop/wake or zero-502 certificate follows from that run.

An isolated file-backed subprocess reproduces the failure without Docker: one observer obtains the expected stable context, but a pair of concurrent production context reads yields one successful result and one SQLite lock refusal. Drizzle's libSQL adapter starts write transactions even for the read-only snapshots. Serialize only the short context-capture operations per DB handle, preserving both transactional snapshots and before/after route checks; agent RPCs and observation windows remain independent. The unchanged concurrency assertion now passes, and a refused routing context does not poison later queued readers. This does not claim cross-process database serialization or a passing hosted idle/Stop/wake cohort; the corrected real cohort must run again.

The covering metadata/idle scheduler/client/coverage run passed **120 tests in five files** without coverage; server typecheck and scoped lint passed. The file-backed proof runs in a child process and removes its owned directory only after child exit. Local Docker remains disabled.

### Real single-service idle/Stop/wake — hosted component verified

[Run 41611317840](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41611317840) passed all ten cases on frozen source `f71e074cf7da56ec46c33fe7b18899fc87cc5038`. The actual scheduler established **311,749 ms** of continuous zero-request coverage after proving that real serving traffic resets it. The production sleep controller stopped the captured immutable app, with the verified catcher route already serving. Real visitor demand caused Start; intentional strict HTTP readiness failure retained the fallback. A new Node/HTTP-agent process reopened persisted readiness, published the app after readiness passed, and did not repeat Start. The ordinary follow-up writer retained the app; its container and the proxy kept their initial IDs.

Independent JSONL/array recounting confirmed **1,788 requests**: **494 application responses** and **1,294 verified waking pages**, with zero 502/connection errors. All **396 samples** inside the failed-readiness interval remained waking pages; **59 samples after completed recovery** were application responses. The two controller PIDs differ, no observation/controller error was recorded, and all five owned containers plus the network were removed. Evidence: `.temp_files/node-sleep-wake-41611317840/independent-verification.json`. This is real sealed HTTP/Docker/Traefik behavior with actual elapsed time, but internal factories rather than public API activation. Basic Auth/IP restrictions, agent opt-out, concurrent services, Stop during wake and pre-Stop restoration faults remain additional acceptance work.

### Shared managed transaction ordering

Preparing concurrent services exposed the same ownership conflict beyond metadata reads. Two controlled DB regressions demonstrate that a second legitimate managed transaction is rejected while the first awaits commit or rollback, even though a transaction on an independent DB succeeds. Queue complete Drizzle transactions per DB handle through commit/rollback, preserving nested savepoints and the existing connection PRAGMAs. The earlier observation-only queue is removed; the transactional snapshots and route comparisons remain intact. This covers managed transactions on one handle, not raw client calls or serialization across different processes/handles. The two regressions were RED before the change and GREEN afterward. The full DB package passed **82 tests in 34 files**, including rollback, independent handles and nested savepoints. The server covering run passed **245 tests in 14 files**, including file-backed read/write concurrency, scheduler/client/coverage, sleep/wake, explicit commands, maintenance recovery and Swarm inventory. DB build, server typecheck and scoped lint passed. This later source still requires full hosted CI and the expanded real cohort.

The source job in [CI 41608355751](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41608355751), frozen wake-settlement source `b1796e82`, reported 13,153 server tests passing and one failure in `proxyNodeSleep.test.ts`: its exact successful-result expectation omitted the new acknowledged routing authority. The expectation now also checks the exact DB head, revision/request identity and written-content digest; all **18 tests in that file** pass locally. This is a contract-expectation correction, not a successful full-CI certificate. The rest of that workflow was still running when its completed source-job log was inspected; do not discard or restart it to recover observation.

### Main integration and expanded guard acceptance

PRs #15–#18 passed their frozen full CI gates and were merged to `main` on 2026-11-03: `8560ea42`, `62d78012`, `b6b8e2ef` and `c1777241`. PR #22 then passed [full CI 41616043392](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41616043392) on `f86d10a53779ae50c55df2c24709f1f5d266f799`, including source checks, real Docker/PostgreSQL integration and all image/runtime smoke steps, and merged as `c3e0214a`. Image publication was skipped for the PR as expected. Git ancestry verifies that all three complete heads from #19–#21 are present in #22; those intermediate PRs were closed as superseded, without dropping their changes or claiming they merged independently. The local main history was reconciled with both integration batches while preserving the prepared source tree. PR #23 is the next direct-to-main manual-wake increment. No production activation or release followed from these component merges.

Expanded [run 41614144107](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41614144107), source `3259a5a8b604e4a5cdfc5a4cfb7af47a54170e19`, stopped at the opt-out fixture's expected-error wording. The operation correctly refused, but the fixture expected an environment hint while the development image still reports 0.18.16 and returns its 0.19.0 upgrade refusal. This is a fixture diagnostic; none of the later concurrent-idle/auth/Stop cases was accepted. Five owned containers and the network were removed. The corrected control requires the advertised capability to be present before opt-out, absent during opt-out, restored afterward, plus the exact observation-refusal family and an untouched runtime/journal. Syntax and scoped lint passed; a new real result remains required.

Follow-up [run 41615171431](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41615171431), source `14544a66536137d59e5e6a521f5f24e340472a72`, then stopped on another fixture defect before idle qualification: its per-service journal helper used `services.id`, which Drizzle rendered as the nonexistent `nodeSleepTransitions.id`. It now selects `nodeSleepTransitions.serviceId`. A local preflight executes the actual fixture helper expressions against fully migrated SQLite for both service IDs; all four current queries succeed, while the prior wrong-column control reproduces the error. Syntax/scoped lint pass. Five owned containers and the network were removed; no expanded acceptance is claimed for this failed run.

### Guarded two-service idle/Stop/wake — hosted component verified

[Run 41616036959](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41616036959) on frozen source `f86d10a53779ae50c55df2c24709f1f5d266f799` passed all 14 cases. Two service entries in the production scheduler established **322,069 ms** and **324,936 ms** of real idle evidence, then their sleep controllers ran concurrently. The agent opt-out control verified advertised capability before/off/restored and no runtime/journal effect. Unauthorized Basic Auth and disallowed-IP requests returned 401/403 without recording the protected service's token or starting it. An authenticated request subsequently started its wake; a real explicit Stop superseded it while strict HTTP readiness was in flight. Its immutable application remained stopped after a fresh poller, while the other service continued serving.

Independent JSONL/array recounting confirmed **2,328 valid responses**: **900 application responses**, **1,428 verified waking pages**, zero 502/connection errors, **400 waking pages during failed readiness**, and **59 application responses after all cases**. New controller/agent PIDs differ, no observation/controller errors were recorded, and all six owned containers plus the network were removed. Evidence: `.temp_files/node-sleep-wake-41616036959/independent-verification.json`. These are isolated real sealed HTTP/Docker/Traefik effects through internal factories. Public API/plugin activation and later source changes are outside this certificate.

### Manual node wake entry point and client feedback

The public manual-wake route previously passed a node's sleeping row to the panel-host wake implementation. Three route regressions reproduced the planned local `docker start web-9` effect through mocked process I/O; seven local-route controls passed. Ordinary node Docker wake now admits the existing durable remote Start command and returns 202 with `pending: true`, leaving readiness and loaded-route confirmation to the ordered worker. Unsupported node Compose/Swarm placement and disabled/unsealed agents refuse without local Docker effects or a new intent. This does not enable automatic sleep or bypass the idle evidence needed for sleep admission.

SDK wake results reuse `ServiceLifecycleResult`. Panel and CLI treat accepted commands as pending rather than reporting the service awake. The panel observes the existing lifecycle query, retains newer completed state, disables repeated wake during verification and binds a delayed acceptance to its original service after navigation. Three API, two initial UI and one CLI regression were RED before the corresponding fixes; two additional UI checks caught repeat submission and delayed-response handling during implementation. The covering runs passed **1,264 server tests in six files**, **164 web tests in four files**, the full SDK package (**384 tests in 34 files**) and **20 CLI tests**. SDK build, server/web/CLI typechecks and scoped lint passed. These checks substitute process/network I/O; real public manual-wake acceptance and final full CI remain required for this later source.

### Public manual wake — native before/after verified

Identical fixtures ran on before source `befc77e269d35016992eff4424b50d3893476e76` ([run 41622494732](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41622494732)) and fixed source `5587e972ab0da9bebc09c15e891c6e64f808ed9e` ([run 41622507659](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41622507659)). Each used a real authenticated panel, its normal lifecycle worker, standard sealed node enrollment, separate owned panel/node Docker daemons and genuine idle/Stop through a private production factory. Observed idle was **315,614 ms** before and **315,775 ms** after the fix.

The before run failed on the harmful-effect assertion: public manual wake changed the stopped same-name panel decoy's `StartedAt` from its never-started value to a real process timestamp. This was an actual isolated Docker mutation, not a fixture setup/import failure or merely an unexpected HTTP code. Its normal deployment and real idle/asleep controls had passed. The fixed run kept that immutable panel decoy never started, acknowledged public 202/pending, held failed strict HTTP readiness behind the catcher, retained the command ID on explicit retry, and completed readiness/routing through the normal worker with the original node container ID preserved.

Independent recounting confirmed **675 valid responses**: **600 verified waking pages**, **75 application responses**, zero 502/connection errors. Both cohorts removed their three outer containers, both owned volumes and the owned network. The dedicated upload accepts only enumerated public JSON files; tokens, DBs and raw logs are excluded. Evidence: `.temp_files/public-manual-wake-fixed-41622507659/independent-verification.json`. This accepts the public manual-wake entry point; idle admission still uses a private real-observation factory. Automatic public sleep/status/plugin activation and full CI for PR #23 remain open.

### Lost pre-Stop acknowledgement — native acceptance in progress

The next isolated cohort is [run 41627779632](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41627779632), frozen source `9eec752efe773c3ae0af1ef6766b44d979506587`. Normal authenticated API deployment and sealed agent enrollment establish the healthy control. A private scheduler must observe and admit genuine five-minute idle before the independent traffic observer starts. A loopback-only forwarder sends the original sealed bytes unchanged to the actual enrolled agent. After verifying its nonce, successful result and exact loaded-routing hash, it holds that response for one second, then drops the panel-facing connection. Production sleep restoration must abort the old idle decision, issue no Stop/Start, clear fallback metadata, confirm an ordinary subsequent writer and leave the immutable application's start/finish timestamps unchanged. Traffic must include at least 20 verified waking pages during the lost acknowledgement and remain on the application after restoration, with no unexpected response or connection failure.

This is a real transport-fault acceptance requirement, not a replacement for the existing queued-writer regression. The fixture's network/sampler checks and covering controller checks passed locally: **22 tests in three files**, then **seven helper tests in two files** after the final observer/delay change. Script syntax, generated sampler syntax, workflow parsing, enumerated JSON-only upload paths and all three pre-Docker hosted-runner guards passed. Local Docker remained disabled. The hosted run is still in progress; no native restoration result is claimed yet. PR #23 retains its frozen head while this separate proof branch runs, without opening another integration PR.

PR #23's [full CI 41622799651](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41622799651) passed on `5587e972ab0da9bebc09c15e891c6e64f808ed9e`: **18,294 tests in 1,160 files**, all **12 tasks**, typecheck/lint/build, post-test checks, real Docker/PostgreSQL integration and the full image/runtime job including RPS source-loss acceptance. The separate serving-generation check also passed. The PR merged to main as `9e79b931e82922cbc47ba23e2949c95d87774110` on 2026-11-03; image publication was skipped for the PR as expected. No new release was published.

### Lost pre-Stop acknowledgement — native transport fault verified

[Run 41627779632](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41627779632) completed successfully on `9eec752efe773c3ae0af1ef6766b44d979506587`. Its private production scheduler observed **315,721 ms** of genuine idle before admission. The loopback-only forwarder verified the real sealed agent's successful nonce/hash-bound loaded-routing acknowledgement, then dropped the panel-facing connection. The sleep controller restored the healthy application, completed its journal with `fallbackRouting: false`, and confirmed a later ordinary writer. No runtime Stop/Start was issued; the original immutable application's start/finish timestamps remained unchanged.

Independent artifact verification counted **640 valid responses**: **216 verified waking pages**, **424 application responses**, zero 502/connection errors, and the last 40 responses all from the application after restoration. All three owned outer containers, both volumes and the network were removed. Evidence: `.temp_files/node-sleep-restoration-41627779632/independent-verification.json`. This proves the stated real pre-Stop lost-acknowledgement path; it does not certify every possible fault timing or activate public automatic sleep. The existing production-renderer queued-writer regression remains the proof for settlement ordering. Integration CI for this later fixture source and the automatic scheduler/coordinator/status/plugin path remain separate work.

### Bounded sleep coordinator — local component checkpoint

`createNodeSleepCoordinator` now reserves at most four execution slots, consumes an opaque idle token only inside a reserved slot, prioritizes expired pending sleep commands and leaves wake journals to the wake poller. It recovers the same Stop identity after a lost acknowledgement, backs off held work for 30 seconds, skips ineligible placements before consuming evidence, and aborts/drains owned work on close. Shutdown before publication completes the unused sleep decision; shutdown with fallback routing leaves restoration recoverable, so the next coordinator restores the application instead of resuming the old idle Stop.

The covering six-file run passed **55 tests**. After the placement filter was added, the coordinator's two-file run passed **17 tests**, including the eight ineligible-placement controls. Server typecheck and scoped lint passed. Network calls are substituted; the actual admission/controller/renderer and managed SQLite transactions are used. The four-slot concurrency proof runs with a real file-backed database in a child process, whose exit precedes Windows cleanup. The memory-only diagnostic reproduced `TRANSACTION_ACTIVE`: its single connection cannot execute an unscoped query while borrowed by a transaction. The identical file-backed proof admitted four services, consumed none of the other two tokens and recorded no error. That diagnostic is not claimed as a production defect or fixed by weakening concurrency.

The coordinator is not yet connected to the production sleeper plugin. Public node sleep/status reporting, automatic wake/maintenance scheduling and full public automatic-cycle acceptance remain required before activation. PR #24 contains only the earlier hosted transport-fault fixture and documentation, with its full CI running on frozen head `feeffe8f6156a55e39e766f992aab320089028c0`; it does not contain this coordinator checkpoint.

### Public automatic cycle candidate — local validation only

The unreleased candidate connects the idle observer, bounded sleep coordinator and wake/maintenance poller to the sleeper plugin's lifecycle. Idle observations run every 15 seconds; pending sleep recovery and wake demand run every two seconds. Close unregisters status, stops timers, aborts and drains the three components. Each service still requires its own `sleepAfterMinutes` setting, eligible ordinary node Docker placement and the sealed agent's advertised capabilities/traffic opt-in. `NINEDEPLOY_NODE_SLEEP_AUTOMATION=off` pauses automatic node sleep, wake and recovery while retaining explicit Start/Wake. The private-factory manual/transport-fault fixtures set this pause so the normal plugin cannot compete with their explicitly controlled admission.

`GET /v1/services/:id/sleep` is a viewer-scoped read-only status endpoint shared by SDK, CLI and panel. It exposes observation duration and coarse observing/sleeping/asleep/waking/held state; no wake credential, immutable target, lease token, runtime owner identity or raw worker reason is returned. App-local observer registration cannot leak coverage across DB handles. The panel removes unsupported manual node Sleep now, shows verified idle coverage and pending wake, and keeps manual wake available for held verification. The CLI's node status does not infer awake from an accepted command. Older panels returning 404 keep an explicit unverified node state.

Local checks passed: 77 server checks in seven files before the later authorization classification, then 1,064 authorization/environment checks in two files; 170 panel tests in four files; all 384 SDK tests in 34 files; 21 CLI checks. Schema/SDK builds, server/web/CLI typechecks and scoped lint passed. The reviewed API snapshot and authorization matrix include the new viewer/read endpoint. A dedicated hosted-only cohort is prepared to prove ordinary public settings, a real traffic request resetting idle, five more idle minutes, automatic Stop, visitor-demand wake, failed readiness, panel restart and automatic recovery with sampled Traefik traffic. Its preflight syntax, YAML/JSON-only artifacts and all hosted guards passed. That native cohort and full CI for this later source are still required; no production/public acceptance or release is claimed here.

The public automatic cohort is now running as [41633395833](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41633395833), frozen source `8f26e19c4af2428807d271ef5a2067e5b3eef854`. Its source tree matches the prepared local candidate before this documentation update. PR #24's separate [CI 41630104741](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41630104741) is still running on `feeffe8f6156a55e39e766f992aab320089028c0`; it does not certify the public automatic-cycle candidate. Neither frozen branch was updated to restart its checks. No additional integration PR or release was opened.

### Public automatic cohort control correction and activity settlement

Run 41633395833 failed at the healthy serving-request control after normal API deployment and the first public idle observation; it did not accept the later automatic sleep/wake/restart cases. All three owned outer containers, both volumes and the network were removed. Its control used `fetch` with a custom Host. A local Node 26.12.1 server proved that this sends the transport host instead, whereas `node:http` sends the requested application Host. The control now uses bounded `node:http`, verifies status and exact application body, and saves a public status/boolean receipt. The real-HTTP regression failed with the prior fetch implementation, then passed unchanged with the corrected transport. Four controls now pass, including unhealthy status, a different backend and an oversized body.

Automatic sleep/wake settlement also now calls the normal audit/activity fan-out only after the Stop receipt or ready application routing is committed. Held, superseded and restoration-aborted work does not claim sleep/wake completion; recovery emits the completion only when it settles. The covering coordinator/poller/audit checks passed **28 tests in three files**; server typecheck and scoped lint passed. Audit remains the application's existing best-effort fan-out, not a new durable notification outbox. The hosted cohort now additionally requires one persisted sleep event, no wake event during failed readiness, and one persisted wake event after panel recovery and confirmed routing. Native acceptance for this corrected later source remains required.

The corrected public cohort is [run 41634736108](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41634736108), frozen source `cd2ca25fbc1ea2cb9974d915155fb9241b8b55be`; it is still running. An independent verifier is prepared to recount its traffic, require the public control/reset/idle and persisted audit receipts, verify its source identity and owned cleanup, and reject private-factory admission. No result is claimed before those artifacts exist. Separately, the Turkish catalog check reproduced 13 missing node-state translations and the obsolete node-unsupported key. The catalog correction passed all 35 checks in the catalog/SleepState/SleepCard run. These translation-only changes are outside the frozen native source and do not restart it. PR #24's source job passed 18,298 tests in 1,161 files; its final image/RPS job remains in progress.

### Public automatic cycle — hosted API/plugin acceptance verified

Run 41634736108 completed successfully on frozen source `cd2ca25fbc1ea2cb9974d915155fb9241b8b55be`. The independent verifier confirmed ordinary public API settings and production plugin timers, with no private factory admission. A healthy application request reset the public idle coverage to zero. Only after **402,743 ms since that request**, with **344,815 ms of conservatively verified idle coverage**, did the normal coordinator complete automatic Stop on the captured immutable node container. Visitor demand then ran the normal wake poller. Failed strict HTTP readiness retained the catcher and sleeping marker; a panel restart recovered the pending wake without changing the acknowledged application's start timestamp. Clearing the readiness fault let automatic retry confirm the application route.

Independent artifact recounting confirmed **791 valid responses**: **677 verified waking pages**, **114 application responses**, zero 502/connection errors, and the final 40 all from the application. The public activity API returned exactly one `service.sleep` event after Stop, no `service.wake` during failed readiness, and exactly one `service.wake` after confirmed routing and recovery. All three owned outer containers, both volumes and the network were removed. Evidence: `.temp_files/node-automatic-sleep-41634736108/independent-verification.json`. This accepts the stated single-node public automatic cycle and restart path; it does not certify public DNS/TLS, every fault timing, never-bound orphan catcher collection or the complete R2–R6/release scope.

The actual new React source components were also rendered in an owned headless Chrome fixture at 1280px and 375px, English and Turkish. Observing, waking, held and paused states had no page overflow or browser errors; automatic waking disabled repeated wake, held/paused kept manual wake available, and awake nodes exposed no manual Sleep now. The long held message wrapped in the mobile render. This substitutes the client boundary and is component visual acceptance, not a real panel/backend browser journey. Evidence: `.temp_files/node-sleep-ui-20261103/result.json` and four screenshots. The owned Chrome and Vite processes were closed.

PR #24 passed [full CI 41630104741](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41630104741), including 18,298 tests in 1,161 files, real Docker/PostgreSQL integration and the final image/RPS cohort, and merged to main as `1b9334f1b07e3b966fd50252b2d7f3c6c112a26a`. Its source excludes this public automatic candidate. Local main history was reconciled while preserving the prepared source tree exactly. No release was published.

### Public candidate integration gate — reader inventory correction

PR #25's first [CI 41637057912](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41637057912), head `49e5bd3a84e37a0edafce6d5f7475f419b23d3f5`, passed 13,198 server tests but failed the single static Swarm runtime-reader inventory check. The new `nodeSleepCoordinator` and `serviceSleepStatus` readers had not been classified. The identical check reproduced locally. The inventory now states their actual boundary: new sleep admission skips Swarm before consuming evidence, recovery revalidates ordinary node Docker authority before effects, and public status returns unsupported for Swarm before consulting node observations or journal identities. An additional status behavior control proves that a Swarm row never consults the node observer. All 34 covering checks in three files passed after the correction. Runtime source and coverage floors did not change. Fresh full CI on the corrected PR head remains required; the old image/runtime job is allowed to finish without being canceled by this test-only update.

The old image/runtime job subsequently passed every step, including PostgreSQL autoscaling and the final RPS source-loss control; the real Docker/PostgreSQL integration job also passed. The workflow remains failed because of the explicit source inventory failure. CI now runs the existing 13-test Swarm runtime guard immediately after build and before the long full suite, with Docker explicitly unavailable for that guard. All 13 checks passed locally. The existing full suite still follows it. The corrected PR update contains only tests, this early CI guard and evidence documentation; it preserves the public automatic-cycle runtime source accepted by run 41634736108.

docs.markdown:
# Resource history, metrics export and durable logs

Status: resource history, Prometheus and OTLP export shipped in 0.18.2;
error-rate and latency alerts are on main for the next release. Validation is
tracked in [competitive delivery](COMPETITIVE_DELIVERY.md).

## Configure resource history

An operator can open **Monitoring → Resource history and metrics export** or use:

```sh
ninedeploy metrics settings
ninedeploy metrics configure --retention-days 30 --log-queue-mb 32
```

The default remains **one day**, with export disabled. Retention accepts 1–90 days.
Raw CPU/memory samples are retained for approximately 24 hours; opted-in history
uses five-minute summaries through seven days and hourly summaries thereafter.
Cleanup aligns with summary boundaries so adjacent tiers do not overlap or leave
a partial boundary bucket missing. Chart queries return weighted averages over
the complete requested interval, bounded to roughly 900 points. Longer charts
therefore smooth spikes. CPU is percent (100 means one core); memory charts use MiB.

Select 1 hour, 24 hours, 7, 30 or 90 days in a service's resource charts. A longer
selection does not recover data already removed under an earlier retention
setting. Reducing retention deletes older summaries during the next cleanup.
The existing per-service visibility checks still apply.

This covers currently collected local and ordinary node-service CPU/memory.
A Swarm service records the average of its tasks on the panel host; tasks on
worker nodes are not measured. Remote Swarm task aggregation, fan-out
destination history and node-only database history remain separate work. Monitoring's panel-host totals stay local.

## Prometheus

Enable **Prometheus scraping**, or:

```sh
ninedeploy metrics configure --prometheus on
```

Scrape **GET /v1/stats/prometheus** using an operator bearer credential. Disabled
export returns 404; unauthenticated or non-operator callers cannot read it.
Use HTTPS and store the credential in the scraper's secret store/file, rather
than embedding it in a shared configuration. A dedicated read-only scrape token
is not provided by this increment; the credential must have operator API access.

Example Prometheus configuration:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: ninedeploy
    scheme: https
    metrics_path: /v1/stats/prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["panel.example.com"]
    authorization:
      credentials_file: /run/secrets/ninedeploy_operator_token
```

Text exposition uses these gauges:

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| ninedeploy_service_cpu_percent | CPU percent; 100 is one core |
| ninedeploy_service_memory_bytes | Resident memory in bytes |
| ninedeploy_service_sample_timestamp_seconds | Collection time in Unix seconds; includes a kind label |

Series include service_id, service and server_id (panel for local services).
Only samples from the last 120 seconds are exposed. Missing/stale samples remain
absent rather than becoming zero. Export is bounded to 10,000 CPU/memory series.

## OTLP/HTTP JSON

Configure the full metrics receiver URL, including **/v1/metrics** where required.
This is OTLP/HTTP JSON, not gRPC:

```sh
ninedeploy metrics configure --otlp-endpoint https://collector.example.com/v1/metrics
# Set COLLECTOR_AUTH securely in your shell/secret manager before this command:
ninedeploy metrics configure --otlp-authorization-env COLLECTOR_AUTH
```

The selected variable supplies the complete Authorization header, for example a
Bearer credential. Its value is never printed by these CLI commands. Omitting
the field preserves a saved credential; explicit removal uses
**--clear-otlp-authorization**. An empty endpoint disables export.

The panel exports every 30 seconds after an initial 15-second delay. The
Monitoring card can test the saved destination immediately and shows the last
attempt/result. Export status is process-local and resets on restart. Each
request has a six-second timeout, rejects redirects, bounds the receiver response
to 16 KiB and reports partial rejection as failure. Failed metric exports are
not spooled; the next cycle sends current samples.

The normal outbound URL policy applies. An internal collector requires the
existing **NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1** operator setting. URL userinfo,
fragments and CR/LF in authorization are rejected. Settings, including the
collector credential, are encrypted in Config Center and participate in master
key rotation. The monitoring API returns only whether a credential is saved.

This exporter handles infrastructure CPU/memory gauges. Existing
**metrics show/flush** commands still refer to the separate kernel event archive;
their backend settings do not configure this exporter.

## Durable captured-log delivery

Each log drain now has an encrypted SQLite queue and persistent cursor per
runtime, host and destination binding. A Swarm service's runtimes are its
tasks: each task's lines are read through the manager wherever the task runs,
with a cursor per task. Capture commits a batch and cursor
together. A stopped source container does not prevent delivery of an already
captured batch, including after a panel restart. A failing destination retries
with exponential backoff (10 seconds up to five minutes); another successful
destination does not need to resend its acknowledged batch.

Delivery is **at least once**. A receiver accepting a request before the panel
records acknowledgement can receive a duplicate. New runtimes start at the
current time, without backfill. Capture is bounded: remote reads return at most
1,000 lines/256 KiB and may clip long lines; local Docker reads are also bounded.
Logs rotated before capture or produced faster than those reads can be lost.
PM2 file logs and secondary Compose services are outside this delivery path.
A durable captured queue is not a guarantee of lossless source collection.

The default queue limit is 16 MiB of payload per destination (configurable
1–256 MiB), with an additional 10,000-batch ceiling. SQLite/encryption overhead
uses additional disk space. Batches contain at most 1,000 entries/256 KiB.
When full, capture pauses without advancing that source cursor or evicting
pending data. An oversized single entry also pauses capture. The log-drain
card shows queue depth, oldest batch, blocked batches and paused sources.

Changing a drain's URL, headers, format, service filter or resolved credential
does not forward old batches to the changed destination: those batches remain
blocked. Reverting to the original binding allows retry, or an operator can
explicitly discard the old queue. Master key rotation re-encrypts the queue
without changing its resolved destination binding. Disabling a drain retains its
queue; deleting the drain or service deletes related queued data.

```sh
ninedeploy log-drains queue 4
ninedeploy log-drains retry 4
ninedeploy log-drains discard 4 --yes
```

Retry schedules delivery for the next cycle; it does not certify delivery.
Discard permanently removes pending batches without rewinding the source cursor.
The panel requires an explicit confirmation for the same operation.

## Log drain targets (G3.4)

Besides Loki, Datadog, Vector, syslog-over-HTTP and plain HTTP, a drain can send to the services below. They use the same shipper, with batches, retries, the durable queue and the egress guard. The body format is the target's own, so the drain's format setting does not apply to them.

| Type | URL | API key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `elasticsearch` (also OpenSearch) | the index or data stream, `https://es.example.com:9200/logs-ninedeploy`; batches go to `_bulk` as `create` actions | `user:password` (basic auth) or an Elasticsearch API key |
| `splunk` | the HEC event endpoint, `https://splunk:8088/services/collector/event` | the HEC token |
| `betterstack` | the source's ingesting host | the source token |
| `newrelic` | `https://log-api.newrelic.com/log/v1` (or the EU host) | a license or ingest key (`Api-Key`) |
| `axiom` | `https://api.axiom.co/v1/datasets/<dataset>/ingest` | an API token |
| `cloudwatch` | `https://logs.<region>.amazonaws.com/?group=<log group>&stream=<log stream>` | `ACCESS_KEY_ID:SECRET_ACCESS_KEY[:SESSION_TOKEN]` |

**Notes per target**
- **Elasticsearch:** answers 200 even when some documents were refused. The shipper reads the `errors` flag and retries the batch, reporting the first reason.
- **CloudWatch:** signed with SigV4 (`PutLogEvents`). The log group and stream are created the first time AWS says they do not exist. The key needs `logs:PutLogEvents`, plus `logs:CreateLogStream` and `logs:CreateLogGroup` if they should be created.
- **Saving a drain:** a URL that does not name what its target needs is refused (422). That means the index for Elasticsearch, and the region, group and stream for CloudWatch.

**Storage:** no migration is needed; the drain type is a text column without a CHECK.

## Search shipped logs

When a Loki drain is enabled, the lines it received can be searched, including
those of containers that no longer exist. On a service, open **Activity Logs →
Search shipped logs** (web UI since G1.5), type the text to find and pick a
window from 15 minutes to 7 days; up to 500 matching lines are shown. The CLI
(`ninedeploy logs search`) and `POST /v1/log-drains/search` do the same, and an
operator can also search across all services there. Searching one service needs
`member` on it, and on a protected lane the lane's admin rights. A member's
window never starts before the service was created, because a reused service
name could otherwise show a deleted service's lines. Without an enabled Loki
drain the search answers that no drain exists; drains of other types cannot be
searched.

## Error tracking (G5.4)

Any Sentry SDK can report a service's errors to the panel. Create the DSN under **Service → Activity → Errors**. It is shown once, as `https://<key>@<panel host>/<serviceId>`. Give it to the SDK as `SENTRY_DSN`. Set `SENTRY_RELEASE` to the commit SHA the service runs, for example from a build argument. The SDKs read both variables themselves:

```js
Sentry.init({ dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN, release: process.env.SENTRY_RELEASE });
```

Without a release, an issue is linked to the deploy that was live when it first happened.

**Ingest**
- `POST /api/<serviceId>/envelope/`, and the older `POST /api/<serviceId>/store/`.
- The key is accepted from the `X-Sentry-Auth` header, from `?sentry_key=` (browser SDKs), or from the envelope's `dsn`.
- Bodies may be plain, gzip, deflate or br, up to 1 MiB uncompressed.
- Only `event` items are stored. Sessions, transactions and attachments are skipped.
- Limits: 600 requests a minute per client and 300 events a minute per service. Past them the answer is 429 with `X-Sentry-Rate-Limits`, which the SDKs honour.

**Issues**
- Events are grouped by fingerprint: the SDK's `fingerprint` when given, otherwise the exception type and its last five in-app frames. Without frames, the normalised message is used, with digits, hex ids and quoted values masked.
- Each issue keeps its count, first and last sighting, and the deploy it first appeared under. That is the deploy whose commit is the event's `release`, otherwise the live deploy.
- An issue can be resolved, ignored or reopened. A resolved issue that happens again reopens by itself.

**Alerts**
- A new issue is audited as `alert.error_new`, and a reopened one as `alert.error_regressed`.
- Both reach the notification channels that receive alerts.

**Access**
- Issue titles are exception messages, and event payloads may carry request headers and user data. Both are for members and up, as are creating, replacing and removing the DSN.
- Viewers only see whether the service has a DSN.

**Bounds**
- A browser DSN is public, so anyone can send events.
- An issue keeps its first 5 events and its latest 15, each payload capped at 32 KiB. A flood therefore cannot evict the first evidence. An SDK retry with the same `event_id` is counted but not stored twice.
- Past 500 unresolved issues in a service, new fingerprints are counted under one overflow issue. Resolving or ignoring issues makes room again, up to a hard cap of 1,500 issues of any status.
- Alerts are limited to 10 per service per hour. The next one is `alert.error_burst`, and then alerts stay quiet until the hour ends. Reaching the issue cap always alerts.
- Alerts name the service and the issue number, never the text the sender chose.

**Retention**
- Events are kept 30 days.
- An issue not seen for 90 days is removed with its events, by the housekeeping step `error-events`.
- The key is stored as a SHA-256 hash in the settings row `error_ingest:<serviceId>`.

**Upgrade**
- Migration `0105_error_ingest` only adds the two tables.

## Error-rate and latency alerts

Two alert metrics read the traffic analytics of one service: `error_rate`, the share of requests answered 5xx in percent, and `latency_p95`, the 95th percentile response time in milliseconds. Add them under **Monitoring → Alert Rules**, or with `POST /v1/alerts` (operator), for example `{ "name": "api errors", "metric": "error_rate", "operator": ">", "threshold": 5, "serviceId": 12 }`.

**How they are measured**
- Each 30-second collector tick sums the minute rollups of the last 5 minutes for the rule's service, across all its domains.
- A service with fewer than 20 requests in that window gets no sample, so its rule keeps its current state: two failed requests on a quiet service are not an outage, and silence is not a recovery.
- The p95 is estimated from the latency histogram (buckets 5 ms to 10 s), so it is exact only to its bucket.
- Fire-after counts collector samples as for every other metric. Because the window is 5 minutes, a short spike keeps the value up for up to 5 minutes.

**Limits**
- Traffic analytics must be on (**Traefik → Traffic**). With it off, these rules never sample.
- They are per service: a rule without a `serviceId` is refused (`error_rate rules are per service`), and so is a patch that clears it.
- Only traffic that passes the panel host's Traefik is counted, as in the traffic view.
- Fired and recovered alerts go to the same channels and subscriptions as the other alert metrics. No migration: `alert_rules.metric` is free text.

## Usage and cost

**Monitoring → Usage and cost** (operators) shows what each service used over the last 24 hours or 7, 30 or 90 days, and what that cost. Group it by service, project or workspace.

What is counted:
- **CPU in core-hours.** One fully busy core for an hour is 1. It comes from the 30-second samples and their summaries described under [resource history](#configure-resource-history). The window uses the same tier boundaries as the charts, so no sample is counted twice.
- **Memory in GiB-hours**, from the same samples.
- **Disk in GB-hours**: once an hour, the panel measures the volumes each service mounts, its data volume and its attached volumes, and stores the total. The panel host reads every volume with one `docker system df -v`; a node's agent measures each volume. If any volume cannot be measured, that service's hourly sample is omitted. Earlier versions could store partial totals. Missing or partial samples make the reported usage lower than the actual total; the report cannot recover those measurements. Disk follows the same retention as CPU and memory.
- **Egress in GB and requests**, from the hourly rows of traffic analytics. Both stay at zero while traffic analytics is off.

Each sample stands for one 30-second interval. A collection cycle the panel skipped, for example while it was restarting, is not counted.

CPU and memory reach back only as far as resource history is kept. With the default of one day, a 30-day window counts one day, and the card says so. Raise the retention to cover longer windows; data already deleted does not come back.

**Cost.** Under *Server costs*, enter what each server costs a month and the currency. The panel host is one of the servers. For a window, the panel:
1. prorates each server's monthly cost at 730 hours a month;
2. splits it among the services on that server: half by their share of its CPU time, half by their share of its memory.

A server that measured nothing keeps its whole cost as *not carried by any service*. A server with no cost entered leaves its services unpriced.

Limits:
- A service is priced on its primary server. Extra placements and Swarm tasks on other nodes are not split out.
- A service tagged into two projects or workspaces counts in both, so group rows do not add up to the total.
- Disk is reported but does not enter the cost split, which stays half CPU, half memory. Database volumes are not counted, since the report covers services.

Routes (operator only):
- `GET /v1/usage?days=30` returns the report, 1–90 days.
- `GET` and `PUT /v1/usage/costs` read and set the costs, for example `{ "currency": "EUR", "servers": [{ "serverId": null, "monthlyCost": 40 }] }`, where `serverId: null` is the panel host. A change is audited as `usage.costs_update`.

SDK: `usage.report({ days })`, `usage.costs()` and `usage.setCosts(input)`.

No migration: the costs are one settings row (`usage_costs`). Nothing new is collected.

## API and SDK

All monitoring settings/export and log-queue management routes require an
operator. Queue responses contain counts and timestamps, never queued log payloads.

| Method and path | SDK |
| --- | --- |
| GET /v1/stats/observability | stats.observability.get() |
| PATCH /v1/stats/observability | stats.observability.update(patch) |
| POST /v1/stats/observability/test | stats.observability.test() |
| GET /v1/stats/prometheus | Authenticated text scrape |
| GET /v1/log-drains/:id/queue | logDrains.queue(id) |
| POST /v1/log-drains/:id/queue/retry | logDrains.retryQueue(id) |
| DELETE /v1/log-drains/:id/queue | logDrains.discardQueue(id) |

PATCH accepts retentionDays, prometheusEnabled, otlpEndpoint,
otlpAuthorization and logQueueMaxMb. Omitted fields remain unchanged.

## Upgrade and recovery

Migration **0096_observability_delivery** adds metric_rollups,
log_drain_cursors and log_drain_batches. Existing service data and the one-day
default are preserved. Save the panel database and master keys together:
encrypted queued logs cannot be recovered without their keys. Do not manually
drop the new tables during a downgrade; older binaries do not deliver this queue.
Use the normal panel backup/restore procedure before any rollback.

docs.markdown:
# Panel Self-Backup NineDeploy can back up **the panel itself** on a schedule: its database, its master key, its `.env` and its Traefik configuration. Each backup is encrypted with a **recovery passphrase** that you choose and keep, then uploaded to one of your S3-compatible backup destinations. It is **off by default**. An upgraded panel behaves exactly as before until an operator turns it on under **Settings → Panel backup**. --- ## 🔑 1. What you must keep (read this first) | Keep this | Where | Why | |---|---|---| | **The recovery passphrase** | A password manager or vault, **not** on the panel server | Every panel backup is encrypted with it. Without it, no backup can be opened, by you or by NineDeploy. | | **The bucket credentials** (endpoint, bucket, access key, secret key) | Same place | A new server needs them to reach the backups. | | **`NINEDEPLOY_MASTER_KEY` / `NINEDEPLOY_MASTER_KEYS`**, *only if you set one* | Same place | When the master key comes from the environment rather than the `master.key` file, the backup does **not** contain it. The settings page shows a warning when this applies. | Why a passphrase and not the master key? The backup contains the master key. Its job is to restore the panel on a new machine after the old one, and its key, are gone. A backup that only the lost key could open would be useless, so it is sealed with a secret that lives outside the server. The panel stores the passphrase **encrypted under its master key** (settings key `panel_backup_passphrase_encrypted`), so scheduled runs need no one at the keyboard. The API never returns it. Master-key rotation re-encrypts it along with the other stored secrets. Changing the passphrase only affects **new** backups. Older objects keep the passphrase they were made with. Keep old passphrases until those backups have aged out of retention. --- ## 📦 2. What a backup contains The artifact is the same archive `GET /v1/system/export` produces (one format, one importer), wrapped in a passphrase envelope: | Member | Content | |---|---| | `_db-.db` | A consistent snapshot of the panel's SQLite database, taken with `VACUUM INTO` while the panel keeps serving. It is never a raw copy of the live WAL files. | | `master.key` | The instance master key file, when one exists. | | `_env-` | The panel's `.env` (from its working directory), when present. | | `traefik/` | The panel's Traefik config directory (dynamic config, ACME store). | | `_meta-.json` | Export time, row counts, `kind: "panel-backup"`, the panel version and whether the master key came from the environment. | **Not included** (each has its own backup path): - **App volumes:** volume snapshots on the Backups page. - **Managed database data:** per-database dumps on the Backups page and the database's Backups tab. - **Docker images and build caches:** rebuilt or pulled again on redeploy. - **Remote nodes' local state:** each node re-enrolls against the restored panel. Objects are written to `/panel-backups/ninedeploy-panel--.ndpb`. ### Envelope format (`NDPB1`) ``` NDPB1:scrypt:::

::\n header line (also the GCM AAD) <16-byte GCM tag> ``` The key is `scrypt(passphrase, salt, 32 bytes, N, r, p)`. Today N=32768, r=8, p=1. Readers accept N between 2^14 and 2^20. Because the header is authenticated, a wrong passphrase, a damaged file, or an object someone swapped into the bucket all fail the same way, and nothing is imported. --- ## ⚙️ 3. Setting it up 1. Add a bucket under **Backups → Destinations** and use **Test** to confirm the panel can reach it. 2. Open **Settings → Panel backup**: - **Schedule:** a 5-field cron expression in server time. Default: `0 3 * * *`. - **Destination:** the bucket from step 1. - **Keep:** how many panel backups to retain (1–365, default 7). - **Recovery passphrase:** at least 12 characters. Type it twice, then store it off the server. 3. Turn on **Scheduled backups** and save. 4. Click **Back up now** once and confirm that the run reports `completed` and the object appears in the list. The same settings are available from the CLI (`ninedeploy system panel-backup set --enable --destination 1 --cron "0 3 * * *" --retain 7 --passphrase`) and through the SDK (`client.system.panelBackup.update(...)`). ### Runs, retention and alerts - **No overlap.** If a run (or a restore) is still in progress when the next tick fires, that tick is skipped and audited as `backup.panel.skipped`. "Back up now" answers `409` in the same situation. - **Retention never deletes the last good backup.** Pruning runs only after a successful upload, keeps the newest *N* (at least one), and always keeps the backup that was just written. A failed run prunes nothing. If a delete fails, the run still counts as completed: the new backup is safe, the run records a warning, and the delete is retried next time. Objects that do not match the panel-backup name pattern are never touched. - **Every outcome is audited.** Runs produce `backup.panel.completed`, `backup.panel.failed` or `backup.panel.skipped`. Settings changes produce `backup.panel.settings` (never with the passphrase in it). Restores produce `backup.panel.restore` or `backup.panel.restore_failed`, plus `system.import`. Audit is the notification fan-out, so a channel subscribed to `backup.` is told when a scheduled panel backup fails. - **Plaintext never stays on disk.** The unencrypted archive is deleted the moment the sealed copy exists. Scratch files live in `/_panel-backup/` and are cleared at boot. ### Keep only one panel writing to a prefix If you restore onto a new server while the old one is still running with panel backups enabled, both panels write to, and prune, the same `panel-backups/` prefix. Disable panel backups on the old server, or point the new one at another destination or prefix. --- ## ♻️ 4. Restoring A restore **replaces** the panel's database, master key, `.env` and Traefik config. The files it replaces are moved to `/_backup-/` first. NineDeploy must be restarted afterwards, just as after any `system import`. Install the **same or a newer** NineDeploy version than the one that wrote the backup. A newer panel migrates the restored database when it starts. An older panel cannot read a newer database. ### A. From the panel (fresh install) 1. Install NineDeploy on the new server and finish the first-run setup. This account is temporary: the restore replaces it. 2. Add the **same bucket** under **Backups → Destinations**, with the same prefix. 3. Open **Settings → Panel backup**. Under *Backups in the destination*, pick that destination. 4. Click **Restore…** on the backup you want, enter the recovery passphrase, and type the backup's file name to confirm. 5. Restart NineDeploy (`sudo systemctl restart ninedeploy`, or restart the container), then sign in with the **old** panel's credentials. The API equivalent is `POST /v1/system/panel-backup/restore` with `{ destinationId, key, passphrase, confirm: "" }`, or `client.system.panelBackup.restore(...)` in the SDK. ### B. Offline (CLI) Use this path if the new panel cannot reach the bucket, or if you have already downloaded the object: ```bash # 1. Download the .ndpb object with any S3 client, e.g. aws s3 cp s3:////panel-backups/ninedeploy-panel-<…>.ndpb . # 2. Open it with the recovery passphrase (works without a running panel) ninedeploy system panel-backup decrypt ninedeploy-panel-<…>.ndpb backup.tar.gz # 3. Import it into the fresh panel (destructive, asks for confirmation) ninedeploy login # prompts for the new panel URL and credentials ninedeploy system import backup.tar.gz # 4. Restart NineDeploy ``` `backup.tar.gz` is a plain `/system/export` archive, so you can also upload it under **Settings → Migration → Import backup**. It contains the database and the master key, so delete it once the import is done. ### After the restore - Remote servers are rows in the restored database. Check that each one shows online under **Servers**. If the panel's address changed, re-enroll any node that cannot reach it. - If the master key came from `NINEDEPLOY_MASTER_KEY(S)`, set the same value on the new server **before** restarting. - Run **Back up now** on the restored panel to confirm the schedule still works from its new home. --- ## 🔌 5. API, SDK and CLI reference All routes are instance-operator only. | Route | SDK | CLI | |---|---|---| | `GET /v1/system/panel-backup` | `system.panelBackup.get()` | `system panel-backup status` | | `PUT /v1/system/panel-backup` | `system.panelBackup.update(patch)` | `system panel-backup set …` | | `POST /v1/system/panel-backup/run` (202, background) | `system.panelBackup.run()` | `system panel-backup now [--wait]` | | `GET /v1/system/panel-backup/remote[?destinationId=]` | `system.panelBackup.list(id?)` | `system panel-backup list [--destination]` | | `POST /v1/system/panel-backup/restore` | `system.panelBackup.restore(input)` | offline: `system panel-backup decrypt` + `system import` | Storage: the configuration lives in the `settings` table. The `panel_backup` key holds the schedule, destination and retention. `panel_backup_passphrase_encrypted` holds the passphrase, sealed. `panel_backup_state` holds the last run and the last success. No schema migration is involved, and an absent row means "disabled".

docs.markdown:
# Plugins SDK & Microkernel Architecture

NineDeploy features an extensible Microkernel architecture allowing developers to hook into the deployment lifecycle, register custom UI navigation menus, and swap core driver implementations.

---

## 🔌 1. Kernel Events & Waterfall Hooks

The kernel exposes two integration surfaces: a typed **event bus** (`ctx.on`) for observing lifecycle activity, and sequential **waterfall hooks** (`ctx.tapHook`) that can inspect — and in some cases abort or amend — pipeline steps.

### Events (`ctx.on(event, handler)`)

The bus is fed from the application's audit stream — every `audit()` call, which
is the one choke point each meaningful state change already passes through (see
`kernel/auditBridge.ts`). These events **fire today**:

| Event | Source |
| :--- | :--- |
| `audit.recorded` | Every audit entry, raw: `{ action, entity, actorUserId, ts }`. Subscribe here for anything the table below does not cover. |
| `deployment.status_changed` | Bridged from `deploy.*` (start / success / failed / rollback / cancel) |
| `service.health_changed` | Bridged from `service.start` / `stop` / `restart` |
| `backup.completed` | Bridged from `backup.create` |
| `alert.triggered` | Bridged from `alert.fired` / `alert.recovered` |
| `plugin.registered`, `plugin.reloaded`, `plugin.status_changed` | Kernel lifecycle |
| `notification.queued` | Emitted by the built-in notifications plugin as an **extension point**. It is not the delivery path: `lib/notifier` owns channels, retries and the delivery log, so consuming this and sending would double every alert. |
| `telemetry.recorded`, `tunnel.route_evaluated` | Built-in telemetry / Cloudflare-tunnel plugins |

**Emitting (r530).** A sandboxed plugin may only emit events in its own
namespace, `plugin.<pluginId>.<name>` (e.g. `plugin.acme-notifier.synced`).
Any other name is dropped, logged once per name and audited once per load as
`plugin.event_rejected` — a plugin cannot forge `audit.recorded`,
`deployment.status_changed`, `alert.triggered`, `telemetry.recorded` or any
other kernel event. Emissions are tagged host-side with
`{ kind: 'plugin', pluginId }` (`EventOrigin` in `kernel/types.ts`); the bus
never hands a plugin-origin emission to a typed `events.on(...)` listener, and
an exact-name `events.onCustom(...)` listener receives one only when it opts in
with `{ acceptPluginOrigin: true }`. Wildcard (`'*'`) listeners see everything
and get the origin as their third argument — the telemetry streamer drops
plugin-origin events there. Built-in plugins therefore only ever act on
kernel/audit-bridge events.

`DomainEvents` in `kernel/types.ts` declares more names than this
(`service.created`, `database.created`, `server.announced`, `config.changed`, …).
They are typed for forward compatibility but **nothing emits them yet** — use
`audit.recorded` and match on `action` if you need one of those today.

### Sequential hooks (`tapHook(name, fn)`)

| Hook Name | Lifecycle Trigger | Capabilities |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `deploy:before` | Prior to build/clone | Inspect the service/target commit; abort deployments |
| `deploy:build_complete` | Image built | Observe image tag & build duration |
| `deploy:healthcheck` | After health probe | React to healthy/unhealthy candidates |
| `deploy:after` | Post-switchover | Send custom Slack/Discord alerts, trigger webhooks |
| `database:before_delete` | Before a database removal | Veto via `allowOrAbort` |
| `database:after_create` | New database provisioned | Provision sidecars, seed data |
| `proxy:sync_routes` | Traefik route sync | Inspect the resolved domains/services |
| `server:before_announce` | Agent enrolment | Validate/reject joining nodes |

```typescript
import { definePlugin } from '@ninedeploy/plugin-sdk';

export default definePlugin({
  id: 'my-custom-hook',
  name: 'Custom Hook Plugin',
  version: '1.0.0',
  init(ctx) {
    // Pick an event from the "fires today" table above. `service.deployed` is
    // declared but not emitted yet — `deployment.status_changed` is its live
    // equivalent.
    ctx.on('deployment.status_changed', (payload) => {
      console.log(`Deployment ${payload.deploymentId} -> ${payload.status}`);
      // Your own events live under plugin.<your id>.* — nothing else is accepted.
      ctx.emit(`plugin.${ctx.pluginId}.deploy_seen`, { status: payload.status });
    });
    const untap = ctx.tapHook(
      'deploy:before',
      async (payload) => {
        // Inspect or amend deployment payload
        return payload;
      },
      // Only `priority` is honoured — the host applies its own per-tap
      // budget (5 s) and rejection-based rollback; per-tap rollback/
      // timeoutMs/id options do not exist (r473 removed the phantom types).
      { priority: 150 },
    );
    void untap;
  },
});
```

The official plugins shipped in-tree are the reference implementations for the
event and hook APIs.

### 🛡️ 2. Permission-Model Process Sandboxing (r468)

NineDeploy executes third-party community extensions in a dedicated **child process running under Node's permission model**, with an asynchronous RPC bridge:

- **Deny-by-default capabilities**: the sandbox process runs with `--permission` and exactly two fs-read allowlist entries (its own bootstrap directory and the package manifest the ESM loader needs). Filesystem read/write outside that, spawning child processes, opening worker threads and loading native addons are all denied by the runtime itself — a plugin that tries gets `ERR_ACCESS_DENIED`, not a warning. The classic exfiltration paths (read `master.key`/`.env`/the SQLite db, fork a shell) are physically closed.
- **Memory Limits**: the child runs with `--max-old-space-size=64` and `--max-semi-space-size=16` (the V8 generation-size equivalents of the old worker limits).
- **Crash Isolation**: if an external plugin throws a fatal exception or crashes its process, the NineDeploy core API and database remain unaffected. The kernel flags the plugin state as `errored` and continues running; a wedged child that ignores SIGTERM is SIGKILLed after a 3 s grace.
- **Scoped RPC Bridge**: sandboxed plugins interact through `PluginContext` APIs (`events.on`, `tapHook`, `scopedConfig.get/set`); the bridge namespaces config access (`plugin:<id>:`) and event emission (`plugin.<id>.`, r530) per plugin id.
- **Plugin ids (r531)**: a sandbox install must use an id matching `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}$` (case-insensitive) that is neither a built-in plugin id (`notifications-dispatcher`, `domain-presets`, `webhook-out`, … — `BUILT_IN_PLUGIN_IDS` in `kernel/pluginLoader.ts`) nor a marketplace catalog id, and may not take over a row installed from a different source. A colliding install is refused with HTTP 409. A row that already collides from an older version is **skipped at boot** with the reason recorded on the row (status `errored`), the built-in keeps running, and enable/disable/reload answer 409 for it — uninstall removes just the stray row.
- **Secret redaction (r533)**: hook payloads and relayed events are copied before they cross the IPC boundary, with secret-bearing fields replaced by `"[redacted]"` — matched by key name at any depth (password/passphrase, secret, token, API key, private key, credential, htpasswd, basicAuth, authorization, cookie, master key — e.g. `databases.passwordEncrypted`, `domains.basicAuth`/`verificationToken`, the `server:before_announce` token), `env`/`envVars`/`environment` objects, `services.composeContent`, and URL userinfo (`repoUrl`). Ids, names, image, branch, commit, ports, status and hostnames pass through. A hook result that still holds a placeholder gets the original value back, so echoing the payload never leaks `[redacted]` into the pipeline.
- **Concurrent hook calls (r532)**: each invocation carries its own `callId` (echoed by the panel-shipped bootstrap), so two concurrent calls of one tap resolve independently.
- **Network (r534)**: not part of the flag set the panel controls. On Node ≥ 25 (`--allow-net` exists; the Docker image and CI run Node 26) `--permission` denies outbound connections, DNS and listening by default and the panel never passes `--allow-net` — a sandbox plugin has **no network**. On Node 22/24 (bare-metal installs on supported 22.23.4+ / 24.22.1+ patch levels) the permission model has no network scope: a sandbox plugin **can** open sockets and `fetch`. Plugin manifests declare no capabilities, so there is no per-plugin grant; `SandboxPlugin.networkDenied()` reports which case the running Node is in.
- **Scrubbed environment (r414, carried over)**: `process.env` is not part of the permission model, so the child still gets only `PATH`/`LANG`/`TZ` — no `NINEDEPLOY_MASTER_KEY(S)`/JWT secret.
- **Remaining trust decision**: the sandboxed plugin can still DO everything its ctx APIs allow — read/write its own namespaced config (including secrets you store there), react to every event (redacted), and participate in deploy hooks. Installing a third-party plugin remains an operator-level trust decision about what it may do through the panel, exactly like granting it a limited API key; the boundary is that it can no longer reach around the API. The install route is admin-gated accordingly.

### 🗂️ 3. Dynamic UI Menus, Widgets & Driver Registries

- **Menu & Widget Slots**: Inject custom navigation tabs and live dashboard widgets:
  - `sidebar:main`, `sidebar:secondary`: Sidebar navigation
  - `dashboard:overview`: Live dashboard telemetry & overview cards
  - `service:tabs`, `service:overview:widget`: Service-level inspection panels
  - `command:palette`: Global command search items
- **ServiceRegistry**: Interchange core storage, DNS (Cloudflare, DNSimple, Namecheap, Route 53, OVH, Porkbun, Hetzner), orchestrator, and deploy drivers dynamically at runtime.
- **ConfigCenter Integration**: Read and persist encrypted plugin configurations in the central key-value store.
