# Secret managers: Vault / OpenBao, AWS, GCP, Azure, 1Password and exec

From 0.14, an environment value can reference a secret held in **HashiCorp Vault** or **OpenBao** (KV version 2) or in **AWS Secrets Manager**. The panel fetches the secret when a deploy starts and passes the value to the container. It never stores the value.

These two providers run alongside the existing instance-wide Infisical or Doppler provider (Settings → Integrations → Vault provider, `/v1/settings/vault`), which is unchanged.

---

## 1. Reference syntax

| Reference | Resolves to |
| :--- | :--- |
| `${{vault:<path>#<field>}}` | One field of a KV v2 secret. `<path>` is relative to the configured mount. |
| `${{aws:<secretId>}}` | The whole `SecretString` of a secret. `<secretId>` is a secret name or a full ARN. |
| `${{aws:<secretId>#<jsonKey>}}` | One key of a `SecretString` that holds a JSON object. |
| `${{infisical:KEY}}` / `${{doppler:KEY}}` | The existing provider, unchanged. |

- **Vault paths** are segments of `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . -` joined by `/`, with no leading `/` and no `.` or `..` segment. Fields use the same characters.
- **AWS secret ids** use `A-Z a-z 0-9 / _ + = . @ : -` (up to 2048 characters), so both names and ARNs work. JSON keys use `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . -`.
- A reference can sit inside a longer value, and one value can hold several:

  ```text
  DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:${{vault:apps/billing/prod#db_password}}@db:5432/app
  STRIPE_KEY=${{aws:prod/billing#stripe_key}}
  LICENSE=${{aws:arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:license-AbCdEf}}
  ```

- A string field is used as it is. Any other JSON value (a number, an object) is passed as its JSON text.
- A string that does not match this grammar is not a reference anywhere, not at deploy time and not at any write gate.

---

## 2. HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao

Configure it under **Settings → Integrations → Secret managers**, with `ninedeploy secrets providers set-vault`, or with `PUT /v1/settings/secret-providers/vault`:

```json
{
  "config": {
    "address": "https://vault.example.com",
    "namespace": "team-a",
    "mount": "secret",
    "authMethod": "approle",
    "approleMount": "approle"
  },
  "credentials": { "roleId": "…", "secretId": "…" }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `address` | `https://` only. `http://` is accepted only with `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`. No credentials, query or fragment. |
| `namespace` | Optional. Sent as `X-Vault-Namespace` (Vault Enterprise, OpenBao namespaces). |
| `mount` | The KV v2 mount (default `secret`). Reads go to `GET /v1/<mount>/data/<path>`. |
| `authMethod` | `token` (credentials `{token}`) or `approle` (credentials `{roleId, secretId}`). |
| `approleMount` | The AppRole auth mount (default `approle`). |

- **KV version 2 only.** A mount that answers without `data.data` is reported as "not a KV version 2 engine". KV version 1 is not supported.
- **Token auth does not renew the token.** Use a periodic token, or AppRole. With AppRole, the panel logs in and caches the client token until 60 seconds before its lease ends. Saving the provider again drops the cached token.
- **A private CA:** start the panel with `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/ca.pem`.
- **A Vault on your LAN** (a private, loopback or link-local address) is refused by the egress guard unless `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1` is set; the error says so.
- **Test** (`POST /v1/settings/secret-providers/vault/test`, optional `{probePath}`) calls `auth/token/lookup-self`, or performs a fresh AppRole login, and then reads `probePath` if you give one.

A minimal setup:

```bash
vault secrets enable -path=secret kv-v2          # skip if the mount exists
vault kv put secret/apps/billing/prod db_password='…'

vault policy write ninedeploy - <<'EOF'
path "secret/data/apps/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF

# Either a periodic token …
vault token create -policy=ninedeploy -period=24h
# … or AppRole
vault auth enable approle
vault write auth/approle/role/ninedeploy token_policies=ninedeploy token_ttl=1h token_max_ttl=4h
vault read auth/approle/role/ninedeploy/role-id
vault write -f auth/approle/role/ninedeploy/secret-id
```

---

## 3. AWS Secrets Manager

Configure it under **Settings → Integrations → Secret managers**, with `ninedeploy secrets providers set-aws`, or with `PUT /v1/settings/secret-providers/aws`:

```json
{
  "config": {
    "region": "eu-west-1",
    "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ninedeploy-secrets",
    "externalId": "ninedeploy-prod",
    "roleSessionName": "ninedeploy"
  },
  "credentials": { "accessKeyId": "AKIA…", "secretAccessKey": "…" }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `region` | For example `eu-west-1` or `us-gov-west-1`. Calls go to `https://secretsmanager.<region>.amazonaws.com/` (`.amazonaws.com.cn` for `cn-` regions). |
| `endpoint` | Optional. A VPC endpoint or a compatible service; `https://` (http only with private egress). |
| `roleArn` | Optional. The panel calls STS `AssumeRole` (regional endpoint) with the stored key and caches the session until 5 minutes before it expires. |
| `externalId` | Optional; needs `roleArn`. |
| `roleSessionName` | Default `ninedeploy`. |
| credentials | `accessKeyId` (`AKIA…` or `ASIA…`), `secretAccessKey`, and `sessionToken` for temporary keys. |

- Requests are `secretsmanager.GetSecretValue`, signed with SigV4. No AWS SDK is involved.
- **Instance and ECS roles (IMDS) are not supported.** The egress guard blocks link-local addresses, so store an access key. Point it at a role with `roleArn` if you prefer short sessions.
- `SecretBinary` secrets are refused; store the value as a `SecretString`. A `#jsonKey` needs a `SecretString` that is a JSON object.
- **Test** (`POST /v1/settings/secret-providers/aws/test`, optional `{probeSecretId}`) calls STS `GetCallerIdentity`, performs a fresh `AssumeRole` when `roleArn` is set, and then reads `probeSecretId` if you give one.

The IAM policy the key (or the assumed role) needs:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:prod/*" }
  ]
}
```

With `roleArn`, the key's own identity also needs `sts:AssumeRole` on that role, and the role's trust policy must allow it (with the `sts:ExternalId` condition when you set `externalId`). A secret encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key also needs `kms:Decrypt` on that key.

---

## 3a. More secret managers (G3.2)

Five more reference forms. All except `op` also accept `#<jsonKey>`, which reads one key of a value that holds a JSON object.

| Reference | Provider | Settings |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `${{ssm:<name>}}` | AWS Systems Manager **Parameter Store**. SecureString values are decrypted. | Uses the **aws** provider above: the same key or assumed role, and the same region. It always uses the regional public `ssm` endpoint, because a custom `endpoint` names Secrets Manager only. The identity needs `ssm:GetParameter` (and `kms:Decrypt` for a customer-managed key). |
| `${{gcp:<secret>[@<version>]}}` | **GCP Secret Manager**. The version defaults to `latest`. | A service account JSON key, plus `projectId` (optional; defaults to the key's project). The account needs *Secret Manager Secret Accessor*. The assertion is only ever sent to `oauth2.googleapis.com`, whatever `token_uri` the key file names. A binary (non-UTF-8) payload is refused. |
| `${{azure:<name>[@<version>]}}` | **Azure Key Vault** | `vaultUrl` (`https://<name>.vault.azure.net`, or the China or US Gov equivalent; other hosts are refused), `tenantId`, `clientId` and a client secret. The secret goes only to Microsoft Entra ID for that vault's cloud. The app needs *Key Vault Secrets User* or a get-secret access policy. A new tenant, client id **or vault URL** needs the secret again: a token for `vault.azure.net` works at any vault. |
| `${{op:<vault>/<item>[/<section>]/<field>}}` | **1Password Connect** | The Connect server `address` and an access token. Each part is a name or a 26-character id. A name that matches nothing, or more than one entry, fails the deploy. A Connect server on a private network needs `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`. |
| `${{exec:<name>}}` | The operator's **exec command** | Off unless the panel was started with `NINEDEPLOY_SECRET_EXEC=1`; without it the provider can be neither saved nor used. See below. |

**The exec provider.** It covers any secret manager that has a command-line client: Bitwarden (`bw`), Doppler, `op`, `pass`, sops, or a script.

- **How it runs:** the operator stores an argv, for example `["/usr/local/bin/bw", "get", "password", "{name}"]`, and a timeout (1–60 s, default 10). At deploy time the panel runs the argv on its host **without a shell**:
  - `{name}` in any argument is replaced by the reference name;
  - the name is also passed in `NINEDEPLOY_SECRET_NAME`;
  - the command gets only `PATH`, `HOME` and that variable, never the panel's own environment.
- **The value:** stdout, minus one trailing newline.
- **Failures:** a non-zero exit, the timeout or more than 64 KiB of output fails the deploy. The first 200 characters of stderr are shown.
- **Names:** reference names use `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . / : @ -`, never start with `-` (as its own argument a name could otherwise read as an option) and never contain a `..` segment. It is still the command that decides what a name may reach: put `--` before `{name}` where the client supports it.

Settings → Integrations → *Secret managers* has a panel for each of these kinds; Parameter Store uses the AWS panel. **Test connection** takes an optional probe:

- gcp, azure, onepassword and exec: a reference name to resolve;
- aws: `probeParameter`, a Parameter Store parameter to read, through the API or `--probe-parameter`.

`ninedeploy secrets providers test|delete` accepts every kind.

The column that names the kind is plain text, so these kinds need **no migration**. Existing text of these shapes in env values stays literal, with a warning, until its provider is configured, as in §6. The new forms do become subject to the write gates and the preview withholding in §4.

---

## 4. Who may use references

The instance-wide **allowlist** that governs Infisical and Doppler references (Settings → Integrations → *Allowed workspaces*, `PUT /v1/settings/vault/allowlist`) governs Vault and AWS references too. The credentials are instance-wide, so only services owned by an operator, or tagged into an allowed workspace, may use them:

- **Writes:** a non-operator cannot save an env value containing a reference unless the service's workspace is allowed.
- **Deploys:** a service that is not allowed fails its deploy with an actionable message. The check runs once, before the first secret is fetched.
- **PR previews** never receive a referenced value; previews withhold them. The preview-only environment refuses references, and templates and service bundles detect them too.
- The allowlist that was seeded from existing usage when it was introduced (r510) grandfathered only services that used Infisical or Doppler references. It does not admit anyone to Vault or AWS.

---

## 5. Behaviour and limits at deploy time

- Each distinct Vault path or AWS secret is fetched **once per deploy**, however many env keys reference it.
- At most **100** distinct Vault/AWS references per deploy, **15 seconds** per provider call, **60 seconds** for all of a deploy's calls together, and **64 KiB** per resolved value.
- A missing field or JSON key, an unreachable provider or a refused credential **fails the deploy**. A half-resolved secret leaking the raw reference into a container would be worse.
- Every call goes through the egress guard: DNS is resolved and pinned, private, loopback and link-local addresses are refused unless `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`, and a redirect is an error, never followed.
- Error messages never contain the token, key, secret id or path; provider response bodies are cut to 200 characters.

---

## 6. Literal until configured

A `${{vault:…}}` or `${{aws:…}}` reference whose provider is **not configured** (no provider saved, the provider is disabled, or its stored credentials cannot be decrypted with the current master key) **stays literal**. The container receives the text `${{vault:…}}` unchanged, and the deploy log warns, naming the env keys (never the values). This is exactly what every release before 0.14 did with such a string, so an install that already had text of this shape deploys byte for byte as before.

Two things do change for such strings from 0.14 on: a non-operator's write is subject to the allowlist, and PR previews withhold them. Both are fail-safe.

Infisical and Doppler keep their old behaviour: a reference to one of them while it is not configured fails the deploy. Deleting a Vault or AWS provider (`DELETE /v1/settings/secret-providers/<kind>`) turns its references back into literal text at the next deploy.

---

## 7. Management API

All routes are operator-only. API tokens need the `settings` scope.

| Route | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `GET /v1/settings/secret-providers` | `[{kind, configured, enabled, config, hasCredential, lastTestedAt, lastTestError}]` for `vault`, `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `onepassword` and `exec`. Credentials are never returned. |
| `PUT /v1/settings/secret-providers/<kind>` | Save. An omitted credential field keeps the stored value, except that a new auth method, AppRole role id or access key id must come with its own secret. Saving clears the last test result. |
| `DELETE /v1/settings/secret-providers/<kind>` | Remove. References become literal again. |
| `POST /v1/settings/secret-providers/<kind>/test` | `{ok, detail}`; probes `probePath` (vault), `probeSecretId` / `probeParameter` (aws), `probeName` (the others). Records `lastTestedAt` and `lastTestError` only. |

A bad address, region, key id or role ARN is a 400 at save time, not a failed deploy later. Saves and deletions are audited as `settings.secret_provider.save` and `settings.secret_provider.delete`, with the kind and switches only, never an address path or a credential. The credentials are one encrypted envelope (`secret_providers.credential_encrypted`), re-encrypted by master-key rotation like every other secret.

---

## 8. Rolling back to 0.13

0.13 ignores the `secret_providers` table and does not know the new reference forms. A container deployed on 0.13 therefore receives the **literal reference string**. Nothing leaks, but the app is misconfigured. Before rolling back, move the affected values into ordinary secret env vars (or into Infisical or Doppler), or redeploy only after upgrading again. The stored provider settings survive a rollback and work again after the next upgrade. See [ROLLBACK.md](./ROLLBACK.md).

docs.markdown:
# Security Audit Remediation — September 2026

This document consolidates the remediation of the September 2026 security
audit across four working sessions. Every item lists the behavior change,
the operator-facing configuration it introduces, and the tests that lock it
in. Commits live on `main` (see `git log --grep "audit"` or the per-area
messages below).

## 1. Cross-tenant data chains (critical)

| Threat | Closure |
|---|---|
| Tagging a service with another tenant's project id leaked that project's decrypted shared env into the attacker's container at deploy time | `POST /v1/services` validates `tagProjectIds` / `tagWorkspaceIds` / `tagLabelIds` against caller visibility (same rule as `PUT /:id/tags`). Defence in depth: `engine/pipeline.ts → filterTrustworthyProjectLinks` re-verifies every `service_projects` link against the owner's workspace seat before decrypting; NULL-workspace projects never inject env |
| Any member could attach another tenant's `nd-svc-*` / `nd-db-*` volume read-write, or delete files from its root via config-repair | `serviceVolumes.ts → assertVolumeOwnership` runs before the docker probe on attach and config-repair: every attaching service must be visible to the caller, `nd-db-*` additionally requires `admin` on every candidate database, orphan/unknown managed names are operator-only |
| A member could attach a database they could merely SEE and read its admin-only password from the container env | `POST /:id/attachments` requires `assertDatabaseRole(..., 'admin')` (same tier as `/credentials`) |
| `visibleDatabaseIds` disagreed with `loadDatabaseForUser` (databases hidden from lists but open by id) | List visibility now derives from project workspace membership — identical rule to the detail loader |

Tests: `servicesCoverage.test.ts`, `serviceVolumes.test.ts`, `rbacRegression.test.ts`, `pipeline.test.ts`, `dashboard.test.ts`.

## 2. Remote agent transport (critical)

- Whether the agent "supports sealing" was decided by an **unauthenticated**
  probe and the plaintext fallback fired by default: one forged probe answer
  sent the agent token (full remote-execution authority) and the decrypted
  service secrets over HTTP. The fallback is now **opt-in** via
  `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT=1`; `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_REQUIRE_SEALED=1`
  remains the stricter alias and always wins.
- A sealed request now **requires** a sealed reply that verifies: plaintext
  responses and envelope failures are refused ("possible tampering").
- Sealed requests carry a fresh **nonce**; the agent echoes it inside the
  sealed reply and the core refuses mismatches — a captured envelope can no
  longer be replayed within the 5-minute seal window.
- Only an affirmative probe answer is cached.
- **Fleet upgrade note:** a node agent older than the nonce-echo change must
  be upgraded (agents and core ship the same binary); to temporarily keep a
  not-yet-upgraded fleet running, set `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT=1`
  on the core and upgrade as soon as possible.

Tests: `agentClient.test.ts` (downgrade/refusal/nonce/replay cases), `agentApp.test.ts`.

## 3. RBAC and API-token scopes

- Fine-grained `nd://scope/{read,write,admin}/<resource>` tokens were stored
  but never enforced — any fine-grained token could use EVERY resource.
  `plugins/auth.ts` now classifies each request (method + route, with
  sub-resource overrides for `env`, `webhooks`, `deploys`, `volumes`,
  `insights`, `domains` under `/services/:id`) and requires a covering
  scope; unclassified paths fail closed for fine-grained tokens.
  `NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_REQUIRE_SEALED`-style coarse scopes (`read`, `write`,
  `operator`) keep their previous meaning.
- `viewer` is now actually read-only: service/project/label/database
  creation requires `member`; domain verification and repo-insight refresh
  require `member` on the service; webhook create/delete require `admin`
  (the webhook secret is a standing deploy credential).
- The `/v1/events` WebSocket applies the same operator narrowing as HTTP
  (a scope-restricted token of an operator no longer sees the global feed).
- Instance-wide branding `PATCH` requires the operator flag.
- **New API tokens default to `['read']` scopes and a 365-day lifetime**
  (previously: unrestricted, never-expiring). Legacy `[]` tokens keep their
  old unrestricted meaning. CLI `tokens.create({ name })` therefore yields a
  read-only token — pass explicit scopes for write/CI usage.

Tests: `plugins/auth.test.ts` (central narrowing + classification),
`rbacRegression.test.ts`, `events.test.ts`, `auth.test.ts`.

## 4. Sessions, SAML, lockout, CSP

- Refresh tokens carry a `gen` claim bound to the session row's expiry:
  rotation advances the row, so a replayed/stolen old refresh token is
  refused **before any DB write** and cannot slide the session. Pre-rotation
  tokens migrate on first refresh.
- SAML: assertion-ID replay cache (checked after signature + digest
  verification), response/assertion `Issuer` must equal the IdP entityID,
  `InResponseTo` refused (the panel never initiates SAML), and
  `Audience` / `Destination` / `Recipient` are enforced when the operator
  configures `spEntityId` / `spAcsUrl` on the provider.
- SAML sign-in is **unavailable** (r354). The assertion consumer was only
  reachable with a Bearer session, so an IdP's browser POST always got 401,
  and the verifier has no XML canonicalization / enveloped-signature
  transform, so it cannot match a mainstream IdP's signature even if made
  public. Rather than expose a hand-rolled XML-DSig verifier to
  unauthenticated callers, `POST /v1/sso/providers` refuses `type: "saml"`
  (`code: "saml_unavailable"`) and `/v1/sso/:name/login` answers the same for
  older SAML rows. Use OIDC. A real SAML login (vetted c14n + transforms,
  SP-initiated AuthnRequest bound to `InResponseTo` and a RelayState cookie)
  is feature-release work.
- Login lockout is two-tier: 5 failures lock the **(account, IP) pair** (the
  guesser locks itself out; the real user is unaffected — the old
  per-account lock was a 15-minute DoS lever), and 25 failures across
  sources lock the account for distributed brute-force. Both land in the
  audit log.
- CSP `connect-src` drops the bare `ws:` / `wss:` grants; same-origin
  WebSockets remain covered by `'self'`.

Tests: `sessions.test.ts`, `sso.test.ts`, `loginLockout.test.ts`,
`securityHeaders` assertions in `app.test.ts`.

## 5. Installer, supply chain and exposure surface

- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` failure no longer falls back to a
  re-resolved install on a production host; opt in with
  `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_LOOSE_INSTALL=1` if you accept the supply-chain risk.
- The compose panel port binds **127.0.0.1** by default
  (`NINEDEPLOY_BIND` overrides); the generated public URL is localhost.
  Terminate TLS via Traefik and set `NINEDEPLOY_PUBLIC_URL`.
- The systemd unit adds `ProtectHome=read-only`. Optionally hand the
  install tree to root with `NINEDEPLOY_HARDEN_OWNERSHIP=1` (future
  updates then need `sudo`).
- Privileged third-party images are pinned: alpine helper sidecars →
  `alpine:3.21` (`lib/inventory.ts HELPER_IMAGE`), cloudflared → `2026.8.3`,
  Adminer → `6.0.1`, Redis Commander → digest
  `sha256:19cd0c49f418779fa2822a0496c5e6516d0c792effc39ed20089e6268477e40a`
  (the project publishes no version tags). Bump deliberately.
- The remote-node agent image reference was corrected from the
  non-existent `ghcr.io/ninedeploy/server:latest` to
  `ghcr.io/ninedeploy/ninedeploy:v<core version>` — provisioning previously
  always failed at pull time; the version match keeps node/core protocol
  (seal/nonce) in lockstep.
- The database Web Studio (Adminer / Redis Commander) publishes on
  **127.0.0.1** only. Redis Commander receives the database password via
  `REDIS_URL` (`REDIS_HOSTS` cannot carry one), so password-protected
  instances list keys instead of an empty tree. PgBouncer sidecars bind
  explicit host ports to loopback and authenticate with SCRAM-SHA-256
  (previously MD5).
- Exec error labels redact `--password=` / `-p` / `-a` values, keeping
  database passwords out of journald, the audit log and notifications.
- `resolveInRepo` refuses build paths that walk through symlinks (dangling
  included) and the generated `nixpacks.toml` escapes control characters —
  a repo-controlled manifest can no longer rewrite the file structure or
  write through an absolute symlink as root.

## 6. Functional races and honesty fixes

- Push webhooks sync `services.branch` immediately but leave `commitSha`
  to the deploy pipeline's success finalize — a failed build no longer
  reports a commit that never ran.
- Domain transfers: the pending-check filters on the clock (an expired
  transfer no longer blocks new ones forever) and acceptance claims the row
  conditionally before moving the domain (accept/accept and accept/cancel
  races resolved).
- Scheduled jobs hold a per-job lock: overlapping cron ticks or run-now
  double-clicks are skipped instead of running twice concurrently.
- Sandbox plugins persist `code`/`manifest` across restarts; a sandbox
  install without code is refused instead of registering an "active"
  plugin that executes nothing.
- The release workflow honors the `workflow_dispatch.tag` input in every
  step (checkout, validation, image tags, GHCR prune, GitHub Release) and
  smoke-checks the pushed multi-arch manifest before going green.
- `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint` and the `r057` test were repaired to green;
  the untracked `deploys-r069` test (which tested a fictional function and
  contradicted the shipped queued-stacking design) was removed — the real
  behaviors are covered in `deploys.test.ts`.

## 7. Known accepted risks (documented, not fixed by design)

- ~~Member-reachable git-host API calls in `sources.ts` are a conditional
  SSRF surface (member-controlled hosts).~~ **Closed (r077):** every
  `sources.ts` route has been operator-only since the RBAC overhaul, all
  its provider hosts are hardcoded, and the outbound calls now run
  through `guardedFetch` like every other panel webhook/API client —
  pinned by a wiring test, so the hardcoded-host invariant cannot drift.
- Exec/spawn everywhere passes arguments as **argv** through
  `lib/exec.ts` / `lib/spawnValidated.ts` (never a shell). Static scanners
  report these as "command injection" sinks; the pattern is the audited
  choke point of this codebase.
- `lib/loginLockout.ts`, `lib/totpReplay.ts` and similar in-process state
  resets on restart — accepted for a single-node self-hosted panel.
- The database Web Studio still serves its own plain-HTTP UI (loopback +
  DB-level credentials). Proxying it through the panel origin (to remove
  the separate port entirely) is a design follow-up that needs live-docker
  validation.
- The web landing bundle was code-split: 1,009 kB → 125 kB raw
  (240 kB → 38 kB gzip).

## 8. Verification status

`pnpm typecheck` 11/11 · `pnpm lint` 8/8 · server 260 files / 3,913 tests ·
web 89 files / 1,479 tests · CLI 617 · mcp+sdk 212 — all green on the
remediated tree. A post-remediation Mimosa deep scan
(`scan-2026-09-09T06-23-32.811Z-b2660f48c9b1`, seal
`sha256:2dd830a6…`) re-raised none of the closed chains; its remaining
candidates were triaged 1:1 against existing runtime tests.

docs.markdown:
# Security & Single Sign-On (SSO)

NineDeploy follows a defense-in-depth security model to protect secrets at rest, API access, user authentication, and system communication.

For 0.10.2 upgrades, read [SSO account linking](SSO_ACCOUNT_LINKING.md): existing accounts must explicitly link their provider before SSO sign-in. Local TOTP requirements remain in force.

---

## 🔒 1. Dual-Vault Secret Encryption & Key Rotation

- **AES-256-GCM Envelope Encryption**: Secrets, database passwords, and environment variables are sealed using versioned envelopes: `v<version>:<iv>:<tag>:<ciphertext>`.
- **Key Rotation**: Multiple master keys can be configured simultaneously via `NINEDEPLOY_MASTER_KEYS=0:<key0>,1:<key1>`.
- **Re-encryption**: Existing secrets encrypted with older keys continue to decrypt seamlessly and are migrated to the active key version upon update.

---

## 🌐 2. OpenID Connect (OIDC) Single Sign-On

Integrate enterprise identity providers for unified authentication — configured per provider from **Settings → SSO** by an operator (no `.env` values involved):
- **Supported Providers**: Google Workspace, GitHub OAuth/Enterprise, Okta, Keycloak, Authentik, Microsoft Entra ID, and any generic OIDC issuer.
- **Automated User Provisioning**: Auto-create user accounts based on verified OIDC claims (`email`, `email_verified`, `name`), with auto-enrollment toggles per provider.
- **Workspace of an enrolled user**: a user an OIDC provider auto-enrolls always owns their own personal workspace. OIDC providers map users into no team workspace: add people to team workspaces with invitations (each carries its own role) or SCIM. The provider's `defaultRole` field is **deprecated**: the API still accepts and returns it so existing clients keep working, but it has no effect on sign-in, and the settings form no longer shows it.
- **Browser-bound hand-off**: the provider's callback is bound to the browser that started the flow twice over — an HttpOnly state cookie on the server side, and a per-tab one-time nonce on the web side. The panel tab that clicks an SSO button stores a random nonce, the server signs it into the OAuth state and echoes it back with the session tokens, and the panel accepts tokens only on its `/auth/callback` route and only when that nonce matches. Tokens pasted into any other link (`/#access_token=…`) are discarded, so nobody can sign your tab into *their* account. The post-login `returnTo` must be a same-origin path. A sign-in started from a page loaded before an update (no nonce) is refused with "please sign in again"; clicking the provider button once more completes it.
- **Domain Restriction**: Each provider takes an optional list of allowed email domains (Settings → SSO → *Allowed email domains*, e.g. `company.com, company.io`). When set, every sign-in, auto-enrollment and account link through that provider must present an IdP-verified email in one of those domains (exact match — list subdomains explicitly); anything else is refused with `sso_domain_not_allowed` before an account is created or a session issued, and logged as `auth.sso_domain_refused`. An empty list (the default, and what every provider has after upgrading) accepts any verified email. With auto-enroll on and no domain list, the settings page warns: for a public provider such as GitHub or Google that means *anyone* can create an account.

---

### SAML sign-in (G3.6)

SAML identity providers sign people in to the panel. Add one under **Settings → SSO → SAML identity providers** with the IdP's metadata XML and the email domains whose accounts may use it. The API equivalent is `POST /v1/sso/providers` with `{ "type": "saml", "name": "corp", "config": { "idpMetadataXml": "…", "emailDomains": ["corp.example"] } }`; instead of the metadata you can give `entryPoint` and `idpCert`. Give the IdP the provider's metadata URL, `/v1/auth/saml/<id>/metadata`. That is the entity id, and its consumer URL is `/v1/auth/saml/<id>/acs`.

**Verification**
- Responses are verified with `@node-saml/node-saml` 5.1.0, which uses xml-crypto with exclusive canonicalization and the enveloped-signature transform. This replaces the hand-written verifier that could never match a real IdP.
- **Request binding:** sign-in is SP-initiated only. A response must answer an AuthnRequest this panel sent in the last 10 minutes, and each request id is accepted once, so a captured response cannot be replayed.
- **Signature and audience:** the assertion must be signed by the provider's certificate and addressed to this panel's entity id, with one minute of clock skew. Signature wrapping is refused.

**Who gets a session**
- Like OIDC, a SAML identity (provider + NameID) signs in only the account it was linked to. The link is made from that account's own signed-in session: Settings → Account → *Link <provider>*, `POST /v1/auth/saml/:id/link`. The IdP must answer with that account's email, and that email must be in `emailDomains`.
- An existing account without the link gets 403 `account_link_required`, and there is no auto-enrolment.
- A link is bound to the IdP configuration (sign-in URL, certificate, issuer), so changing it asks everyone to link again.
- With `emailAttribute` set, only that attribute is read as the email.
- An account with two-factor authentication signs in with its password and code instead.
- The session reaches the browser the same way as an OIDC sign-in: through `/auth/callback`, only in the tab whose nonce started it.
- It carries `amr: "sso"` and `idp: "sso:<id>"`, so a workspace can exempt it from its 2FA requirement.

**Testing:** the flow is checked end to end with a real AuthnRequest and RSA-SHA256 signed responses. The tests cover linking, a success, replay, another key, another audience, wrapping, an unsolicited response, the link, domain and account checks, and a forged RelayState.

## 🔑 3. Multi-Factor Authentication & Passkeys

- **Passkeys (WebAuthn / FIDO2)**: Passwordless biometric authentication (Touch ID, Face ID, YubiKey) with hardware-backed security.
- **Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)**: RFC 6238 compliant 6-digit TOTP with QR code setup and ±30s clock-drift tolerance.
- **Recovery codes (0.16.3)**: turning 2FA on hands out ten single-use recovery codes, shown once. At sign-in, one of them stands in for the authenticator code ("Lost your authenticator? Use a recovery code"; the CLI takes one at the same prompt). Only their SHA-256 is stored; a wrong one counts toward lockout like a wrong 2FA code. Settings → Account shows how many are left and creates a new set, which needs the password and a current 2FA code and replaces the old one. Turning 2FA off or enrolling again deletes the set. Accounts that turned 2FA on before 0.16.3 have no codes until they create a set. API: `GET`/`POST /v1/auth/2fa/recovery-codes`, `recoveryCode` on `POST /v1/auth/login`.
- **Workspace-enforced 2FA (G1.4)**: a workspace admin or owner can require every member to sign in with a second factor (Workspaces → *Require two-factor authentication*, or `PUT /v1/workspaces/:id/two-factor` with `{ "required": true }`).
  - **What counts:** what the session proved, not what the account holds. A sign-in with TOTP, a recovery code or a passkey marks the session `amr: "mfa"` (a JWT claim that survives refreshes).
  - **Who is held:** any other session of a member gets 403 `two_factor_required` from every route except `GET /v1/auth/me`, `GET /v1/auth/status`, `GET /v1/auth/2fa/requirement` and logout.
  - **Accounts with no second factor:** they may also set up TOTP or a passkey, then sign out and sign in again with it. An account that already has one only signs in again, so a session holding just the password cannot add a factor of its own and pass with it.
  - **SSO exemption:** sessions from the SSO providers the workspace lists in `ssoExemptProviders` (`oidc:<id>`, `sso:<id>`) are exempt, for an IdP that enforces MFA itself. Such a session carries `amr: "sso"` and `idp`. GitHub sign-ins carry no provider and are never exempt.
  - **What is not held:** API tokens the member already holds keep working; a held session cannot create new ones.
  - **Turning it on:** the admin's own session must pass the requirement (409 `enrol_first`). Sessions signed in before an upgrade carry no `amr` and sign in again. It is audited as `workspace.two_factor.set`.
  - **Storage:** no migration is needed; it is a settings row per workspace.
- **Argon2id Password Hashing**: State-of-the-art memory-hard password hashing with automatic salt generation.

---

## 🛡️ 4. Brute-Force Lockout & Rate Limiting

- **Per-Source Lockout**: 5 failed sign-ins (wrong password or wrong 2FA code) for one account from one source lock *that source* out of that account for 15 minutes. A source is one IPv4 address or one IPv6 /64. The real user, signing in from anywhere else, is unaffected — a stranger who knows an email cannot hold its owner locked out.
- **Per-Account Lockout**: 25 failures for one account inside a sliding 15-minute window, from more than one source, lock the account for 15 minutes from every source (logged as `auth.lockout`). Failures from sources that already locked themselves keep counting, so spreading 5 guesses each over many addresses still trips it. A successful sign-in clears only that source's own failures; it never lifts a lock early.
- **Responses do not leak state**: a locked account, a wrong password and an unknown email all answer `Invalid email or password`, and an unknown email pays the same password-hash verification as a real one.
- **IP Rate Limiting**: Tiered token bucket rate limits on public endpoints to prevent credential stuffing and DoS attacks.

### Panel IP allow-list (O4)

**Settings → Security → Panel access** (operator; `GET`/`PUT /v1/settings/panel-access`; SDK `settings.panelAccess`). It is off by default. When it is on, only the listed addresses can use the panel. Entries are IPv4 or IPv6 addresses or CIDR ranges, at most 64.

What the list covers:
- **Signing in:** password, passkey, 2FA, token refresh, OIDC and SAML start and callback, SSO under `/v1/sso`, and the remote-MCP consent page (`/v1/oauth/authorize`).
- **Signed-in sessions:** every panel API request and WebSocket that carries a session.
- **Tokens, optionally:** API and remote-MCP tokens, only when **Also restrict API and MCP tokens** is on. It is off by default, so CI jobs and AI agents keep deploying from anywhere.

What it never covers:
- requests without a user credential: git, registry and deploy webhooks, badges, status pages, the CI runner protocol, SCIM, error ingest, the OAuth token endpoint and SAML SP metadata;
- the app traffic Traefik hands the panel: wake, forward-auth checks and maintenance pages;
- loopback, i.e. the panel's own in-process calls.

How it works:
- The check uses the route the router matched, not the raw URL, so a percent-encoded path cannot slip past it.
- A save is refused when the new list would exclude the address making it. The card shows the address the panel sees for you, with **Add my address**.
- Apps behind panel sign-in ([forward auth](TRAEFIK_INGRESS.md)) also need a listed address to sign in, because that sign-in is a panel sign-in.

**Locked out?** See [TROUBLESHOOTING.md §14](TROUBLESHOOTING.md#-14-locked-out-by-the-panel-ip-allow-list). In short: set `NINEDEPLOY_PANEL_ACCESS=off` and restart the panel. The list stays stored and is ignored until you remove the variable. On bare metal, an SSH tunnel to `127.0.0.1:3000` also works, because loopback is always allowed.

**Limits:**
- The client address follows `NINEDEPLOY_TRUST_PROXY`. With the default (`1`), the `X-Forwarded-For` of a peer on a private network is trusted. A container on the panel host's networks can therefore claim any address. The list is not a boundary against workloads on the same host.
- The same applies to a client the panel sees through a private hop. In Docker mode, with port 3000 published on `0.0.0.0`, Docker's userland proxy can make some clients appear to come from the bridge gateway, for example an IPv6 client reaching an IPv4-published port. Such a client's own `X-Forwarded-For` would then be trusted.
- The list is reliable when clients reach the panel only through its HTTPS domain. Traefik then sets the real client address.
  - Keep port 3000 reachable from Docker, because Traefik forwards to it through the Docker gateway. A panel bound to `127.0.0.1` is cut off from its domain.
  - Block port 3000 from the internet with a firewall in front of the host instead.
  - The Doctor page warns when the panel port is reachable over plain HTTP.
  - `NINEDEPLOY_TRUST_PROXY=false` stops the spoofing, but then every client behind Docker's userland proxy appears as the bridge gateway. Prefer the HTTPS domain.

## 🕳️ 5. Egress Controls

Operator-supplied URLs whose targets are normally public — notification channels, log drains, push delivery, git clones and PR inspections, OAuth token exchange, the marketplace catalog and `templates_source` — are resolved through a guarded fetch that refuses private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT and multicast addresses (including the cloud metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`). Self-hosted LAN remotes keep working with `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`.

The guard is deliberately **not** applied to the OIDC issuer, the S3 endpoint, the log-search backend or the telemetry endpoint: self-hosted Keycloak, MinIO and Loki normally *are* on a private address, so guarding those would break working installs. All of them are operator-only settings, and an operator can already run host commands through a service — the guard is defence in depth against a copy-pasted URL, not a privilege boundary.

The 0.14 secret managers (HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao, AWS Secrets Manager and its STS calls) **are** guarded, and never follow a redirect: a Vault on a private address needs `NINEDEPLOY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=1`, and instance metadata credentials are refused. The Infisical and Doppler calls go to their fixed public hosts. See [SECRET_MANAGERS.md](./SECRET_MANAGERS.md).

docs.markdown:
# SSO account linking

Starting with 0.10.2, a verified provider email does not automatically link to an existing local account. NineDeploy records the provider and stable subject after explicit linking, or atomically when SSO creates a new account. Subsequent sign-ins use this identity record.

For an existing account, sign in with its password/passkey, open account settings, and link the provider. The API is `POST /v1/auth/oidc/:slug/link` with the interactive access token. It returns `{ "authUrl": "..." }`; navigate the same browser to that URL. The callback checks the initiating session is still live, the account's token version is unchanged, and the verified provider email matches the local account. API tokens cannot initiate linking. Successful browser linking returns to `/settings?oidcLinked=1` without issuing new session credentials.

If sign-in returns `account_link_required`, sign in locally and link the provider. Legacy SSO-only accounts have no historical identity mapping: use the password-reset email flow to recover local access, then link the provider. Configure a working system email channel before upgrading an installation that relies exclusively on SSO. NineDeploy does not infer links from old audit logs or matching email addresses.

Changing an OIDC provider's issuer or client ID invalidates its existing links. Users must link the new provider configuration again. Deleting the provider also deletes its links.

Mailbox-based password recovery revokes all existing sessions, API tokens, passkeys, and SSO links atomically with the password change. Register passkeys and link SSO providers again after recovery. This prevents credentials planted before mailbox ownership was proved from retaining access. An ordinary authenticated password change keeps its existing behavior.

Accounts with local TOTP enabled must continue using password and code for sign-in until an SSO second-factor challenge exists. Linking from an already authenticated local session is permitted, but it does not disable that requirement.

# Support matrix

<!-- Generated by apps/server/test/serviceCapabilities.test.ts from lib/serviceCapabilities.ts. Do not edit by hand: run the test with ND_UPDATE_SUPPORT_MATRIX=1. -->

Which service features work where. The panel reads the same evaluation from `GET /v1/services/:id/capabilities` and disables a control before you save it. The routes refuse with the same reasons.

✅ works · 🟡 works partly or is held at run time · 🚧 being built · — refused when saved

| Feature | Docker (panel host) | Docker from an image (panel host) | Compose (panel host) | PM2 (panel host) | Docker (node) | Compose (node) | Docker (Swarm) | Docker (panel host + node fan-out) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maintenance mode | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — [1] | — [1] | ✅ | — [2] |
| Custom error pages | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — [3] | — [3] | ✅ | — [4] |
| Panel sign-in on a domain (forward auth) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — [5] | — [5] | ✅ | — [6] |
| Restart-loop limit | ✅ | ✅ | — [7] | ✅ | — [7] | — [7] | — [7] | ✅ |
| Inline Dockerfile | ✅ | — [8] | — [8] | — [8] | 🟡 [9] | — [8] | — [8] | ✅ |
| File mounts | ✅ | ✅ | — [10] | — [10] | ✅ | — [10] | ✅ | ✅ |
| Autoscaling | ✅ | ✅ | — [11] | — [11] | 🟡 [12] | — [11] | 🟡 [13] | ✅ |
| Scale to zero | ✅ | ✅ | — [14] | — [14] | 🚧 [15] | — [14] | 🟡 [16] | ✅ |
| Canary releases | ✅ | ✅ | — [17] | — [17] | 🟡 [18] | — [17] | 🟡 [19] | ✅ |

## Notes

1. Maintenance mode is for services on the panel host for now
2. Maintenance mode is not available for a service that also runs on nodes
3. Custom error pages are for services on the panel host for now
4. Custom error pages are not available for a service that also runs on nodes
5. Panel sign-in is for domains of services on the panel host for now
6. Panel sign-in is not available for a service that also runs on nodes
7. The restart-loop limit is for docker services on the panel host and PM2 services, not Swarm
8. An inline Dockerfile is for docker services that build from source, not from an image or a compose file
9. On a node, the service must build on the panel host (Service → Settings → Build on: panel); a build on a node or a build server would not have the file
10. File mounts work for docker services only (on the panel host, a node or Swarm), not for compose or PM2 services; remove the files (Service → Volumes → Files) to deploy it.
11. Autoscaling applies to docker services only
12. On a node, requests-per-second scaling needs an agent with proxy traffic observation turned on (NINEDEPLOY_AGENT_PROXY_TRAFFIC=on)
13. Swarm services are not autoscaled: they run the replica count set on the service
14. Scale to zero applies to docker services only
15. Scale to zero on nodes is being built (R2); until it is accepted, a node service does not sleep
16. Scale to zero does not apply to Swarm services; the setting is kept but nothing sleeps
17. Canary releases apply to docker services only
18. On a node, a canary needs a single replica, the strict HTTP healthcheck and an agent with proxy traffic observation
19. Swarm services skip the canary and use Docker’s native rolling update

Checks of the live environment are not in this table. They run when you save or deploy. Examples: whether Traefik can reach the panel for maintenance pages and forward auth, and whether a node agent advertises an operation.

# Real Swarm artifact and recovery acceptance

## Support matrix on real tasks — 2026-11-06

[Hosted run 42238384185](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/42238384185) (runtime-readiness, `swarm_support=true`) passed on `abd8eb45`. It builds the candidate image and runs `node scripts/smoke-multinode.mjs --swarm-only`, whose `swarmSupportChecks` exercise each row of the matrix in [DEPLOYMENTS.md §7](DEPLOYMENTS.md) against a two-task service on a real single-manager swarm in DinD:

- logs: 88 lines from both tasks, in time order;
- Stop → 0/0, Restart → 2/2, and the route serves again;
- `docker service scale <svc>=0` outside the panel: the runtime patrol scaled it back to 2/2, status still `running`;
- inspect and the File Browser on the service name reached a task on the panel host;
- `/v1/stats` reported the 128 MiB per-task limit, the two tasks averaged;
- a health path answering 404 through Traefik read healthy on the dashboard;
- `Container running` readiness deployed a service whose port answers nothing;
- `docker service rm` behind the panel's back: the patrol marked the service `error`;
- refused: volume attachment (422 `swarm_unsupported`, nothing created), TCP readiness (400), sleep (400 `cannot_sleep`); autoscaling offers no metric.

The same checks run in every release's `swarm-artifacts` cohort. Not covered: metrics of tasks on worker nodes (only the panel host's tasks are sampled), distributed workers, and Swarm autoscaling, which is not offered.

## Artifact and restart cohort — 2026-11-03

Status, 2026-11-03: the corrected hosted cohort passed, and its downloaded public receipts passed independent verification. This closes the single-manager artifact/restart cohort in R2, not the entire runtime or release program. Local Docker remains disabled.

Integration checkpoint: after PR #25 passed all required checks and merged as `977390d7279268b3ab8dffd0dde133fa40668c01`, [PR #26](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/pull/26) opened with frozen head `817af47a4bfa17b3cdae90f4d810a61e892df5f1`. It is the only open integration PR. Its prepared source tree was unchanged when accepted main history was merged. [Full CI 41650523274](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41650523274) and serving checks are running; real Docker/PostgreSQL integration has passed. This PR contains the Swarm cohort and release gate, not the later R3 restore adapter. No new release was created.

Accepted evidence: [run 41644236264](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41644236264), frozen source `1e2214e3ae765e1d414f89149649abb9c38bfee1`. All four cases completed: Docker-to-Swarm migration retired the previous Docker container; promotion retained the first image config ID and commit after repository HEAD advanced; a panel restart recovered the original pending deployment with its captured second image; recorded rollback returned to the first image and commit. Promotion and recovery made no additional Git fetch. The worker also asserted no fetch during recorded rollback.

Independent recount of the downloaded traces found **7,171 source and 6,003 target requests: 13,174 exact application HTTP 200 responses**, with no errors or 502. Source traffic contains both image bodies and ends with 40 first-image responses after rollback; every target response remains the promoted first image. Recovery and rollback preserve the source native service, manager and encrypted overlay identities. Four owned outer containers, both named volumes and the network were removed. Evidence is retained in `.temp_files/swarm-runtime-41644236264/swarm-runtime-41644236264/independent-verification.json`; verifier: `.temp_files/verify-swarm-runtime-41644236264.mjs`. This fixture is not yet integrated through its own full-source PR gate. Earlier preparation/failure checkpoints below are historical.

The release matrix now requires a separate `swarm-artifacts` cohort against the pushed candidate image, with no failure bypass and a 15-minute step bound. Promotion and npm publication depend on the entire matrix. Its evidence upload enumerates public JSON receipts on success or failure and excludes private Git repositories, raw logs and environment data. The existing matrix guard failed four checks before this addition; afterward all 82 covering checks in five files passed, including the eight-cohort schedule, existing release/security policies, real Git helper and sampler controls. Lint and diff checks passed. This wiring has not yet run against a numbered release image and does not constitute publication.

The cohort uses owned panel/node Docker daemons on a GitHub-hosted runner. A smart HTTP Git fixture serves two real commits. Normal authenticated API deployment builds the first repository-backed Docker image. The operator then initializes/enables an actual single-manager Swarm, selects Swarm placement and deploys through the normal worker.

Required cases:

1. Docker-to-Swarm migration: healthy task/image identities and encrypted overlay are confirmed; the captured previous Docker container is removed. The source release reports an available recorded Docker artifact. Public service and deployment commit identities must agree with the actual selected image in every case.
2. Pinned artifact promotion: advance repository HEAD to the second commit, then promote the first artifact to another Swarm service. Its native task must run the original config image ID and commit without another Git fetch. The source uses image-native health; the target uses an explicit command healthcheck.
3. Native restart recovery: deploy the second commit behind real native-image readiness, restart the panel after the pending journal and candidate exist, then release readiness. The original deployment and native service ID must settle with the captured candidate image ID, no new Git request, no unresolved journal and a persisted recovery outcome.
4. Recorded rollback: restore the first source artifact while repository HEAD remains at the second commit. Native task image ID and recorded commit must return to the first artifact without fetching/rebuilding from current source.

Independent HTTP observers run through the real Traefik proxy throughout source migration/update/restart/rollback and after target promotion. Only HTTP 200 with the exact baked first/second fixture bodies is accepted; status 502, unknown bodies, response errors and deadlines remain failures in the trace. Before readiness is released, only the original source body may serve. Final source samples must be the first body again. Cleanup must remove every owned outer container, both named volumes and the network. Uploaded evidence contains enumerated public JSON receipts, not Git data, raw logs, service environment or encrypted journal payloads.

Local preflight passed script/generated-CGI/sampler syntax, workflow parsing, JSON-only upload paths and all three pre-Docker hosted guards. Two files passed six helper checks: actual smart HTTP shallow clones of both commits and the original pinned commit, plus sampler controls for both application bodies, status 502, foreign bodies and oversized responses. These do not prove native Swarm behavior; the hosted result and its exact source will be recorded here.

The first hosted cohort is [run 41641877386](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41641877386), frozen source `7e91d9f210c4f4aa801289cf4700f565d9165185`. Its tree matches the prepared local source before this documentation update. It is running independently of PR #25; no additional integration PR was opened. PR #25's initial full source job failed only the omitted runtime-reader inventory classification; that same check reproduced locally, and the correction passed 34 covering tests. Its old image/runtime job is still allowed to finish before the test-only PR update starts a fresh exact-head gate.

That first run completed with failure at the initial traffic-observer baseline, before Docker-to-Swarm migration. The ordinary repository deployment and operator Swarm initialization/enabling had completed. The observer incorrectly addressed the node's `ninedeploy-proxy`, while this cohort uses the panel's `ninedeploy-traefik`. The sampler regression now checks its transport target against the production panel container constant: all five cases failed on the wrong target, then all six sampler/Git helper checks passed after correction. Baseline collection is also inside the protected diagnostic block now, so a future early failure preserves its traffic and redacted recovery state. Four owned outer containers, both named volumes and the network were removed. No native Swarm scenario was accepted by this failed run.

The corrected cohort is [run 41644236264](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41644236264), frozen source `1e2214e3ae765e1d414f89149649abb9c38bfee1`; its real Swarm step is in progress. Its tree matches the prepared candidate before this documentation update. The corrected public-node PR #25 now has fresh [CI 41643863613](https://github.com/ninedeploy/ninedeploy/actions/runs/41643863613) on `65d15f69f71eb0e63e59dd1600e7455089e331a8`; its early Swarm runtime guard has already passed, while its full source/image checks continue. This Swarm fixture is not part of that PR, and no additional integration PR or release was opened.

Distributed workers, public DNS/TLS, storage/data migration, every native failure timing and final source/release/upgrade/artifact certification remain separate acceptance. Never-bound node wake catcher collection and R3–R6 also remain open in [Competitive delivery](COMPETITIVE_DELIVERY.md).

docs.markdown:
# Template mirrors: Coolify and Dokploy

NineDeploy can convert two community template catalogs into its own compose-stack format:

- the Coolify compose templates (`coollabsio/coolify`, `templates/compose`);
- the Dokploy blueprints (`Dokploy/templates`, `blueprints/`, MIT, added in G4.7).

Each converter writes a bundle that the Hub can load as a remote source (Settings → `templates_source`), or that a maintainer can promote into the bundled registry after a smoke run.

The tools never download anything themselves. You clone the catalog first.

---

## 1. Building a bundle

```bash
# Coolify
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/coollabsio/coolify /tmp/coolify
git -C /tmp/coolify sparse-checkout set templates/compose
pnpm --filter @ninedeploy/server exec tsx scripts/buildTemplateMirror.ts \
  --src /tmp/coolify/templates/compose --out ./templates-coolify.json

# Dokploy
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Dokploy/templates /tmp/dokploy-templates
pnpm --filter @ninedeploy/server exec tsx scripts/buildDokployMirror.ts \
  --src /tmp/dokploy-templates/blueprints --out ./templates-dokploy.json
```

- **Output:** each script prints how many entries it converted and why it skipped the rest.
- **Validation:** the bundle is checked by the production registry parser before it is written.
- **Not verified yet:** every entry carries `requires: "… · not runtime-verified"` until it has been smoke-run.

---

## 2. How a Dokploy blueprint is converted

A blueprint keeps its settings outside the compose file:

- `[variables]` hold generators;
- `[config.env]` is written to the stack's `.env`;
- `[[config.domains]]` routes a service;
- `[[config.mounts]]` writes files.

The converter folds the env into the compose file. It substitutes inside the parsed string values, as Docker Compose does, so a value containing `: ` or `#` cannot change the file's structure. Each generator becomes the `SERVICE_*` token that makes the same kind of value at deploy time. The value is kept across redeploys.

| Dokploy | NineDeploy |
| :--- | :--- |
| `${domain}` | `${SERVICE_FQDN_<routed service>}` |
| `${password}` / `${password:N}` | `${SERVICE_PASSWORD_<N>_<VAR>}`: N alphanumerics (16 by default) |
| `${base64}` / `${base64:32\|64\|128}` | `${SERVICE_REALBASE64_<N>_<VAR>}`: base64 of N random bytes |
| `${hash:32\|64\|128}` | `${SERVICE_HEX_<N>_<VAR>}`: N hex characters |
| `${username}` | `${SERVICE_LOWERCASEUSER_<VAR>}` |
| `${email}` | `${SERVICE_LOWERCASEUSER_<VAR>}@example.com` |

Rules that match Dokploy's own behaviour:

- **Variables:** one variable is one token, so a database and its app get the same password.
- **Precedence:** a generator name wins over a variable of the same name, as in Dokploy.
- **Env references:** an env value may refer to another env key, with or without a `:-default`, as Compose interpolates a `.env` file.

A blueprint is **skipped with its reason** whenever there is no faithful equivalent:

- it uses file mounts;
- it routes more than one service, port or sub-path;
- it routes no service;
- it uses `${uuid}`, `${jwt}`, timestamps or `${randomPort}`;
- it asks for a base64 or hash length other than 32, 64 or 128;
- it uses a variable only Dokploy provides (`DOKPLOY_*`);
- its compose file has a shape the Coolify mirror also refuses: host ports, host networking, build contexts or `env_file`;
- it reaches the host. That means it bind-mounts a host path (`/root:…`, the Docker socket), a path that leaves the stack anywhere in it (`../files/…`, `./a/../../x`, `~/…`) or an interpolated source; declares a volume with `driver_opts`, another driver or `external`; declares top-level `secrets` or `configs`, a volume or network with a fixed `name`, or an external network or one with another driver; or gives a service a key outside the safe list (image, command, environment, volumes, depends_on, healthcheck, …). That list leaves out `build`, `env_file` (and `pull_policy: build`), `privileged`, `pid`, `ipc`, `devices`, `cap_add`, `security_opt`, `volumes_from`, `userns_mode`, `sysctls`, `runtime` and every other key that can loosen isolation. Named volumes, `./` paths and the read-only `/etc/localtime` and `/etc/timezone` stay. The check runs on the blueprint and again on the converted file.

On the catalog of 2026-10-27, **383 of 586 blueprints converted**. With the host-access rules of 2026-10-29, 322 convert. The largest skip groups were file mounts (91) and more than one routed service (38).

---

## 3. Promoting entries

A converted entry only reaches the bundled registry after it has started in an isolated smoke run:

```bash
node scripts/smoke-template-runtime.mjs --registry=./templates-dokploy.json --ids=dokploy-n8n,dokploy-umami
```

The script runs `compose up` with generated `SERVICE_*` values, probes the routed port and then runs `compose down -v`. `scripts/promote-templates.mjs` then moves the passing entries in.

On 2026-10-29, 30 Dokploy entries were smoke-run and 26 passed. A security review then withdrew six of them, leaving 20 in the Hub. Trilium Next bound the host's `/root`. iHateMoney, Kener and Statping-ng bound `../files` outside the stack, which the converter now refuses. FileGator starts with a publicly known admin login, and ByteStash with open sign-up and debug mode. A started stack is not enough: a promoted entry must also be safe to expose by default. The same review was then applied to the first batch, and 18 more were withdrawn. Only AList and Healthchecks stayed; each reason is in the evidence file. A second batch of 30 left one, Dagu, after the same review; `runtime-verify-2026-10-29-dokploy-2.json` records why each other one stayed out. Reasons include mutable `latest` tags, open registration, auth switched off, a first visitor becoming admin of an app that runs code, fixed passwords, and the converter's host-access rules. Each withdrawal is recorded as a failure, with its reason, in the evidence file. The evidence is `apps/server/test/fixtures/runtime-verify-2026-10-29-dokploy.json`. Etherpad, Wiki.js and Kutt exited before they were ready, and Cloud Commander listens on 8000 where its blueprint routes 80.

A third round, on 2026-10-31, filtered before running anything. Of the 324 blueprints that convert, those already tried, those with an image not pinned to a version, a literal credential, or open registration or auth switched off in their environment were set aside, leaving 138. A reading of each one's first-run behaviour left 11: each sets its admin login or API key from a generated value. Rejections at this stage included known default logins (Umami, Grafana, BookStack, Wallabag, Zabbix), a first visitor becoming admin (n8n, Strapi, Immich, Forgejo, Docmost), open sign-up (Linkwarden, GlitchTip, GitLab), phpMyAdmin's auto-login, Keycloak in `start-dev` and Directus's `postgis:13-master` image. All 11 started in the smoke run. Each was then started again and asked, without credentials, for its admin pages, APIs, install and sign-up pages; every answer had to be a login, a 401 or 403, a locked installer or a missing page. Ten passed and are in the Hub: 9Router, Dolibarr, Graylog, Kimai, Meilisearch, Miniflux, OpenObserve, Ponos, PrivatePaste and Typesense. YOURLS stayed out: its install page answers without a login and the stack does nothing until someone runs it, and its MySQL 5.7 is end-of-life. The evidence is `runtime-verify-2026-10-31-dokploy-3.json`.

A fourth round, on 2026-11-01, took the 125 blueprints the third round had set aside only because an image was not pinned. Apps the Hub already has, as a native or a Coolify entry, were dropped, which left 56. Reading each one's first-run behaviour left eight. The rest were rejected for reasons like those in round three, plus self-hosted modes without any auth (Domain Locker, go-whatsapp) and a fixed `admin:admin` superuser (Bugsink). FreeScout dropped out because its image, `tiredofit/freescout`, is gone from Docker Hub. The other seven were pinned by hand to the newest release at least two weeks old: Flatnotes `v5.5.5`, Omni-Tools `0.6.0`, HortusFox `v6.3`, MAZANOKE `v1.1.7`, Kokoro Web `0.1.3`, Cut `0.1.0` and Rustrak `v0.18.1`. Nothing else in their files was changed, apart from two wrong upstream descriptions in the Hub (HortusFox, MAZANOKE). All seven started in the smoke run. Without credentials:

- Flatnotes, Kokoro Web and Rustrak answered their APIs with 401.
- Rustrak refused registration without an invitation (403).
- HortusFox sent every page to its login, and its API answered 403.
- Cut's admin page and link creation required the owner's password.
- MAZANOKE and Omni-Tools are static pages that work in the browser and keep nothing on the server.

The evidence is `runtime-verify-2026-11-01-dokploy-4.json`.

A stack that fails is left out; often its upstream file is to blame. The Dokploy Ghost blueprint is an example: it has no `depends_on` or healthcheck, so Ghost restarts until MySQL is ready, and the smoke run reports "exited before readiness".

## 4. Apps that are open before they are set up

The bar above came after the native catalog and the 175 Coolify entries of 0.15.7, which were promoted because they started. On 2026-11-01 the whole bundled Hub was reviewed for what an app does before anyone has set it up. Each template where that is open carries `openFirstRun`, and the deploy wizard and the Hub detail show a warning:

| `openFirstRun` | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `first-visitor-admin` | The first person to open it creates the admin account or runs the installer. | n8n, Uptime Kuma, Immich, WordPress, Portainer |
| `default-login` | It starts with a publicly known login. | Mealie, Nginx Proxy Manager, BookStack, Joplin |
| `open-signup` | Anyone can create an account. | Vaultwarden, Rallly, Karakeep |
| `no-auth` | It has no login of its own. | Dozzle, Node-RED, Ollama, Qdrant, Prometheus |

The review marked 174 templates. When such an app also has the Docker socket, the warning says that whoever gets in first controls the server. A test makes sure every template that reaches the host Docker is either marked or named with the generated value that closes it (WUD, Autobase).

Three Coolify entries were withdrawn, because they combine host Docker access with an open first run: Portainer (the socket, first visitor becomes admin), Authentik (the socket, an initial-setup flow that sets the `akadmin` password) and Glances (privileged, host PID namespace, the socket and no login). The native Portainer CE, Dockge and Dozzle stay, with the warning. `runtime-verify-2026-10-10.json` records each withdrawal. A stack installed from a withdrawn template keeps redeploying; only the Hub no longer offers it.

The marks come from reading each app's documented first-run behaviour, not from running all of them. An unmarked template is not a promise that it is closed.

**The bar for promotion:** the stack starts in the smoke run, every image is pinned to a version (no `latest`, no `pull_policy: always`), and nothing is open by default. That rules out a known default login, open registration, auth switched off, a first visitor becoming admin, and a form that reaches arbitrary hosts. A blueprint that needs a manual first step to be safe stays in the remote bundle (Settings → `templates_source`), not the bundled Hub.
