docs.description: The complete upstream guide to workspaces, roles & access, synchronized with the product repository.
docs.markdown:
# Workspaces & Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

NineDeploy provides multi-tenant Workspaces, allowing engineering organizations to partition services, databases, secrets, and servers into isolated scopes with team access controls.

---

## 🏢 1. Workspace Scoping

Every resource in NineDeploy belongs to a Workspace:
- **Services & Containers**
- **Managed Databases & Volumes**
- **Domains & SSL Certificates**
- **Secrets & Environment Variables**
- **Connected Servers & Remote Agents**

Users can seamlessly switch between Workspaces from the dashboard header or CLI without re-authenticating.

---

## 👥 2. Role Hierarchy & Permission Matrix

NineDeploy has four role levels **within each workspace**, plus one flag that
sits outside the workspace model entirely (see §2.1).

Roles rank `owner > admin > member > viewer`. On a service, your effective role
is the **highest seat you hold across the workspaces that service is tagged
into**; being the service's creator, or an instance operator, counts as `owner`.
From 0.15 a project or environment grant can raise that role, never lower it
(§2.3).

| Permission | Owner | Admin | Member | Viewer |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Transfer / delete the workspace | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Workspace settings (name, slug, description) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Invite, remove and re-role members | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Delete a service · re-tag it into other workspaces | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Create services · edit service & build config · set limits | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Trigger deploys, rollbacks, cancels · start/stop/restart | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Edit environment variables · manage domains | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| View the dashboard, services, metrics, deploy logs | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

Enforcement lives in `assertServiceRole` (`apps/server/src/lib/resourceAccess.ts`)
and is covered by `apps/server/test/workspaceRoleEnforcement.test.ts`.

Managed databases follow the same hierarchy through `assertDatabaseRole`; a
database's workspace is the one its **project** belongs to:

| Permission | Owner | Admin | Member | Viewer |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Delete the database · take/restore a backup · reveal credentials | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Start / stop / restart · change CPU & memory limits | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| View the database, its size, backups and logs | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

> **Two deliberate exceptions** stay instance-operator-only whatever your
> workspace role, because they reach past the workspace boundary:
> **database Studio** (it binds a port on the host) and **volume-scope
> backups** (they belong to no database, so there is no workspace to derive a
> role from).

> **Still panel/operator-only:** log drains and instance settings. Tracked in
> ARCHITECTURE.md §16.4.

### 2.1 Instance operator — not a workspace role

A separate flag, `users.is_instance_operator`, controls everything that is not
scoped to a workspace:

- managing users, SSO/OIDC providers and instance settings
- system export/import, the self-updater, host firewall rules
- the container file browser, `docker exec`, volume deletion
- **host-privileged deploys**: PM2 services, Compose stacks, deploy lifecycle
  hooks and Docker-socket templates all execute code on the host itself

Rules:

1. The **first** account on a fresh instance receives it (`/setup`, the first
   `/auth/register`, or the first SSO auto-enrolment).
2. Everyone else must be granted it by an existing operator — Settings → Users →
   *Make operator*, or `PATCH /v1/users/:id/operator`.
3. **Creating a workspace does not confer it.** Before 0.3.5 the flag was
   inferred from holding `owner`/`admin` in any workspace, and since any user
   can create a workspace they own, any user could self-promote to full instance
   control — including host code execution. Migration `0038` moved the flag onto
   the user row to close that path.
4. The last remaining operator cannot be demoted or deleted.

On upgrade, the flag is backfilled to the bootstrap user and to the
owners/admins of the **oldest** workspace only. If someone legitimately needs it
and was missed, an existing operator re-grants it from Settings → Users.

### 2.2 API tokens

API tokens carry scopes, enforced on every request:

| Scope | Effect |
| :--- | :--- |
| `read` | safe methods only (`GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS`) |
| `write` | any method, but the request always runs as a **non-operator** |
| `operator` | no extra restriction beyond the owner's own authority |

A scope can only ever narrow what the owning account can do — asking for
`operator` as a non-operator is refused at creation. Tokens created before 0.3.5
have an empty scope list, which still means *unrestricted*; `ninedeploy token
list` labels those, and re-issuing them with an explicit scope is recommended
(a `write`-scoped CI token cannot reach the host-privileged deploy paths).

### 2.3 Project and environment access grants (0.15)

A grant gives one user a role on part of a workspace: a project, an
environment, or both. Grants are **raise-only**:

```text
effective role on a resource = max(seat role in the resource's workspace(s),
                                   highest role of the user's matching grants)
```

- A grant never lowers a role. To keep a seat admin to `viewer` on
  production, give the seat `viewer` and grant `member` or `admin` on the
  other environments.
- `owner` is never grantable. Operators stay `owner` everywhere.
- With no grants, every permission is exactly what it was in 0.14 (proven
  over 4839 access decisions by `test/accessGrantsEquivalence.test.ts`). A
  grant only ever adds access, for its one user.

**What a grant covers**

| Grant | Covers |
| :--- | :--- |
| Project P | The project itself, the databases in P, and the services linked to P |
| Environment E | The services whose environment is E |
| Project P + environment E | The services linked to P **and** in E. Not the project row, and not P's databases |

Databases have no environment, so an environment grant never covers one.
Every grant also requires the service to be **tagged into the grant's
workspace**: a project link alone never reaches another workspace's service,
even when someone linked that service to this workspace's project. A grant's
project and environment must belong to the grant's workspace; a project moved
to another workspace stops matching its old grants at once, and the move
deletes them.

**Guests.** A user with grants in a workspace but no seat there is a guest. A
guest sees only the granted projects, environments and the resources they
cover, and works on them within the granted role. A guest gets no
workspace-level right: member lists, invitations, labels, email templates,
creating projects and workspace settings all stay refused, as for any
non-member, and probing a resource that is not granted answers 404. In 0.15
guests cannot create services or databases, because new resources are tagged
by seat. `GET /v1/access/me` (`ninedeploy access me`) lists a user's own
grants and the workspaces they reach only through grants (`guestWorkspaces`);
the workspace list (`GET /v1/workspaces`) is unchanged and shows seats only.

**Who can grant**

- Workspace `admin`s and `owner`s, up to their own role capped at `admin`, and
  instance operators (up to `admin`). A grant above your cap answers 403
  `grant_exceeds_role`.
- An admin can grant only to an account they already share a workspace with,
  or that already holds a grant in this workspace. Any other email answers the
  same 404 as an unknown one, so the route cannot be used to find out which
  emails have accounts. Operators can grant to any account.
- One grant per user and target (a duplicate is 409); change its role instead.

Manage grants in Workspaces → Access grants, with `ninedeploy access grants
list|add|update|remove`, or `GET/POST /v1/workspaces/:wid/access-grants` and
`PATCH/DELETE /v1/workspaces/:wid/access-grants/:grantId`. `GET
/v1/projects/:id/access` (project admin) lists everyone who reaches a project
and how (`operator`, `seat`, `grant`). The grant routes have no fine-grained
token scope; the read-only MCP tools `list_access_grants` and `my_access` need
a coarse token. Every write is audited as `workspace.access_grant.create`,
`.update`, `.delete`, `.suspend` or `.reinstate`.

**Suspending a grant.** `PATCH …/access-grants/:grantId {"suspended": true}`
(CLI `--suspend`) keeps the grant listed but stops it counting on the next
request; `{"suspended": false}` (`--reinstate`) makes it count again. The
workspace admin's hold and the identity provider's hold are kept separately,
and a grant is suspended while either exists.

**Lifecycle with seats and SCIM**

- Removing a member from a workspace deletes their grants there, so they do
  not stay behind as a guest.
- SCIM deactivation in a workspace puts an IdP hold on the user's grants
  there; SCIM re-activation lifts it (a grant an admin also suspended stays
  suspended). Only SCIM lifts an IdP hold: an admin reinstate answers 409
  `grant_suspended_by_idp` while it stands or while the user is SCIM-suspended
  in the workspace, and a new grant for such a user answers 409
  `user_suspended_by_idp`. A SCIM delete removes the user's grants.
- Deleting the user, the workspace, the project or the environment deletes the
  grant. A deactivated account reaches nothing.

**Rolling back to 0.14** ignores the `access_grants` table, so every effect is
a loss of access: guests lose everything and elevated roles fall back to the
seat role. Tell guests before you roll back. See [ROLLBACK.md](./ROLLBACK.md).

---

## ✉️ 3. Team Invitations & Member Management

1. **Invite Links**: Admins generate time-limited invitation tokens or send direct email invites.
2. **Role Assignment**: Assign appropriate roles upon invitation or update existing member privileges.
3. **Revocation**: Removing a member immediately revokes their workspace tokens and active sessions.

### 3.1 Email templates

A workspace admin can replace the subject and text of the emails the workspace sends, under **Workspaces → Email templates** (web UI since G1.5), with `ninedeploy email-templates`, or with `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /v1/workspaces/:wid/email-templates`. **Preview** renders what would be sent; **Reset to built-in** deletes the override.

- Variables such as `{{workspaceName}}` are filled in when the email is sent. A template whose email carries a link must keep it: an invitation override without `{{acceptUrl}}` is refused.
- The password reset is about the user's account, not one workspace, so it is always sent with the built-in text and cannot be overridden.
- Custom emails are sent from the instance's own mail server, so overrides can only be saved for workspaces an instance operator owns; elsewhere saving is refused and the built-in text is used.
- A template marked *not sent yet* is stored, but nothing sends that email yet.

docs.markdown:
# Competitive roadmap: 2026-11

**Drawn up on 2026-11-09** against `main` at e85dbf45 (0.18.25). The tree had 12 modified files from another session; they are not part of this plan.

**Sources:**
- three read-only reviews run on the same day: code health and structural debt, competitor state, and product and adoption;
- the competitive gap report in `.temp_files/competitive-gap-20261109/REPORT.md`, which pins 12 competitor sources;
- spot checks of the claims these rely on, against the source.

The working notes are git-ignored:
- `.temp_files/compet_20261109/` holds the competitor issue rankings, advisory counts and raw release notes;
- `.temp_files/competitive-gap-20261109/` holds the pinned competitor sources.

This plan follows on from [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md) and [GAP_ROADMAP.md](../GAP_ROADMAP.md), whose items are all done except R2. It does not re-plan R2 (node ordered lifecycle, autoscaling and sleep acceptance, 0.19.0), because another session owns it; see [COMPETITIVE_DELIVERY.md](../COMPETITIVE_DELIVERY.md).

Every item follows the rule every release follows: installed servers upgrade in place; migrations are additive only; new behaviour is opt-in or keeps the old default; and `smoke:upgrade` exercises the item after an upgrade.

---

## 1. What changed: features are no longer the bottleneck

Six weeks of roadmap work closed almost every feature gap found in October. What decides whether NineDeploy beats its rivals now lies elsewhere.

**Adoption is near zero.**

| Signal | NineDeploy | For comparison |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub stars | 16 | Coolify 65.8k, Dokploy 38.3k |
| Forks | 3 | |
| Issues ever opened | 0 | |
| Commits by one author | 1,925 of about 1,980 | |
| Tags in the last 30 days | 47 | |

The repository also has:
- no importer from another platform;
- no screenshots in the README;
- no CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY or CODE_OF_CONDUCT file.

**The rivals are closing in on our differentiators.**
- Coolify 4.5.1 to 4.7.0 (2026-10-20 to 11-09) shipped workspace-enforced 2FA, compose build skip, per-resource RBAC for members and tokens, update channels (stable, preview, nightly), and image scanning with API and MCP tools.
- Dokploy 0.31.0 shipped moving services between servers and audit-log export.
- GAP_ROADMAP's G5 heading, "None of the Docker-based rivals has these", is no longer true as a group claim.

**Structural debt now causes silent data loss in ordinary operations.**
- About 25 per-entity `settings` key prefixes hold feature state.
- They are untyped.
- They are orphaned when their entity is deleted.
- They are dropped on export, import and clone (§3).

**The capability story is inconsistent.**
- The server has 45 distinct `*_unsupported`, `*_unavailable` or `*_refused` codes.
- Several docs contradict each other or the code (§2).

**Security is a selling point we don't use.**

| Platform | Event in 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Coolify | 61 GitHub advisories, 16 critical | Counted on 2026-11-09 |
| Dokploy | 56 GitHub advisories, 33 critical | Counted on 2026-11-09 |
| Dokploy | A fresh instance was taken over through its open setup page | [#5156](https://github.com/Dokploy/dokploy/issues/5156) |
| Railway | Breach disclosed on 10-21 | [changelog](https://railway.com/changelog/2026-10-23-october-21-security-incident.md) |
| Northflank | Breach disclosed on 10-30 | [BleepingComputer](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/northflank-security-breach-leads-to-abuse-of-customers-ai-api-keys) |

NineDeploy already has:
- argv-only command execution;
- a setup token on first boot;
- signed releases;
- real restore verification.

These are told nowhere a buyer would look.

**Hence the order of this plan:**
1. Truth: one contract for what works where.
2. Structural debt.
3. Adoption.
4. Parity across runtimes.
5. Reliability and data.
6. New modules, last.

Priority: **P0** means fix now, because it is wrong or loses data today. **P1** is the next releases. **P2** comes after P1. **P3** is a strategic choice for the owner.

Size: **S** means at most a patch. **M** is one or two patches. **L** is a multi-patch package. **XL** is architectural.

Status: ⬜ not started · 🟨 in progress · ✅ done (with the release that shipped it)

Usage and cost reporting exists (`usageReport.ts:49`). | Owner decision on the target market first. If agencies: CPU/memory/service caps per workspace, then an export for billing. | P2 | M | ⬜ (approved 2026-11-09: agencies) |
| X8 | **The plugin marketplace.** | All 16 catalogue entries are `implemented: false` placeholders (`pluginLoader.ts:563-575`). | Hide placeholders from the UI now (S). A real third-party registry is a later decision. | P1 / P3 | S / L | ✅ narrowed (2026-11-09): the page already labelled placeholders honestly. PITR, Sentry ingest and Tailscale entries now point to the built-ins; the rest say "Not available" instead of "Planned" |

**Not planned:**
- a Kubernetes runtime (a different market: Kubero, Canine, Tsuru);
- Caddy;
- our own analytics, replay or RUM suite (link to Umami, PostHog or GlitchTip instead, REPORT G07);
- integrated mail.

---

## 8. Order of work

Each phase ships as patch releases. R2 continues independently in the other session.

| Phase | Items | Exit evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **1: Truth and debt** | C2, S1, S2, S3, S4, O4, X8 (hide), S8, A7 | Docs agree with code. No orphaned rows after a delete, proven by a test that deletes every entity kind. Export, import and clone round-trip every declared feature. Panel allow-list proven, including its exemptions. |
| **2: Contract and first impressions** | C1, C3, A5, A2, A6, S7 | Capability API drives the UI. The support matrix is generated. Time to HTTPS on a clean host is measured. Stable channel exists. Browser journeys run in CI. |
| **3: Switching and parity** | A1 (step 1, then 2), A3, A4, P1, P2 (maintenance, forward auth) | Import plans for one fixture each from Coolify, Dokploy and CapRover. The simpler UI passes the same journeys. Worker-task diagnostics proven on two daemons. |
| **4: Data** | O1, O2a, O2b, P3, A1 step 3 | Recovery from losing the host to a chosen point. A major upgrade with verified rollback. Preview copies for MySQL and Mongo. |
| **5: Expansion** | X1, X2, X3, X4, O3, O5, P4, S5, S6 | Each item's own acceptance. |
| **Owner tracks** | A8 (with phase 2), X6 and X7 (after phase 3), A9 and O6 (deferred) | See §9. |

## 9. Owner decisions (2026-11-09)

1. **Release channels (A6): approved; details left to us.**
   - Two channels. **current** is today's patch stream and stays the default, so upgrades behave as before. **stable** is opt-in.
   - Stable moves to the newest release that is at least **7 days** old and has no later release that fixes a regression it introduced.
   - Sooner when a release fixes a security issue: stable takes that fix, and the security bullet in the release notes says so.
   - The self-updater and `install.sh --channel stable` follow the chosen channel.
2. **Public launch (A7): approved.**
   - It happens once phase 2's exit evidence exists: screenshots, a measured first-run flow and a generated support matrix.
   - The community files ship in phase 1 regardless.
3. **Template slugs (A8): approved.** Rename `coolify-*` with redirects and credit upstream.
4. **Signing (A9): over time.**
   - No certificates yet.
   - The desktop app stays out of the README headline until signed builds exist.
5. **Swarm's scope (P5): left to us; decided as a stateless deployer.**
   - Stateful workloads belong on Docker nodes, where volumes, managed databases, backups, PITR and tunnels already work.
   - A shared-storage contract would be an XL project with new data-loss modes. The current refusals are safe.
   - C1 states the limit, and the UI offers "run on a node" when a stateful option is refused on Swarm.
   - Revisit only if users ask for it.
6. **Target market (X6, X7): both agencies and AI-agent workflows.**
   - X6 (agent sandboxes) and X7 (workspace quotas and a billing export) move from P3 to **P2**.
   - Both still come after phases 1–3.
7. **Sustainability: sponsorship only.**
   - Add `.github/FUNDING.yml` for GitHub Sponsors in A7.
   - No paid tier, no paid support and no hosted control plane.
8. **Cloud accounts (O6): later.** Arranged when the item comes up.

## 10. Claims to retire or qualify

- "Only we have MCP": Coolify and Easypanel have MCP.
- "No Docker rival scans images": Coolify 4.7.0 does.
- "None of the Docker-based rivals has these" (the GAP_ROADMAP G5 heading).
- "GitOps manages the whole instance": the schema is narrower (X3).
- "Swarm support" stated as multi-node parity (P1, P5).
- "Error ingest replaces Sentry": there are no source maps or traces yet (X1).
- Any "fastest", "most secure" or "largest catalogue" claim without a measurement.

docs.description: Dated project evidence or work in progress. This is not a promise of released runtime support.
docs.markdown:
# Persistent TCP/UDP ingress and MonoSIP migration

Status: kernel rule foundation merged in PR #30. Publication authority acceptance
is in progress. No production deploy mode is enabled.

## Confirmed trigger

Normal Docker deploys publish direct host ports on the application container. The
Docker builder stops the previous runtime to free those ports before starting the
candidate. Traefik can still reference the previous runtime during this interval.
Readiness runs after candidate startup; it cannot keep an already stopped runtime
serving. Source inspection does not prove a particular production failure started
during image pull. Capture timestamps and immutable runtime IDs before attributing
the observed first 502 to a specific phase.

The reported bindings are explicit IPv4 `10.6.6.9`, TCP/UDP 5060, UDP 3478 and UDP
10000–10100. A container port base of 10000 already represents 10000–10100 in the
Docker formatter. The editor now displays the full range without changing the API.

## Network contract

Application containers must not own stable host ports in this mode. A separate
port keeper reserves them; a kernel DNAT publication selects the application
target. DNAT must preserve the original client IP and source port. A generic
userspace proxy that substitutes its own source tuple cannot silently replace
this path: SIP address handling and STUN XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS depend on that tuple.

The first implementation supports explicit unicast IPv4 bindings only. Wildcard
addresses, IPv6, allow lists and unsupported firewall backends must fail preflight
without stopping a serving runtime. Existing direct-publish behavior remains the
default until migration and recovery are certified.

Only the service's owned nft table may be replaced. Publication uses one atomic
transaction at NAT priority -101, ahead of Docker's destination NAT. Existing
conntrack bindings continue using their original backend. Forwarding grants must
require the owned connmark, original destination tuple and retained backend
address. They must execute after DOCKER-USER so operator drops retain precedence.
Never flush a global ruleset or change Docker's default forwarding policy.

Conntrack preservation is not SIP dialog migration. Repeated registration packets
can keep an old UDP flow alive; active calls and ARI applications have their own
state. Retirement requires an explicit transport/application drain policy. A
timeout must report an unresolved drain rather than claim lossless retirement.

## Publication authority and runtime integration still required

`PersistentPortPublisher` now records intent before either routing plane changes,
retains both targets after an uncertain acknowledgement, and can resume from a
durable journal. It compares the actual nft table, chains and rule expressions
against the expected publication: a matching comment alone is insufficient.
Retirement requires a confirmed generation, no pending intent and a completed
drain observation followed by another kernel readback. Retention is bounded to
three targets; further deploys must wait instead of forcibly stopping active flows.
The journal also records retirement intent before issuing an immutable
runtime stop. A lost stop acknowledgement blocks later publication/reuse until
that retirement is reconciled. The runtime reference is removed only after stop
and forwarding-grant cleanup acknowledge completion.

The version 3 journal records the observed source publication of each pending
intent. An unresolved handoff can roll back only to the last confirmed immutable
target, after that target passes readiness again. The rollback receives a new
revision; it never replays an old revision. This allows recovery when the pending
candidate has become unhealthy, including a lost acknowledgement after kernel
commit. Unknown kernel state and an unhealthy fallback refuse mutation. The
candidate remains retained while its existing flows drain; rollback does not
authorize immediately stopping it. An unresolved first deploy has no invented
fallback target and remains held for recovery.

The hosted acceptance adapter runs compiled worker modules inside the target
Docker host network namespace. The worker holds its own OS authority and durable
journal scope, and executes nft/iptables mutations locally through inherited
descriptor 3. A bounded confirmation challenge binds a fresh token, service,
owner, revision, immutable target and publication fingerprint. The existing
fixture coordinator writes Traefik configuration, observes the loaded target,
and only then acknowledges that exact challenge. EOF, stale/mismatched ACK,
timeout and cancellation leave unresolved intent rather than authorizing cleanup.

The native process-death check kills that worker while its local nft child
survives. A competing worker must remain fenced until the child commits the
actual table and finishes. In the unfenced control the competitor completes
before that same child commits. Both cases retain the pending durable intent.
The native fixture also checks held TCP/UDP flows, source tuples, disk recovery,
uncertain acknowledgements, rollback and refusal to retire active targets.

This worker engine and its hosted IPC fixture are not a production deployment
mode. Owned helper/keeper image provisioning, full lifecycle integration, trusted
routing-controller adoption, host reboot restoration and shared-state policy
remain required. Never substitute a Docker API exec child for a local kernel
mutator that inherits the target worker's locked descriptor.

`withPersistentPortHostAuthority` provides the Linux worker lock primitive. It
locks an owned private state directory's regular lock file through `flock`, keeps
the open file description in the worker and passes it to each mutator as file
descriptor 3. It closes its reference without explicitly unlocking a surviving
child's reference. Unsupported platforms, writable state directories, hard-linked
lock files, invalid deadlines and escaped command contexts are refused.

`withPersistentPortJournalStore` scopes one service journal to that same host
lock. It snapshots the service claim before waiting, refuses foreign or unsafe
existing entries, bounds decoded state, and commits through a private exclusive
nonce file, file fsync, atomic rename and directory fsync. Reads and writes cannot
escape the authority scope or follow a replaced state directory. FIFO entries
are opened nonblocking and rejected by type. Uncertain failures preserve the
installed intent and never authorize runtime deletion; private orphan files are
left for separately owned recovery when cleanup cannot be proved safe.

The Linux filesystem acceptance exercises process death before and after rename,
lost durable acknowledgement, reload under fresh authority, sync ordering,
malformed/oversized state and alias/ownership guards. Process-death tests do not
simulate storage-device power loss. This store is not yet wired to the production
publisher, managed host namespace or service cleanup paths.

The native process-death acceptance kills the worker while a child is still
running. In the fenced case the competitor enters only after the child finishes;
in the unfenced control it enters before the child finishes. This validates lock
lifetime, not the complete production worker: production target-host provisioning,
trusted helper image, managed state-volume ownership and pipeline callbacks still
need wiring. Every kernel mutator must use the inherited-descriptor command path.

1. Persist binding ownership, service generation, immutable Docker IDs, backend
   addresses, keeper identity, firewall capability and publication revision.
   Serialize per-service operations and reject stale revisions. Reconcile kernel
   state after panel/agent restart before permitting cleanup.
2. Validate explicit addresses, port conflicts, Docker firewall topology and
   source-preserving return routing before any serving-state mutation. Refuse
   unsupported nodes before build/deploy consumes a stop-first fallback.
3. Prepare a candidate without published ports, retaining the old application.
   Shared persistent state must explicitly permit concurrent application access.
   Readiness evidence must belong to this candidate ID and deployment generation.
4. Install narrow forwarding grants for old and candidate targets. Publish the
   new DNAT revision only after readiness, then publish and acknowledge Traefik's
   web route. A partial/uncertain acknowledgement retains both runtimes and both
   forwarding grants while authority reconciles or rolls back.
5. Stop the old target only after both routing planes confirm the desired
   generation and its retained flows/application state have drained. Cleanup must
   reject any runtime still referenced by an active or unresolved publication.
6. Adopt existing direct mappings through a separately journaled migration. Port
   ownership cannot be assumed merely because a short preflight bind succeeded.
   Recovery must distinguish the old direct publication, an installed DNAT table
   and a committed keeper before deleting anything.

## MonoSIP v1.8.0: embedded database blocks naive overlap

The operator confirmed the default PostgreSQL in `/data`, not an external
`DATABASE_URL`. The official v1.8.0 installer places this cluster under
`/data/postgres`. Never start two PostgreSQL instances on that directory. Never
delete `postmaster.pid`, wipe the cluster, enable reset-on-failure, or copy live
PGDATA as a database backup.

The same image also embeds Asterisk and stores persistent generated configuration,
recordings and encryption/session secrets. Moving only PostgreSQL does not prove
that two all-in-one replicas can safely serve calls. The v1.8.0 API registers fixed
ARI application names (`monosip-inbound`, `monosip-flow`, `monosip-outbound`), so
control-plane overlap needs explicit application-level verification as well.

Before a live change:

1. Inventory the immutable image, actual volume/mount identity, database major,
   extensions, roles, database name, app migration state, Asterisk configuration,
   recordings and the existence of `/data/.monosip-secrets`. Keep secret values
   out of logs and reports. Confirm the original container still serves.
2. Take an online logical backup using the embedded PostgreSQL tools and an
   encrypted/permission-restricted backup of non-database state. Restore into an
   owned disposable PostgreSQL 17 instance. Check restoration, schema, constraints,
   row counts and application health using copies. A backup without a restore
   rehearsal is not a migration gate.
3. Rehearse a topology with independent PostgreSQL and a separately owned PBX,
   preserving secrets and recording/configuration paths. Verify application
   migrations and ARI ownership before enabling any overlapping web candidates.
   Do not attach a rehearsal candidate to production trunks or send real calls.
4. Plan the final write boundary: an online dump alone misses subsequent writes.
   Use a bounded maintenance cutover with a final consistent export/restore unless
   a separately verified replication path exists. Keep the original data and image
   intact. State clearly that this initial migration has a maintenance window.
5. Verify admin login, encrypted SIP secret access, extensions, trunk registration,
   inbound/outbound calls, WSS, RTP in both directions, STUN and recordings. Inspect
   an actual normal redeploy through public HTTP and SIP clients. Roll back before
   allowing incompatible writes if a gate fails; a new database with newer writes
   cannot be discarded by blindly starting the old database.

These are pending operational gates. No live data has been read, migrated or
modified by the kernel acceptance.

## Acceptance and evidence boundaries

`scripts/smoke-persistent-port-ingress.mjs` refuses to run outside a GitHub-hosted
runner and creates an owned privileged Docker-in-Docker daemon. Its inner networks,
firewall rules, test IP, applications and port keeper are disposable. Cleanup
removes that daemon and its anonymous volumes; it does not enumerate/delete user
containers.

The acceptance checks TCP/UDP on 5060, first/middle/last RTP ports, STUN binding
responses, client source preservation, readiness-held target publication, retained
old flows, new-flow handoff, rollback and web traffic through actual Traefik.
SIP/RTP packet round trips use synthetic endpoints, not a real PBX call test.
Passing this lab proves the network primitive only. It does not certify database
migration, SIP dialog HA, durable ownership, restart recovery or production pipeline
integration. Those remain explicit gates above.

Primary references:

- [MonoSIP v1.8.0 installation](https://github.com/MonoSIP/MonoSIP/blob/v1.8.0/docs/INSTALL.md)
- [MonoSIP v1.8.0 ARI client](https://github.com/MonoSIP/MonoSIP/blob/v1.8.0/apps/api/src/asterisk/ari.ts)
- [nftables stateful NAT](https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Performing_Network_Address_Translation_(NAT))
- [PostgreSQL server startup and data-directory ownership](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/server-start.html)
- [util-linux flock descriptor and child-lifetime semantics](https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/blob/master/sys-utils/flock.1.adoc)
